slides.alt: 1912 photograph of the Whitney Laboratory of Seismology: a timber-beamed room with concrete piers carrying tall pendulum seismographs and their drums, with windows along one wall. It is the Whitney Vault named in the sentence; Wood is not pictured.
slides.credit: Photo: T. A. Jaggar, 1912, USGS, PD

slides.alt: Photograph from HVO's 1912 logbook, dated February 4, 1912 and initialed by Jaggar: the wooden Technology Station on Kīlauea's rim behind a picket fence, with a man standing in the doorway. It shows the first small building the observatory work grew from; the man is not named.

Photograph from HVO's 1912 logbook, dated February 16, 1912 and initialed by Jaggar: a plain wooden building frame under construction on open ground, with workers beside it. It shows the first permanent observatory building going up, the construction the card's funding row refers to.

two cylinders wrapped in paper seismograms, one covered in short spikes from an earthquake swarm and one with the dense bands of harmonic tremor, mounted on the wall of the Jaggar Museum at the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory. It shows what the paper era produced, ink traces on paper drums, not Wood’s arrival or the half million items themselves.

Photograph from June 6, 2024 of an HVO field engineer burying the cable for a new seismometer at a Kīlauea Southwest Rift Zone station that already carries GPS and high-resolution gas equipment, with solar panels and a radio dish beyond. It shows the three signal families the sentence names, earthquakes, deformation and gases, at one modern site; it does not show the early observers' instruments.
slides.credit: Photo: M. Warren, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: Photograph from June 2018 of a temporary GPS station on the floor of Kīlauea's caldera: a yellow tripod carrying a GPS antenna, with a solar panel and radio telemetry, steaming crater wall behind. It shows the GPS tool in the sentence's list of later deformation systems, used to track the summit subsidence; it does not show Jaggar-era surveying.
slides.credit: Source: USGS Volcano Hazards Program, PD

slides.alt: Photograph of an HVO geochemist at the rim of Halemaʻumaʻu photographing an FTIR spectrometer on a tripod pointed into the gas-filled crater; the page dates the image to July 2016. It shows gas being measured at Kīlauea, the window the sentence adds. The geochemist is not named.
slides.credit: Source: USGS Volcano Hazards Program, PD

slides.alt: a silhouetted HVO scientist and three instruments on tripods at the rim of Halemaʻumaʻu against glowing gas and steam during the summit eruption on September 29, 2021. It shows several kinds of observation made side by side; it is not a picture of the hypothetical in the sentence.
slides.credit: Photo: D. Downs, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: Photograph of a smoked-drum seismic recorder in a museum case: a black, soot-coated cylinder on its axle beside a wooden instrument box. It is the kind of drum the sentence describes; the case is part of a National Park Service exhibit, cropped here from the original exhibit photo.
slides.credit: Photo: Ed Shiinoki, NPS, Public domain

slides.alt: Close photograph of a paper seismogram at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park showing the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake as a dense band of pen traces, with handwritten notes "Japan Earthquake" and a local 4.6 event. It shows paper seismograms still in use at the park's HVO displays in 2011, two years before HVO ended paper seismograms. The photographer's caption does not name the recorder type.

USGS photograph from summer 2017 of the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's archive: aisles of steel shelving packed with labeled cardboard boxes of paper seismograms, with handwritten labels such as "Smoke Records." It is the physical paper archive behind the sentence.

slides.alt: Photograph taken July 24, 2018: a deep crack runs across the ash-coated Jaggar Museum overlook deck on Uēkahuna Bluff beside an interpretive sign, with the enlarged Halemaʻumaʻu crater behind it. It shows summit-collapse damage to a building-side structure next to the observatory; it does not show monitoring equipment.
slides.credit: Photo: Jon Christensen, NPS, Public domain

slides.alt: Photograph taken July 8, 2021 of the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory building on Uēkahuna Bluff behind a fence and an AREA CLOSED sign, closed because of structural damage from the 2018 eruption. It shows the building the sentence is about, as it stood after the evacuation.
slides.credit: Photo: Larry D. Moore, CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: two HVO scientists inspect a seismic station with a solar panel in forest on Mauna Loa in April 2019. It shows one field site of the distributed network; it does not show what the observatory does not know. Resized once to 4600 px wide from the 5184 px original.

Two HVO field technicians in orange work on a volcanic gas monitoring station on a slope of dark tephra at Kīlauea summit, one lying on a cardboard sheet to reach the cracked solar panel while the other works behind it. It shows a station of the network being dug out and repaired, the kind of change that makes any instrument count depend on its date.
slides.credit: Photo: L. DeSmither, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: an HVO scientist in a helmet aims a laser rangefinder across Halemaʻumaʻu at the lava lake on December 28, 2020, to turn the lake surface into a measured distance and depth. It shows one change at the volcano being turned into data; it is not the whole of the sentence.
slides.credit: Photo: M. Patrick, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: an HVO geologist in an orange helmet and high-visibility vest documents a lava fountain in Halemaʻumaʻu with a camera on a tripod from the caldera rim on May 5, 2026. It shows one change at the volcano being documented, in the spirit of the carousel’s close; it is not the limitations or the evidence the frame points readers to.

onScreen: The Observatory That Turned a Volcano into a Century-Long Signal A volcano does not announce an eruption in a language made for humans.
No single change means the same thing every time.
The technology of volcano monitoring is therefore not one heroic sensor. It is a system for making fallible observations comparable across time, and for deciding when a pattern justifies action.
On Kīlauea’s rim in 1912, the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory began continuous, systematic study of Hawaiian volcanic and earthquake activity. Jaggar is conventionally identified as its founder.

“A century of data” can sound like possession of the volcano’s whole history. It is a century-scale body of data made by particular institutions, instruments, categories, and decisions about what to measure.
Jaggar reached Hilo on January 17, 1912, traveled to Volcano House, and began surveying the lava lake that afternoon. But an observatory could not survive as one scientist looking into a crater.
Demosthenes Lycurgus, who operated Volcano House, led local fundraising. Hilo businesses contributed $1,785 toward construction.

Carnegie Laboratory director Arthur Day and E.S. Shepherd came to collect volcanic gases and remeasure temperatures. Dodge joined them in descending into Halemaʻumaʻu to obtain samples before the gases mixed with air.
Seismologist H.O. Wood arrived with Jaggar in June and put the mechanical instruments into operation in the Whitney Vault.

A monitoring institution emerged through collaboration among local supporters, field workers, assistants, outside laboratories, publication networks, and instruments, not through a lone moment of invention.

widening of the pit.

posts.title: Anatomy class, but the microbes are made of clay
posts.summary: A former dentist turned designer rebuilt the anatomy lesson as four hands-on exercises and tested them at Dutch Design Week 2026. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, walked through them with him.* *This piece follows the lessons back to the old anatomy theaters, the textbooks they answer and the research on whether hands-on teaching works.

slides.alt: Small clay models of microbes in pink, green, purple and orange on a lit table, with a tablet aimed at them. Slide text: Anatomy class, but the microbes are made of clay.

A pavement A-board with a lilac Queer Anatomy Theater poster showing a pale round shape. It marks the venue at Plug in City. Slide text: Queer Anatomy Theater by Kuang-Yi Ku, shown at Plug in City during Dutch Design Week 2026.

Kuang-Yi Ku, in glasses and a black and red jacket, explains the project at the entrance, with visitors behind. It goes with how the work turns anatomy into lessons you take part in. Slide text: It turns anatomy lessons into exercises you take part in, after the old anatomical theaters.

The lit Queer Anatomy Theater lightbox with a tablet in front of it showing the same box in AR, and small clay microbes in pink, green and orange on the table. Slide text: Lesson Four uses clay and AR to show sexuality, microorganisms and other species.

A hand points at a tablet held up to a lit table of small clay microbes in pink, green and purple; on the screen an AR layer draws lines over a clay figure. Slide text: In the maker's words, microbes are living within our body.

Kuang-Yi Ku, in glasses and a red and black jacket, sits beside his lit Queer Anatomy Theater box, with a tablet and small clay microbes on the table and a screen behind. Slide text: I am an anatomist, so I was extremely intrigued by this work. It asks who else lives in the body.

Kuang-Yi Ku in a seated interview against a dark purple curtain. It goes with his path from dentistry to design. Slide text: Kuang-Yi Ku practiced dentistry from 2009 to 2015, then studied Social Design at Design Academy Eindhoven.

posts.title: The source-file question
posts.summary: A special effects company, a sculptor and a software contractor each handed over finished work without settling who owned it. The courts that sorted it out show why the finished file, the working files and the right to reuse them are separate things.

slides.alt: Two computer monitors running Adobe Premiere Pro, a video editor: the project panel and timeline of an open edit on the left screen, the program monitor on the right. This is the kind of project file that sits behind a finished video.

onScreen: Imagine a brand paying $2,000 for one video
and still never receiving the project file behind it.
The brand may receive a finished MP4, PDF or PNG that looks completely done.
The editable project file is a different thing:
it carries the footage, layers, fonts and access that a finished export does not.
Linked footage, fonts, links and license files can sit outside the final export,
unseen until someone asks for them.
Before delivery, ask exactly what the next person can open, change and reuse.
Deliver the finished video, and define what stays editable.

posts.title: The Year Hawaii Rewrote the 329 Card
posts.summary: Acts 46, 241 and 269 of 2025 changed who can certify a patient, how, what it can cost, who can grow for a patient and who can sell hemp. Here is what the printed texts say, what the 2026 numbers show, and what they leave open.

onScreen: The year Hawaii rewrote the 329 card Acts 46, 241 and 269 of 2025: certification, telehealth, fees, caregivers and hemp sellers.
Three laws in 2025 Act 46 was approved May 14. Act 241 followed on June 27, and Act 269 on July 2.
A new way to qualify A primary treating medical provider can certify a condition not on the debilitating list. A hospice provider can certify hospice care.
Who counts as a primary treating provider A Hawaii physician or APRN, licensed in the state, primarily responsible for your treatment and ongoing care.
Telehealth is allowed No initial in-person visit is required. The provider must be in Hawaii and meet the same standard of care. OMCCR's guidance starts September 18, 2025.
A cap on certification fees No more than three times the Department's registration fee. OMCCR's fee page caps it at $105 for one year and $315 for three.
The Department can inspect files It may inspect the files behind a certification, and suspend or revoke a provider who refuses.
Caregivers can grow again Act 46 restored caregiver cultivation, retroactive to January 1, 2025. Fines can reach $5,000 per violation, and each day counts separately.
Five patients A caregiver may serve up to five patients. Each growing location may be used for not more than five patients.
A cultivator license starts in 2028 From January 1, 2028, Act 241 Part IV makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a Department license.
Hemp sellers must register Since January 1, 2026, hemp product retailers and distributors need a certificate: $50, valid five years. Topicals and tinctures are exempt.
What we know and what we do not
Education, not legal advice OMCCR's own guidance sheets say they do not replace legal advice, and neither does this. For your situation, ask a Hawaiʻi attorney.

posts.title: What a colon actually looks like, versus the art
posts.summary: Atelier Van Lieshout parked a gut-shaped clinic on a square in Eindhoven for Dutch Design Week 2026 and called it speculation. Here is the artwork, the real anatomy it borrows, and what the medical literature and the law say about cleaning out a colon.

slides.alt: A close pass of a pale green walk-in sculpture shaped like an intestine, with a porthole window and sculpted veins, on a city square. It is the art the carousel compares with real colon anatomy. Slide text: What a colon looks like, versus the art.

A wide view of Ketelhuisplein in Eindhoven with a long pale green intestine sculpture lying across the square between towers. It introduces Colonic Cleansing Clinic by Atelier Van Lieshout. Slide text: Colonic Cleansing Clinic, a walk-in sculpture of the human gut by Atelier Van Lieshout.

The tail end of a pale green walk-in gut sculpture on a city square, marked with a red cross and the words Colonic Cleansing Clinic, with sculpted tubes trailing onto the paving. Slide text: It belongs to Sanitas Futurum, the studio's project on the future of health and care.

Code-drawn diagram: the small intestine (about 3.05 m) and the large intestine (about half the length of the small intestine) drawn as straight tubes on one meter scale. It gives the length behind the walk-in colon sculpture. Slide text: Your large intestine is about half as long as your small intestine.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from OpenStax data

slides.alt: The pale green gut sculpture with its large oval window, a domed porthole and an open side door, where a visitor with a backpack steps through; a tour member in a magenta coat stands in the foreground. Slide text: The sculpture has one opening you can walk through. The real large intestine ends at the anal canal.

The presenter in a green jacket stands beside the sculpture's red cross and the lettering Colonic Cleansing Clinic. It goes with the studio framing the work as speculation, not medical advice. Slide text: The studio frames it as speculation, not medical advice. Thank you to Atelier Van Lieshout's presenter for explaining it.

posts.summary: A refund link hidden on purpose. An exit named after an epic about a war. A tax form that takes most of a working day. The public papers behind each one show who built the experience, who was warned, and what the law already asks of them.

posts.title: Threat, trap, network: the Hornet Trap
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, a design team showed a hornet trap with a camera and a decision rule. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, saw the demo. Here is the invasive hornet it targets, why ordinary traps do more harm than good, and what the research says about finding nests.

slides.alt: A gray teardrop-shaped nest form with a scalloped surface hangs from a cut branch inside a glass case, in a concrete hall with plants. Slide text: Kill, release or tag.

A presenter in a black hoodie, holding a small microphone, explains the trap to press tour members wearing receiver headphones in the exhibition hall. Slide text: Accenture Industrial Design showed a smart trap for the yellow-legged hornet at Dutch Design Week 2026.

A broken, papery hornet nest in a glass case, its brown outer layers torn open to show rows of comb cells. Slide text: One mature nest can raise up to about 13,000 hornets over a season. Most are not out at once.

Prototype trap parts on a white light table: hand-drawn sketches, printed plastic housings, cone-shaped funnels, a mesh piece and circuit boards in rows. Slide text: The aim is to catch the invasive hornet and spare native insects.

A clipped line from the study's results: Overall, 213 individuals of V. velutina have been trapped in the two sampling seasons (104 in spring and 109 in autumn), accounting for 1.02% of the total trapped insects. Slide text: Why that matters: in standard traps the target hornet was about 1 percent of the catch.
slides.credit: Source: Lioy et al. 2020 (PMC), CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A hand holds a phone over a dark demo table with token slots, while others look on; the table's screens are blurred. Slide text: In the demo, the trap's camera sorts what it sees: bees go free, spring queens are killed, summer workers get tagged.

Four photos from a 2018 study: a yellow-legged hornet held on a plate while a tiny radio tag is fitted, the tagged hornet from the side, a hornet hovering at a beehive, and a nest in a birch tree. Slide text: Tagged hornets have led researchers to hidden nests up to 1.33 km away.

posts.title: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide
posts.summary: Heʻeia Fishpond is enclosed by a stone wall about 1.3 miles long, and its gates admit water and small fish while keeping grown fish home. Floods, mangrove, a fish die-off and a stream diversion broke that system. The studies and reports on its rebuilding show what the gates do, and what they still lack.

slides.alt: Looking across the shore toward Heʻeia Fishpond in Kāneʻohe Bay: the long, low line of the pond wall and its tree-covered stretches sit on calm water, with the green Koʻolau ridges rising behind in low light. It opens the story on the place itself, the pond named in the first sentence.

A published map from a 2019 study: the island of Oʻahu, then a satellite view of the Heʻeia land division outlined in yellow, with Heʻeia Stream drawn in blue from the Koʻolau ridge through the Hoi wetland to the pond, shaded red, at the edge of Kāneʻohe Bay. It shows where the fresh water comes from that mixes with the tide inside the pond.

Photos from a 2019 study of two gates at Heʻeia Fishpond, labeled Nui and Kahoʻokele: water rushes through a stone channel under a wooden frame, and a row of upright slats crosses a channel with calm water and mountains behind. These are mākāhā, the gates the slide names.

A grid of 24 blue scatter plots from a 2019 study, one row for each of six gates at Heʻeia Fishpond and one column each for spring flood, spring ebb, neap flood and neap ebb tides. Each plot shows how much water passed through that gate as the water level changed, logged every 20 seconds. It shows water moving through the openings; fish are not measured in this figure.

From a hillside of green shrubs at Heʻeia State Park, the long straight wall of Heʻeia Fishpond runs across calm blue water toward the Koʻolau mountains, January 2019. It shows the wall the slide says no source credits to one designer.

The middle section of the Heʻeia Fishpond wall in April 2010: a low wall of stacked blocks runs out across calm water, and on the near end white plastic buckets, boulders and broken coral are piled, ready to be moved. It shows material gathered by people for the wall.
slides.credit: Photo: Kanu Hawaii, CC BY 2.0, cropped

slides.alt: A dense band of dark green red mangrove at Heʻeia Park in July 2004 lines the edge of still water, with the Koʻolau and the raised H-3 freeway behind. Red mangrove is the invasive tree that keepers at Heʻeia have had to clear from the pond's edge for years.
slides.credit: Photo: Forest and Kim Starr, CC BY 3.0

slides.alt: A dense band of dark green red mangrove at Heʻeia Park in July 2004 lines the edge of still water. Clearing this invasive tree is part of the ongoing upkeep the slide describes.
slides.credit: Photo: Forest and Kim Starr, CC BY 3.0

slides.alt: An outline map of Heʻeia Fishpond from a 2019 study, for a spring flood tide in 2018. Blue arrows at each gate are sized by that gate's share of the incoming water: 51 percent and 28 percent at two seaward gates, 13 percent at a third, and 2 percent or less at the others. It shows the exchange concentrated through a few mākāhā.

Heʻeia Fishpond seen from Heʻeia State Park in October 2011: the pond wall curves out into the water with the town of Kāneʻohe and the Koʻolau mountains behind, and overhead wires cross the frame. It shows the enclosed water the sentence says stays brackish.

A photo from a 2019 study of the broken seaward wall of Heʻeia Fishpond: a low, ragged line of blocks crosses open water under a grey sky. A 1965 flood opened this gap, and it stayed open until 2015. It shows the storm damage and the physical work of keeping a coastal wall.

An aerial photo from a 2019 study of Heʻeia Fishpond: a long curving wall encloses a wide pond, with mangrove-covered shores and the Koʻolau mountains behind. It shows the pond the card's facts describe.
An aerial photo of Heʻeia Fishpond and its curving wall, from a 2019 study.

A line chart from a 2017 study of water temperature inside Heʻeia Fishpond and out in Kāneʻohe Bay from March to December 2009, with two shaded bands where fish died in the pond's net pens. It shows the kind of temperature research the slide says is under way.
A line chart of 2009 water temperatures in Heʻeia Fishpond and Kāneʻohe Bay, from a 2017 study.

A published map from a 2019 study of Heʻeia Fishpond's wall, marked with the years each stretch was cleared of mangrove and rebuilt, from 2005 to 2018, and the names of the gates. It shows practitioners restoring the pond, section by section, year after year.

A photo from a 2019 study of the rebuilt seaward wall of Heʻeia Fishpond: a stone-walled channel with upright wooden slats sits under a plank walkway, the new gate Kahoʻokele, with calm water and green hills behind. It shows the mākāhā the slide names.

onScreen: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide The kuapā curves through Kāneʻohe Bay, built from stone and coral without becoming an impermeable barrier.
Inside, those flows make a brackish environment where limu and other food for fish can grow.
A mākāhā is often translated as a sluice gate.
The openings permit water and small fish to move. Juvenile fish can enter.
No reliable source identifies one person who designed Heʻeia Fishpond. Its wall is therefore not only a structure.
It is evidence of coordination: people selecting and moving material, reading a difficult coastal environment, organizing labor, maintaining a shared food system, and transferring knowledge.
The labor did not end when the wall was completed. Its productive capacity depends on continuous mālama: clearing channels, repairing storm damage, maintaining gates, observing fish and water,
controlling predators or invasive species, coordinating harvests, and caring for relationships upstream and downstream. Loko iʻa are living systems.

The physical system at Heʻeia makes that labor legible. Paepae o Heʻeia describes a wall built in compact layers that slow water loss, preserve a base level at low tide, and concentrate more exchange through seven mākāhā.
Together they help maintain brackish conditions favorable to limu and fish.

Restoration practitioners face watersheds altered by development, sediment and nutrient changes, invasive species, unreliable recruitment of juvenile fish, warmer water, storms, regulation, funding constraints, and the sheer physical demand of maintaining a coastal structure.

posts.title: Paid work is not automatically work made for hire
posts.summary: In 1985 a sculptor delivered a statue to a Washington charity, and four years later the Supreme Court ruled that the charity was not its author under the work-made-for-hire rule. A decade before the statue, a five-person firm had given NASA its best-loved logo. One federal rule decides who owns work like this, and payment is only one small part of it.

onScreen: Your testimony is data How a Hawaii law differs from an agency rule, and how to testify.
Two doors change a rule A law goes through the Legislature. A rule goes through an agency. Each has its own public step.
A law starts as a bill Only a legislator can introduce a bill. It needs three readings in each chamber, on separate days, before the governor acts.
A rule starts with an agency Chapter 91 asks for 30 days' notice of a public hearing. The agency must fully consider every written and oral submission.
One fee, both doors Act 241 caps certifier fees at three times the Department's registration fee. The multiplier is law. The registration fee is set by rule.
The 2027 session: January 20 The Constitution sets 10:00 a.m. on the third Wednesday in January. No 2027 calendar was posted on November 15, 2026.
Testimony needs a hearing You can testify only on a bill with a scheduled hearing. Ask the committee chair to schedule it, and read the notice's instructions.

posts.title: The Lines That Changed the Land
posts.summary: Between 1846 and 1855, Hawaiʻi asked thousands of people to turn the land they lived on into written claims, testimony, surveys and awards. The laws, the award books and the surveyors' own accounts show how the lines were drawn, who drew them, and why courts still read them today.

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page of October 12, 1850: a pen-and-ink plat of a parcel with a creek along one edge, hachured hillside and neighboring-land names, the tail of a courses-and-distances description above it, a costs list and the commissioners' signatures below. It is an actual parcel made legible as a drawing, a description and a signed document, which is the sentence this story opens with.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.003_jp2.zip/1846.003_jp2%2F1846.003_0081.jp2 (vol 3, leaf 81 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission page signed by surveyor A. F. Turner in July 1850: a description of a Honolulu lot that starts at the corner of Nuuanu and King Streets and runs by bearings and chain lengths to the point of commencement, with a hand-drawn plat showing the Bethel Chapel and neighboring lots beside it. It shows a boundary put into words, measured and drawn on one page.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.004_jp2.zip/1846.004_jp2%2F1846.004_0039.jp2 (vol 4, leaf 39 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: The top of a handwritten Hawaiian-language page in the first Land Commission award book, under the names of three commissioners, J. Y. Kanehoa, John ʻĪʻī and Z. Kaauwai. It says the notice ran in the Polynesian newspaper on February 14, 1846, and it is headed as a notice to everyone holding a land right across the Hawaiian islands. It is the commission's call for written claims, the thing a claimant presented in place of the land.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.001_jp2.zip/1846.001_jp2%2F1846.001_0030.jp2 (vol 1, leaf 30 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page of October 27, 1852, headed with an award number (Helu 570B), with two ʻāpana described by bearings and distances and signed by surveyor S. P. Kalama, two hand-drawn plats of the parcels at the bottom, and the commissioners' signatures with the fee line at the top. It shows the pieces the card lists: an award number, a survey and a metes-and-bounds description on one document.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.008_jp2.zip/1846.008_jp2%2F1846.008_0390.jp2 (vol 8, leaf 390 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: a rusted metal target on a post set in a mortared lava-rock pier, a Hawaii Territorial Survey triangulation station called LUKE, with the Wailuku valley and clouded mountains behind it. It shows a physical mark left by Hawaiian land surveying; it is a later Territorial-era station, not a Māhele-era survey, a metes-and-bounds description or a patent.

Part of a handwritten Land Commission page for claim 539, Kukuihaa uka at Hōnaunau, Kona, Hawaiʻi: the line "The rights of Native tenants, if any, must be respected," then a boundary that starts at a rock marked with a cross on pāhoehoe lava, follows a small stone wall up to a pile of stones, and runs by bearings and chain lengths back to the start. It shows a boundary known through landmarks restated as courses and distances.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.003_jp2.zip/1846.003_jp2%2F1846.003_0040.jp2 (vol 3, leaf 40 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission page in Hawaiian with ruled lists of bearings and chain distances for three separate ʻāpana, the neighboring holding named at the end of each line, a handwritten column of sums in the right margin, and three hand-drawn plats with a chain scale below. It shows a description that was calculated, copied into the file and drawn.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.010_jp2.zip/1846.010_jp2%2F1846.010_0040.jp2 (vol 10, leaf 40 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission page from November 1853: a description of a Honolulu lot at Puaa by bearings and chain lengths signed by surveyor A. F. Turner, a hand-drawn plat with a scale of one chain to an inch, and below it the start of another award, number 7767, with a ruled fee table and the commissioners' signatures. It is the kind of award document descendants search, with its limits visible: one surveyor's lines on one date.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.010_jp2.zip/1846.010_jp2%2F1846.010_0294.jp2 (vol 10, leaf 294 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

slides.alt: Two surveyors, rodman Harry Kawamoto and topographer J. O. Kilmartin, standing at the Mauna Kea triangulation station on the cinder plateau of Hawaiʻi Island on October 25, 1925; the station was set by the Hawaiian Government Survey in 1892. It shows the field measurement behind the boundary lines the sentence asks readers to read first as measurements.
slides.credit: Photo: J. O. Kilmartin, USGS, 1925, PD

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page dated September 3, 1853: award number 4779 at Wailua, Koʻolau, Maui, a description by bearings and distances signed by surveyor A. F. Turner, a small plat of a long narrow parcel beside a stream, and the four commissioners' signatures over a paid fee. It is one of the instruments the sentence means: a signed document that holds the boundary without anyone going back to the land.
slides.url: https://archive.org/download/esrp260351545/1846.003_jp2.zip/1846.003_jp2%2F1846.003_0444.jp2 (vol 3, leaf 444 of the Land Commission awards item https://archive.org/details/esrp260351545)

onScreen: The Lines That Changed the Land Before land can be sold as a parcel, it must be made legible as one.

A boundary must be described in words, followed across the ground, measured, calculated, drawn, attached to a name or number, accepted by an institution, and preserved in a document another institution will recognize.
A claimant did not present land itself to the commission.
A boundary known through a stream, a wall, a planting area, a ridge, a neighboring holding, or the memory of people in a place could be restated as a sequence of courses and distances.
The description could be calculated, copied, mapped, indexed, compared, and carried into a later dispute.
The lines on a cadastral map therefore deserve to be read twice. First as measurements: carefully made descriptions that allowed a boundary to be found again.

Second as instruments: documents that could transfer, divide, mortgage, foreclose, and settle a claim without anyone returning to the ground the boundary describes. Educational information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Frets for the notes between the notes
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, in a garden at a former squat in Eindhoven, a design student showed RN Collins the first guitar they had ever built. Its frets sit where a standard guitar has none. This piece looks at what a fret does, why some music lives between the frets, and what a hand has to do on a neck like this.

Whose data counts? Trials for 10 widely used drugs (not cannabis studies) left Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander participation unreported for 6. Where reported, it was below population share.
Hawaiʻi’s own survey was opt-in The state’s 2022 patient survey reached about 10 percent of registered patients. Its report says the results do not represent all patients.
Door one: newcomers OMCCR says the National Cannabis Study is for residents beginning medical cannabis who are cannabis-naive. OMCCR adds that optional blood tests come with results.
Door two: already using OMCCR points current users to Realm of Caring’s registry. The page says it is for regular users, and also that no use is required.
Door three: a cancer study COSMIC follows adults newly diagnosed with certain cancers. The federal trial listing names 13 Hawaiʻi sites. OMCCR’s 2025 newsletter said 12.
Ask: who reviewed this study? Federal rules for human research require an institutional review board to review the research they cover. Ask which board approved the study you are considering.
Ask: who sees my name? A consent form must say how far the confidentiality of files identifying you will be kept, and whom to contact with questions about your rights.
Ask: who gets my data later? Consent forms must say whether your information, with identifiers removed, may be used for future research or shared with other investigators.
Ask: can I stop? The rule requires a statement that taking part is voluntary, refusing carries no penalty, and you may stop at any time without penalty.

A certificate can limit disclosure Federal law issues certificates of confidentiality to federally funded research that collects identifiable sensitive information. They limit disclosure to people outside the research, with exceptions.

posts.title: Who Made This So Hard?
posts.summary: When a person "fails to submit," someone else wrote the demand. In 2023, federal and state papers showed who, for millions of Medicaid renewals. This is what those papers say, and what the law already admits about deadlines.

slides.alt: A paragraph of a 2024 federal bulletin saying CMS found an issue in 29 states that wrongly ended coverage for over 400,000 children and families in multi-member households.

Bar chart. Coverage ended for 20.7 million people: 14.3 million for procedural reasons and 6.5 million found ineligible. Coverage renewed for 55.1 million: 37.6 million from data on file and 17.5 million from a returned form.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from MACPAC data

Two items from a printed regulation: (6) We gave you incorrect or incomplete information about when and how to request administrative review or to file a civil suit. (7) You did not receive notice of the determination or decision.
A Federal Register rule summary from the Social Security Administration, marked Final rule, revising past relevant work by reducing the relevant work period from 15 to 5 years.

The rule says renew from data the agency already has. Ask the person for a form only when that is not possible.
States must meet every federal renewal rule by December 31, 2026. CMS set that date in 2024.
Social Security's deadline rule admits the agency can be the cause. Wrong agency information, or a notice that never came, can be good cause.
A demand can shrink. In 2024, Social Security cut its work history question from 15 years to 5.
The new Medicaid work rule keeps the same order. States check the data first, then ask the person.

posts.title: Glass, mirror and a breathing rhythm
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Rive Roshan showed tall columns of glass and mirror with light that rose and fell like a breath. One of the makers said the team picked that pace themselves. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, filmed the stop. Here is the work, the building it stood in, and the muscles that a slow breath puts to work.

slides.alt: Light moving through a tall column of ribbed glass and mirror, glowing cyan and pink in a dark hall. It is Beacons of Hope, whose light rose and fell at a pace one of the makers said the team set by feel. Slide text: Paced by feel, not by sensors.

A tall glass-marquetry column of ribbed glass and mirror glowing cyan and pink, with visitors around it in a dark hall. It is one of the Beacons of Hope columns by Rive Roshan. Slide text: Beacons of Hope is a set of standing glass-marquetry columns by Rive Roshan.

A ribbed glass column lit pink and white in the foreground, with visitors and a second column further back. It goes with the light engineered by Studio Ravenhorst. Slide text: The light was engineered by Studio Ravenhorst.

Textbook figure of a person in side view breathing in: arrows show air entering, the diaphragm contracting and moving down, the external intercostal muscles between the ribs contracting, and the chest cavity expanding. Slide text: On an in-breath your diaphragm contracts and moves down. Muscles between your ribs help lift and widen the chest.

One of the makers of Beacons of Hope explains the piece to a small group beside a glass column lit pink and blue; a visitor with headphones listens. This is the moment the maker described how the rhythm was set. Slide text: One of the makers said the team set the rhythm by feel. A version driven by data was in the works.

posts.title: Who donates a brain, and who decides?
posts.summary: The law says a signed gift belongs to the person who signed it. The national brain bank network still asks the family to sign at the time of death. A medical examiner can keep a brain without asking anyone. This is the chain of consent behind a donated brain, read from the statute, the court opinions and the studies of the people who signed.

onScreen: Who donates a brain, and who decides? Illinois law says that once a donor signs, a person other than the donor "is barred from changing, amending, or revoking" the gift.
The brain banks still ask the family. The NIH brain bank network tells donors that "a consent form must be signed by the next of kin at the time of death."
A license sticker is not enough. The network's own answer: the sticker on a driver's license "does not give brain banks permission to receive a brain."
No signature? A ladder decides. Illinois lists 11 classes, from a health care agent and a spouse down to a close friend. No one lower may decide if someone higher can be reached.
Signed is not the same as done. At Rush in Chicago, most signers in two studies came to autopsy. Among African American signers, 53.4 percent did, as of 2012.
A coroner can keep the brain. In 2008 Ohio's top court held that families had no protected right in organs a coroner removed and kept for testing.
Sometimes it is one phone call. Asked by phone on the day of an autopsy, 69.7 percent of families said yes: 74.1 percent of White families and 57.0 percent of Black families.

posts.title: Everything moist seems alive
posts.summary: Shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, MU in Eindhoven filled a dark hall with mist, pipes and pools, and a choir turned it into a performance. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, was there with the press tour. Here is the room, the idea behind it, and what a body does with its own water.

slides.alt: A gray cylinder on a wooden plinth releasing a plume of mist in a dark exhibition hall. Slide text: Everything moist seems alive.

A dark wall with the printed title Maison the Faux, Everything Moist Seems Alive, and booklets below. It names the installation at MU. Slide text: An installation of mist and dripping water by MAISON the FAUX and Studio Boris Acket,. curated at MU by Angelique Spaninks.

The Waterbar at MU: a bartender behind rows of glasses lit by tea lights, under the word WATERBAR on a dark green wall. This is where visitors got one glass of still, sparkling or salty water. Slide text: At the Waterbar, each visitor got one glass: still, sparkling or salty. No one knew which. You could drink it or give it to the art.

A hanging form covered in small tan nodules, lit against a dark wall near the bar. It is a suspended sculpture by the artist Roni(a) Johansson, as Dezeen credits it. Slide text: A form covered in small nodules, hanging by the bar.

The performance at MU: a performer in a long dark robe and a tall white headdress stands before wooden crosses and candles against a blue-lit glass wall, with a second robed performer and video screens behind. It shows the room turned into a performance. Slide text: At 15:30 the room became a performance.

A sheet of water pours from a glass tank raised on a steel frame into a wide glass basin below, lit by a bright lamp in a dark hall, while the audience watches from the floor. It shows the moment the wall of water was let loose at the end of the performance. Slide text: It ended with a wall of water let loose.

A clipped line from the OpenStax textbook: human beings are mostly water, ranging from about 75 percent of body mass in infants to about 50 to 60 percent in adult men and women, to as low as 45 percent in old age. Slide text: Most adult bodies are about half to 60 percent water, depending on age and body fat.

A clipped passage from the OpenStax textbook: the ICF makes up about 60 percent of the total water in the human body, about 25 liters in an average-size adult male. Slide text: Most of that water, about 60 percent, sits inside your cells. The rest is outside them, including your blood plasma.

A clipped passage from the OpenStax textbook: each day about the same volume, 2500 mL, of water leaves the body as it takes in; most as urine through the kidneys, and some by evaporation from the skin and in air expelled from the lungs. Slide text: MU's host said water never really goes away. Your body agrees: you lose water through your kidneys, skin and lungs, and take it back in every day.

posts.title: Partnership Ads and Spark Ads: two permission trails
posts.summary: Meta and TikTok both let a brand pay to show a creator's post to people who never followed the creator. On both apps the creator gives permission with a switch and a code. The switches look alike. They do not do the same things, and neither one holds the whole deal.

slides.alt: Diagram: three boxes joined by arrows, the creator's post, the brand pays, and the ad shows the creator's name. Below: Meta's version is Partnership Ads and TikTok's is Spark Ads, with a different permission on each app.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Meta, TikTok data

slides.alt: Diagram of Meta's three ways for a creator to give a brand permission: a toggle for one tagged branded post, a code for any one post, archived ones too, and account-level permission for ads from her handle with no post needed.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Instagram data

slides.alt: Diagram of Meta's three ways for a creator to give a brand permission: a toggle for one tagged branded post, a code for any one post, archived ones too, and account-level permission for ads from her handle with no post needed.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Instagram data

slides.alt: Diagram of TikTok's three ways for a brand to get a creator's post for a Spark Ad: pick posts from a linked account, use a code the creator sends for one post, or have Ads Manager post to an authorized account.

slides.alt: Diagram of four off switches. Meta: with the code off, running ads keep running; with the partner removed, running ads pause. TikTok: a video cannot be deleted while authorized, and its code can be deleted only once its ads end or it expires.

slides.alt: Diagram in two boxes. The switch shows that a permission was on. No Meta or TikTok page read for this piece says the switch holds the fee, the countries, edit rights or final approval; those live in the deal itself.

posts.title: The hemp timeline: eight years and three laws
posts.summary: How federal hemp law got from the 2018 farm bill to December 11, 2026, told date by date from the enacted texts and the Federal Register.

slides.alt: Rows of young hemp plants, Cannabis sativa, set in white plastic mulch with grass between the rows and trees behind, on a Maryland farm. Slide text: Hemp law, 2018 to December 11. Hemp rows on a Maryland farm in a USDA photo from 2020. The federal rules for this crop have moved in dated steps since 2018.

A crop of Public Law 115-334, page 132 Stat. 5018: section 12619, Conforming Changes to Controlled Substances Act, adding that the term marihuana does not include hemp. Slide text: Dec. 20, 2018: hemp leaves the drug law. The 2018 farm bill defined hemp at 0.3 percent delta-9 THC and wrote that the term marihuana "does not include" hemp.

A crop of the first page of Public Law 119-37: An Act making continuing appropriations and extensions for fiscal year 2026, dated Nov. 12, 2025, H.R. 5371. Slide text: Nov. 12, 2025: a rewrite in a funding law. Public Law 119-37, a stopgap spending act, rewrote the hemp definition in section 781 of its agriculture division.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 558: the opening of section 781, effective 365 days after the enactment of this Act, amending section 297A of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946. Slide text: It set a one-year clock. Section 781 opens "Effective 365 days after the enactment of this Act." That pointed to November 12, 2026.

A crop of the first page of Public Law 119-103: An Act making continuing appropriations and extensions for fiscal year 2027, dated Sept. 2, 2026, H.R. 6500. Slide text: Sept. 2, 2026: another funding law. Public Law 119-103 held most of the rewrite back until December 11, 2026. Only the ban on cannabinoids the plant cannot make started November 12.

A crop of Public Law 119-103, page 140 Stat. 989: section 106, making funds available until the earliest of three events, the third being December 11, 2026. Slide text: Dec. 11: the stopgap's end date. The same law set its stopgap funding to end December 11, 2026, so the next funding bill could move the hemp date. Check GovInfo.

The United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., its white dome and east front under a blue sky with light clouds. Slide text: At least five hemp bills waited. On Nov. 11, 2026: S. 3686, H.R. 7024, H.R. 6209, H.R. 9830 and H.R. 10079, none past referral. Check Congress.gov on the day.

posts.title: The Machine Inside the Mountain
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. In 1913 a sugar company drove a tunnel under the Koʻolau Range to carry stream water across Oʻahu. The mountain answered with more water than anyone had measured. This part follows the building of the ditch and what it took from the streams.

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1916 photograph looking down a timbered tunnel in the Waiāhole project: curved wooden arch forms overhead, a plank wall on the right and narrow rail tracks on the floor leading into the dark. The report's own caption reads 'Portion of tunnel, showing forms for arch of tunnel roof' and does not say which tunnel or heading. It opens the story inside the mountain, on the machine itself.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: USGS map of the Waiāhole Ditch System: a blue dotted line starts at the Kahana tunnels in the windward valleys, runs south past Waikāne and Uwao tunnels and Gates 30 and 31, passes under the Koʻolau at the North Portal, comes out past Adit 8 and crosses central Oʻahu to Reservoir 155. Black outlines mark the Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole watersheds the ditch draws from.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of two large riveted steel pipes arching over a cut in a hillside at Waikakalaua Gulch, with a railway track running through the cut below. The report's caption calls them steel pipes crossing a branch of the Oahu Railway, the larger one the new 72-inch pipe. They are the part of the route where the conduit crosses a gulch instead of a tunnel or ditch.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: First page of Act 111, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1998, the law that let the state buy the Waiāhole water system. Section 2 opens: Water belongs to the people and the State should be the steward in managing and ensuring the allocation of this resource for the highest and best use in the public interest.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of a worker in a hat standing before two concrete-framed gates with hand wheels above them, set into the mouth of a finished section of the conduit. The report captions it 'Gates at a section of finished conduit.' It shows the kind of gate the sentence means, the control that moves in minutes.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Printed paragraph from page 111 of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion: For the reasons fully explained below, we affirm in part and vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The caption of the opinion as printed on page 97 of the Hawaiʻi Reports: In the Matter of the Water Use Permit Applications ... for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing. No. 21309. Supreme Court of Hawaiʻi. Aug. 22, 2000.

Letterhead of the State of Hawaiʻi Commission on Water Resource Management, dated December 24, 1997. The letter tells the parties that the Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Decision and Order for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing are enclosed: the decision the Supreme Court later reviewed.

Black-and-white 2019 photograph of two large siphon pipes crossing Kipapa Gulch side by side: on the left a newer siphon behind a concrete intake with a wooden screen, on the right the historic riveted-steel siphon behind a rusted grate. The survey caption says the historic one is no longer in use and the newer one is in use. It shows the fixed physical network of the Waiāhole Ditch carrying today's water through 1916-era works.

Lines of type from page 6 of Kluegel's 1916 report: the highest intake at 790 feet, and the length of the main tunnel through the Koolau Ridge, 14,567 feet, or 2.76 miles, with the North Portal at 752 feet and the South Portal at 724 feet. The usual facts, which the slide says are not the only questions.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph inside the main tunnel: a wall of dark rock with water jetting and spraying out of it into the bore, and two men with lanterns standing near the floor. The report's caption reads 'Water issuing from water-bearing rock in the main tunnel, 10,550 feet from the South Portal, March 23, 1915,' and explains that the lanterns are held by men beside a drill. It shows the mountain's own stored groundwater, the landscape process the tunnel tapped.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1914 photograph of six tunnel workers in work clothes and caps standing together underground in front of a rock face, with a drill rig and air hose across the foreground. The report's caption reads 'Japanese professional tunnel men, Main Tunnel, July, 1914,' and its text credits them with most of the drilling and mucking. It puts the people who built the tunnel in the frame.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Paragraph from page 178 of a 1913 USGS report, written about 1911, before the ditch: Waiāhole Stream rises in springs about 1,000 feet above sea level, its flow is fairly constant, and a part of the water is used for irrigating rice and taro lands in the lower part of the valley.

Typed lines from page 3 of a 2025 Hawaiʻi Senate bill on the Waiāhole water system, listing who depends on it today: Aloun Farms, the Hawaii Agriculture Research Center, Larry Jefts Farm, Mililani Nursery, Mililani Agricultural Park, Sugarland Farms, Waiawa Nursery, Waikele Farms, livestock ranchers, Mililani Memorial Park and the Waiawa correctional facility.

A Parshall flume on the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-8): a concrete channel that narrows in the middle so one depth reading gives a flow rate, with smooth fast water and tall grass on the banks. By 2019 a laser sensor upstream had replaced it. It shows a gauge, the subject of the line.

Page 728 of a 1921 territorial Supreme Court opinion setting out the deals made before the tunnel was dug: a fifty-year lease of Kahana's surplus water from May 27, 1916, and a December 30, 1912 deed of water rights in Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole for $257,500, each subject to the valley residents' water for household use and irrigation.

The start of the conclusion of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion, page 189: For the reasons stated in this opinion, we vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for additional findings and conclusions ... regarding the following, beginning with an interim instream flow standard for windward streams.

Faded photograph from a 1913 USGS paper, captioned Velocity-area gaging station, Waiāhole Stream: two men measure the stream by wading it, one seated in the water and one holding a rod, while men in hats watch from the grassy bank. A flow measurement, the thing the line says cannot decide allocation on its own.

A metal gate set into the concrete wall of the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani, with a staff scale marked in one-foot steps and a narrow concrete footbridge at right, photographed for the National Park Service HAER survey in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-4). The 1916 machine still decides, gate by gate, where today's water goes.
slides.credit: Photo: David Franzen, HAER, Public domain

slides.alt: Line chart from the USGS low-flow study, Figure 34: daily water released at Gate 31 to Waiāhole Stream from January 1999 to late 2004, a jagged blue line mostly between 5 and 25 million gallons a day, above a flat pink line for the Commission's targeted restoration flow of 4, then 4.8 million gallons a day.

onScreen: The Machine Inside the Mountain Inside Oʻahu’s Koʻolau Mountains, the Waiāhole tunnel still helps decide where water goes.
The project therefore did not simply capture rainfall after it entered a ditch. It recruited an entire mountain watershed.
Intakes, tunnels, ditches, siphons, reservoirs, and gates turned flow into a controllable route.
Once farms, towns, ecosystems, and institutions depend on a route, infrastructure becomes governance.
A gate can change flow in minutes. Deciding the lawful and sustainable flow can take years.
In 2000, the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court affirmed part of the Commission on Water Resource Management’s decision, vacated part and sent issues back.
Waiāhole’s present consequence is therefore a continuing design problem: how should a fixed physical network serve changing public purposes?
Ask which landscape processes it recruited,
whose labor made it durable,
what uses it displaced,
which dependencies formed around it,
what the gauges can and cannot tell us,
and which past decision is hiding inside the present baseline.

onScreen: Finding a certifying provider What to expect in Hawaiʻi, what the state does and does not vouch for, and five questions to ask.
Who can certify Physicians and APRNs can certify when they have a bona fide relationship with you. Hospice providers can certify hospice patients.
OMCCR lists but does not vouch The list is not exhaustive. The Department of Health does not endorse providers or guarantee the list, and encourages patients to research them.
Ask about cannabis education OMCCR’s patient page says meeting a provider who has completed medical cannabis education is advisable. Its specialist list was under development on October 11, 2026.
The first visit can be telehealth Act 241 says the relationship need not start with an in-person visit. OMCCR says telehealth certification has been allowed since September 18, 2025.
Telehealth has rules The provider must be physically in Hawaiʻi during the visit. Telehealth must meet the same standard of care as an in-person visit.
A form alone is not enough OMCCR says an online questionnaire alone does not meet the standard of care. Each patient must be assessed individually.
What a visit may include Providers told OMCCR what to expect: bring ID, medical files and your medication list; expect a history review and a check for drug interactions.
The fee has a cap A certifier’s fee may not exceed three times the state registration fee, $105 for a 1-year certification. Fees must be disclosed first.
Rules moved after September 2024 That month’s newsletter said telehealth was for renewals only. Act 241 and OMCCR’s September 2025 guidance now allow telehealth for first visits.

posts.title: Sleeping in a monastery
posts.summary: For Dutch Design Week 2026, RN Collins stayed at Hotel Mariënhage in Eindhoven. The hotel sits in a complex built over a medieval castle mound. Two figures in black habits look out of its stained-glass windows, and a robot dog hides in one of its paintings.

slides.alt: An arched stained-glass window shows a friar in a black habit. He holds a book marked with a cross, framed in purple and yellow glass. Slide text: RN Collins's Dutch Design Week hotel sits in a monastery complex with a 15th-century wing.

Through a window, a courtyard lawn and hedges lead to a brick monastery wing. A church with two spires and a modern tower stand behind. Slide text: Hotel Mariënhage sits in the former school and chapel buildings of an Augustinian monastery complex.

An arched stained-glass window shows a figure in a black habit and white headcloth. The figure holds small scales in one hand and a red heart in the other. Slide text: A second window: a figure with scales and a red heart. The cover's label reads 'Aegidius Columnius', most likely Giles of Rome, an Augustinian theologian. The hotel has not confirmed it.

Through a window, a red-brick building with white windows stands over a green courtyard garden. Slide text: Kunstwacht Eindhoven says the friars bought it in 1890. The last ones left in 2017. Now it is a hotel, with a ceremony house next door.
A woman in a black hoodie looks up in a white atrium under skylights and a hanging light installation. Slide text: Saturday morning in the corridors: "I don't know why I'm whispering."

A dark-tiled hotel bathroom at night with a round mirror ringed in blue light above a white basin, and a glass shower with a second blue-ringed mirror behind it. Slide text: Night two: blue rings in the bathroom, gold curtains in the bedroom.

A black four-legged robot with an arm for a head, painted in among peaches, grapes and a basket in a dark old still life, with a tennis ball by its front foot. Slide text: In a corridor painting, someone added a robot dog to an old still life.

Two drawn hind-leg skeletons side by side. In the flat-footed leg the red ankle bones sit low, on the ground. In the leg that stands on its toes, the same red ankle bones sit high above the ground. Slide text: A dog's hock is its ankle.

An old anatomy plate of a dog skeleton, hind legs only. The paws rest on the toe bones, and the ankle joint sits high above the ground, angled back like a knee. Slide text: Dogs stand on their digits, so the ankle rides high and looks like a knee bending backward.

posts.title: Embed, host or repost? Big Buck Bunny on YouTube
posts.summary: A rabbit cartoon from Amsterdam was made to be shared, and its makers put it on YouTube themselves. That makes it a clean test case. Showing YouTube's player on a web page, holding the file and uploading a fresh copy look alike to a viewer. The license, YouTube's terms and the courts treat them as three separate acts.

slides.alt: A frame from Big Buck Bunny, taken at 1:15 from the Blender Foundation's own 1080p release file: the large gray cartoon rabbit smiles behind white flowers in a meadow. It is the free, Creative Commons licensed film the sentence names.

Page 8 of the Ninth Circuit's 2023 opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the paragraph that ends: Importantly, the embedding website does not store a copy of the underlying image. It is the court's own statement that an embed is not a new copy.

Section 3, License Grant, of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: a worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive, perpetual license to reproduce the work and include it in collections. It is the clause that permits the broad reuse the sentence names.

The start of section 4(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code, the credit clause: anyone who distributes or performs the work must keep intact all copyright notices and give credit reasonable to the medium, beginning with the name of the original author. The entrance of YouTube's headquarters at 901 Cherry Avenue in San Bruno, California, with a YouTube sign on a hedge-covered wall, photographed August 9, 2010. It is the company that hosts uploaded copies on its own servers, the host the sentence names. It does not show where any file is stored.

Page 9 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram: the host server can control whether embedding is available and can delete or replace the image, and the browser shows whatever the host server supplies. It is the court's account of an embed showing the host's own copy on another page.

Page 34 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the passage that says BuzzFeed and Time embedded but did not store the underlying photographs, so they did not directly infringe. It is the court applying the point that an embed makes no new copy of the file.

slides.alt: Paragraph 44 of the EU Court of Justice's 2018 Renckhoff judgment: posting a work on another website gives rise to a new communication, independent of the one first authorized, which may stay available after the author removes the original. It is the court's statement that a repost is a separate copy needing its own permission.

Section 4(a) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: you must include a copy of, or the web address for, this License with every copy of the work you distribute or perform. It is the license link the sentence says to keep with the file.

Section 3(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: an adaptation must clearly label that changes were made, for example with the line The original work has been modified. It is the modification note the sentence asks for. Captions and transcripts are not license terms and are not shown.

A chart titled Host, embed or repost, with three boxes. Host: the file is on YouTube's servers, allowed by the uploader's license to YouTube. Embed: the file stays on YouTube and the page holds code that calls the player, allowed by YouTube's Terms. Repost: a separate copy that may outlast the original, allowed for this film by CC BY 3.0 and its conditions. It lays out the route choice the sentence asks for.

Section 106 of Title 17 of the United States Code, Exclusive rights in copyrighted works, from the 2023 edition printed by the Government Publishing Office, cropped to the heading and the first three rights: to reproduce, to prepare derivative works and to distribute copies. posts.title: The per-container cap: how the new hemp law measures a package
posts.summary: The 2025 hemp law caps finished products at 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Here is the text, the definition of a container, the federal data on children that framed the debate, and what is still undecided.

slides.alt: Young hemp plants, Cannabis sativa, growing thickly in raised beds inside a plastic-covered high tunnel in Crawford County, Indiana, with a water tank behind; no people in frame. Slide text: The new hemp cap counts the package. Hemp in an Indiana high tunnel, June 2022. A 2025 law caps the THC in each package of finished products made from it.
slides.credit: Photo: B. O'Connor, USDA NRCS, PD

slides.alt: A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: clause (iv), excluding final hemp-derived cannabinoid products with greater than 0.4 milligrams combined total per container of total THC and similar-effect cannabinoids. Slide text: 0.4 milligrams per container. A final product is not hemp if its container holds over 0.4 mg combined of total THC and THC look-alikes, as HHS decides.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 560: the definition of container as the innermost wrapping, packaging or vessel in direct contact with the product, and the exclusion of bulk shipping containers. Slide text: The container is the innermost pack. The law names "a jar, bottle, bag, box, packet, can, carton, or cartridge." Bulk shipping boxes and outer wraps do not count.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: intermediate products excluded above 0.3 percent combined total, and when marketed or sold as a final product or directly to an end consumer. Slide text: Ingredients get a different line. Intermediate products are limited to 0.3 percent combined, and may not be marketed or sold to an end consumer at all.

A crop of an FDA web page: national poison control centers received 2,362 exposure cases of delta-8 THC products from January 1, 2021 to February 28, 2022; 41 percent involved patients under 18; 82 percent of unintentional exposures affected children. Slide text: FDA's 2022 count: 41 percent were under 18. Poison centers took 2,362 delta-8 THC cases in 14 months. 41 percent involved people under 18. FDA notes these are self-reported calls.

A crop of an FDA web page, point 5: delta-8 THC products should be kept out of the reach of children and pets, with a paragraph on packaging such as gummies and candies and sales at convenience stores and gas stations. Slide text: FDA's concern was the package. FDA warned of packaging "that may appeal to children" and sales where there may be no age limit. Its advice: keep products out of reach.

A crop of the Federal Register, December 23, 2025: Executive Order 14370 saying some full-spectrum CBD products will once again be controlled as marijuana when section 781 goes into effect because of the per-container threshold. Slide text: Full-spectrum CBD is caught too. A December 2025 executive order says some full-spectrum CBD products will be controlled as marijuana once the per-container cap applies.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 561: item (D), additional information and specificity about the term container. Slide text: Still open: what counts as a container. FDA was told to give more detail on "container" within 90 days. As of Nov. 12, 2026, nothing was in the Federal Register.

posts.title: How Regulatory Categories Conceal Scientific Uncertainty
posts.summary: Federal law sorts one plant, Cannabis sativa, into hemp, Schedule I marijuana and Schedule III drugs. The statutes, rules, letters and court papers behind each label show where the numbers came from, what the agencies did not know, and which questions are still open.

onScreen: A cannabis plant can cross a legal border without moving. Federal law draws the hemp line at 0.3 percent THC, dry weight.
The number becomes a procedure: dry-weight basis, plus a measurement of uncertainty.
Labs must report uncertainty, and USDA doesn't standardize how they calculate it.
Scheduling isn't a literature review. It translates evidence into eight statutory factors.
The Schedule I listing shows where marijuana was placed, not what was found about it.
Aug 29, 2023: HHS recommended Schedule III. A recommendation isn't a rule.
May 2024: a proposed rule to move marijuana to Schedule III. A proposal isn't a final classification.
Status as of Nov 15, 2026: an April 2026 order moved FDA-approved and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III. Replies on the broader rule were due Nov 5. No decision found yet.

posts.title: One elder's yes is not a community's yes
posts.summary: When outsiders want a people's consent, to dig on their land, to study their blood or to sell what they know about a plant, someone has to say yes. The hard question is who. This is how courts, treaties and communities have answered it, read from their own pages.

onScreen: One elder's yes is not a community's yes. In 2008 Suriname asked a human rights court whom to consult: the Saramaka captains, one captain or the Gaa'man. The court said the Saramaka decide.
Chosen by the people themselves. In 2007 the UN adopted a declaration, 143 to 4. Peoples take part in decisions "through representatives chosen by themselves."
Four men gave DNA. Their leaders were avoided. After a 2010 genome study of four San men, the San wrote: "In Genomics research, our leaders were avoided."
Come in through the door. The San Code of 2017 names the San Council to manage research. A San leader asked researchers to come through the door, not the window.
Two systems, two answers. The office for 12 of 13 Wet'suwet'en houses opposed a gas pipeline. All five elected bands signed benefit deals. A court called the people "deeply divided."
Two peoples, one levy. A government-led study found the Khoi and San hold the traditional knowledge of rooibos. Under a 2019 deal, processors pay them 1.5 percent of the farm gate price.
Where the yes gets checked. The 143 Parties to the Nagoya Protocol must take steps so that traditional knowledge used there was obtained with community consent. The US is not a Party.

posts.title: Two thirds of Google searches now end without a click
posts.summary: A clickstream study found that 68 percent of US Google searches in early 2026 sent no one anywhere. Here is what that number measures, what the other studies found, what Google says, and what the 2024 forecast of a search collapse got right and wrong.

slides.alt: A chart titled In 2026, what happens after a Google search. Three arrows lead from a Google search box to 32 percent a click, 39 percent nothing and 29 percent another search, beside the words 68 percent zero-click searches and 232 clicks per 1,000 searches to the open web.

A bar chart of US Google searches with zero clicks: 45.01 percent in 2016 and 50.33 percent in 2019 from the Jumpshot panel, 60.45 percent in 2024 from Datos, and 68.01 percent in 2026 from Similarweb.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from SparkToro data

slides.alt: Four bars: searches with one or more clicks, 41.50 percent in 2024 and 32.00 percent in 2026; searches followed by another search, 21.40 percent in 2024 and 28.68 percent in 2026.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from SparkToro data

slides.alt: A bar chart of clicks to the open web per 1,000 Google searches: 360 for the United States in 2024, 374 for the European Union in 2024, and 232 for the United States in 2026.

slides.alt: Two pairs of bars for the top result's click rate. March 2025: forecast 4.0 percent, measured 2.6 percent, minus 34.5 percent. December 2025: forecast 3.7 percent, measured 1.6 percent, minus 58 percent.

slides.alt: Three bars: clicked a result with no AI summary, 15 percent; clicked a result with an AI summary shown, 8 percent; clicked a link in the summary, 1 percent.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Pew data

posts.title: Late to breakfast
posts.summary: A design studio in Eindhoven served breakfast inside its own exhibition during Dutch Design Week 2026. RN Collins reached the door five minutes before the listed end. This is that morning, told from her footage, and the research on what a welcome is made of: who can see whom, who checks on whom, and where the word comes from.

posts.title: Who Is Supposed to Supply What the Law Requires?
posts.summary: A man asks a judge for a lawyer. A clerk hands back divorce papers. A mother cannot pay $2 a page. Court rulings, rules and orders show who has been told to supply what the law demands.

slides.alt: A 1963 Supreme Court opinion page, headed Gideon v. Wainwright, 337, quoting a judge who says he cannot appoint counsel because Florida allows it only in capital cases, and Gideon's reply that the Supreme Court says he is entitled to counsel.

Typed court text saying the cities estimated about 1,700 transferred cases, chose a proposal paying $17,500 a month, which works out to $10 per case for April 2012, and that this makes effective help virtually impossible.

Typed order text setting, from January 1, 2026, 47 felony case credits, 120 misdemeanor case credits and 250 commitment case credits a year for a full-time appointed attorney, with a phase-in of at least 10 percent a year.

A 1971 Supreme Court page head, Boddie v. Connecticut, 373, above a paragraph saying the clerk of the Superior Court returned the papers because no entry fee had been paid, and efforts to get a waiver were to no avail.

A page of a 1996 Supreme Court opinion, headed 108, M. L. B. v. S. L. J., listing $1,900 for the transcript at 950 pages at $2 per page, $438 for other documents, $4.36 for binders and $10 for mailing.

A paragraph of a 1974 Supreme Court opinion saying there is no equality of treatment merely by providing students with the same facilities, textbooks, teachers and curriculum, because students who do not understand English are foreclosed from any meaningful education.

Federal Register text: Executive Order 14224 of March 1, 2025, Section 3, making English the official language and revoking Executive Order 13166, while saying nothing in the order requires any change in agency services.

Federal rule text headed section 35.160 General, above paragraph (3): a public entity shall not rely on a minor child to interpret or facilitate communication, except in an emergency involving an imminent threat where no interpreter is available.

In April 2012, two cities' defense contract came to $10 a case. A federal judge said that made real help "virtually impossible."
Washington limits a public defender's year to 47 felony credits. Or 120 misdemeanor credits, from January 1, 2026.
A Connecticut clerk sent back divorce papers. No fee was paid. In 1971 the Supreme Court said the poor could not be shut out of divorce court.
Mississippi wanted $2,352.36 before a mother could appeal. The case ended her parental rights. In 1996 the Court said cost could not bar her.
Same books, same teachers: "no equality of treatment." The Supreme Court, 1974, on students who did not speak English.
In 2025 an executive order revoked the 2000 language access order. It said it did not require any agency to change its services.
A public entity may not rely on a child to interpret. Except in an emergency, a federal disability rule says, since 2010.

In 2000, Hawaii became the first state to enact medical cannabis through its legislature. Governor Ben Cayetano approved Act 228 on June 14, 2000.
Will Espero: a supporter votes yes. A champion builds coalitions and spends political capital. He chaired the 2015 conference committee that passed the dispensary bill, Act 241.
In 2024, the Hawaii Senate passed SB 3335 to legalize adult use. Two House committees amended it. It went no further.
In 2026, HB 1624 proposed a constitutional amendment for adult use. In February, Speaker Nadine Nakamura said neither House bill would move ahead.
In a survey of 1,009 people in Japan, 57.5% said legal adult use would not affect a visit to Hawaii. From a 2025 report for the Hawaii Department of Health.
Guam legalized adult use in April 2019. The same report found no significant rise or fall in visits from Japan or South Korea, using data through December 2020.
D.C. voters approved Initiative 71 in November 2014. Certified count: 115,050 for, 49,168 against. It legalized possessing small amounts for personal use.
Congress then barred D.C. from using its funds to go further. The March 2024 spending law says no D.C. funds may be used to enact a law that legalizes recreational use of a Schedule I drug.
Marijuana under a state medical license is now federal Schedule III. In effect April 28, 2026. Other marijuana stays Schedule I. Current as of Nov. 15, 2026.

posts.title: The Windbreak Decree
posts.summary: In 1958 the Netherlands exempted hemp grown as a windbreak from part of its drug law. The decree, the 1976 Opium Act, a 1999 rewrite and a 2019 experiment law show how one farm rule was named in court, narrowed, dropped and finally replaced.

slides.alt: A bearded man on a canal bank in Amsterdam in 1969 holding up the gardening newspaper De Amateur-Tuinder.
Two men among tall hemp plants in an Amsterdam garden bed in 1969, one holding a spade, a third person partly hidden behind them.
Two Dutch ministers in the parliamentary chamber in 1976, a woman seated over papers and a man standing at a microphone.
Printed Dutch text of article 11 of the 1976 Opium Act, four numbered paragraphs, the last ending with the words ten hoogste 30 gram.

Herbarium sheet of Cannabis sativa L., the leafy top of one whole pressed plant that was mounted with its roots, collected by J. Akkerman on August 13, 1975 at the rubbish dump in Krommenie, North Holland, the year the bill was before parliament. Naturalis Biodiversity Center, Leiden.
Dutch Justice Minister Dries van Agt speaking at a microphone in the Tweede Kamer debate on the Opium Act, March 2, 1976.

onScreen: Nov 19, 1971: a defendant asked the prosecution's chemist whether he'd considered "the windbreak decree of 1958." The decree was real. The name was his.
Before 1976, Dutch law prohibited dried tops of flowering plants. A green seedling in a pot did not clearly fit. In May 1971, seedlings sold for a guilder each, opposite a police station.
The 1976 Act was signed by Health Minister Irene Vorrink first, Justice Minister Dries van Agt second. Its two lists sorted drugs by risk.
Nothing was legalized. Under article 11, 30 grams or less of hemp or hashish fell to the lowest tier: still an offense, but a minor one.
The new definition: every part of the plant except the seeds. The law remembered as tolerance brought the living plant inside it.
Tolerance came from prosecutors, not the Act. Their guidelines of October 1976 gave no priority to having drugs for personal use or to small soft-drug sales.

posts.title: The license expired. The episodes didn’t.
posts.summary: Friends left Netflix in the United States at the end of 2019 and turned up on HBO Max five months later. The show itself stayed with the studio that made it. A contract ran out, and the dated papers around it show exactly what moved, where and when.

onScreen: Friends left Netflix in the United States at midnight on December 31, 2019.
The 236 episodes hadn't changed. Netflix's license to stream them had run out.
Streaming availability can change when a licensing window ends,
the way Friends left Netflix once WarnerMedia built its own service, HBO Max.
Warner Bros. Television, the studio behind Friends, had licensed the show to Netflix for years
before WarnerMedia decided to carry it exclusively on HBO Max instead.
The real evidence of that handoff was a reported five-year, $425 million licensing deal,
not a “leaving soon” banner inside the Netflix app.

posts.title: Sectie-C, 2015 to 2024: a former factory site in the Dutch Design Week archive
