posts.title: A bus stop you'd want to lean on
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Luca Ortmann's Waiting for the Bus put yellow steel rails, lamps and ledges on the Demer, a shopping street in Eindhoven. RN Collins filmed them on a Sunday evening. This piece follows the objects back to a Berlin graduation project, the street back to 1942, and the body back to the bones that carry a wait.

slides.alt: A group of people stands around a tall yellow arch-shaped frame on a shopping street at dusk, one person leaning on it. Slide text: An anatomist watches where people put their weight. On the Demer, one leaned on the design.

A yellow steel lamp on a shopping street at dusk, its stem looping around a small round yellow table with three paper cups on it; shoppers pass behind and the shop signs are blurred. Slide text: Waiting for the Bus by Luca Ortmann was made to turn a temporary bus stop into a place to wait.

A yellow steel tube and a low yellow rail, each fixed with bolts to a rounded yellow base plate on sunlit paving; a passer-by is blurred. Slide text: Yellow steel tubes, bolted to movable base plates.

Textbook drawing of the pelvis from the front, labeled hip bone, sacrum, acetabulum and ischial tuberosity, with a small inset showing the pelvis between the spine and the thigh bones. Slide text: Standing: the pelvis passes the body's weight to the legs. Sitting: the sitting bones carry it.

A yellow three-bar steel rail on a rounded yellow base plate on pale paving at dusk, shop fronts behind with their signs blurred. Slide text: A rail to lean on. It was free to use on the Demer during Dutch Design Week 2026.

posts.summary: Where a Hawaii medical cannabis patient may grow, what a lease or an association can say about it, and where the statutes stop.

onScreen: Renters, HOAs and the patient gardener What Hawaii's lease, condo and planned community statutes say about medical cannabis. Education, not legal advice.
Chapter 329 speaks to landlords once. Section 329-125.5 bars refusing to lease to a patient for status alone, unless the landlord would lose a federal benefit.
The rental rule: section 521-39. A lease clause allowing eviction of a tenant with a valid 329 certificate is void, with one smoking exception.
The smoking exception has two parts. The lease must already allow eviction for tobacco smoking, and the cannabis must be smoked. Both must be true.
Association documents can switch it off. Section 521-39 does not apply where condominium or planned community documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis.
Condominiums: section 514B-113. Condo documents allowing listed discriminatory practices against a resident with a valid certificate are void, with the same smoking exception.
Planned communities: section 421J-16. Same wording for planned community associations. Both keep the duty to give reasonable accommodations to people with disabilities.

posts.title: Before opening hours
posts.summary: On the first Saturday of Dutch Design Week 2026, two young designers were still drilling their sign in a building that squatters took over in 1990 and bought two years later. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, filmed the morning. The footage shows the build; the residents' own written history explains how the building came to be theirs.

slides.alt: A white building with tall orange letters reading BURGERS rises beside a tree, a small yellow pavilion at its foot. Slide text: Squatted in 1990. Bought in 1992.

posts.title: A voice can sound like someone who said no, and the company can say it doesn’t
posts.summary: In May 2024 a ChatGPT voice called Sky was paused after Scarlett Johansson said it sounded like her. OpenAI said the voice belonged to a different actor. Both statements are public. What they leave open is an old question about who owns the sound of a person.

posts.title: The Species Gap
posts.summary: What plant produced it? State cannabis law asks licensed laboratories to certify a great deal about a cannabis product, but arguably not the threshold question of what plant produced it.

slides.alt: Figure 2 of Xiang and colleagues (Genes, 2025): four agarose gels. THCAS and CBDAS bands, genes found only in cannabis, appear in the five cannabis and hemp seed lanes and not in hops, related plants, tea or tobacco. A DNA test that tells cannabis from other plants.
slides.credit: Source: Xiang et al., Genes 2025, CC BY

slides.alt: Herbarium sheet of Cannabis sativa L. at the University of Neuchâtel: a whole pressed plant, from the root to the leafy flowering top, collected on the lakeshore at Neuchâtel on 4 October 1974. Reference specimens like this are how botanists check what plant a material came from.

A flowering Andrographis paniculata plant with narrow green leaves and slender seed pods against a dark green background. The article names this herb as the cheaper plant substituted for the bitter tonic Swertia chirata.
slides.credit: Photo: V C Balakrishnan, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.alt: Figure 1 of Xiang and colleagues (Genes, 2025): an agarose gel with four DNA bands amplified from cannabis, THCAS and CBDAS, the THC and CBD synthase genes behind chemotype, and rbcL and matK, two plant barcodes for species identity.
slides.credit: Source: Xiang et al., Genes 2025, CC BY

slides.alt: California regulation section 15714, Required Testing, listing the nine tests a licensed lab must run: cannabinoids, foreign material, heavy metals, microbes, mycotoxins, moisture, pesticides, solvents and terpenoids.

Colorado marijuana Rule 4-215, Contaminant Testing, with its table of required tests for flower: water activity, mycotoxins, residual solvents, elemental impurities, pesticides and microbial contaminants.
California regulation section 15726, Certificate of Analysis, requiring a lab to issue a COA for each sample containing the results of all required analyses.

Top of page 1 of Congressional Research Service Insight IN12620, Change to Federal Definition of Hemp and Implications for Federal Enforcement (December 3, 2025): Congress enacted P.L. 119-37, Division B, with a provision that reimposes federal controls over certain hemp products.

Passage from FDA's 2016 Botanical Drug Development guidance saying trained staff should identify the plant species against a voucher specimen and that a genetic method such as DNA barcoding may be developed.
Michigan's enactment of UCC section 2-314, implied warranty of merchantability, including (f): goods must conform to the promises or affirmations of fact made on the container or label.

Rule 4-205 of Colorado's marijuana rules, 1 CCR 212-3, Regulated Marijuana Testing Program: Mandatory Testing. Test batches may be tested for potency or contaminants such as pesticides, microbes, mycotoxins, molds, metals and solvents; no plant identity test is listed. One of the five rule sets on the card.

California's cannabis rule 4 CCR 15014.1, Equity Fee Relief: who counts as a qualified equity applicant or licensee, one of the groups the slide names, for the state's licence fee waivers and deferrals.

Contents of Article 5, Laboratory Testing and Reporting, in California's cannabis rules: required testing, moisture, residual solvents, pesticides, microbes, mycotoxins, foreign material, heavy metals, cannabinoids, terpenoids and the certificate of analysis. No section tests which plant the product came from.

onScreen: The Species Gap: what plant is it? State Testing Law and the Case for Molecular Authentication of Cannabis
What plant produced it? State cannabis law asks licensed laboratories to certify a great deal about a cannabis product, but arguably not the threshold question of what plant produced it.
Herbal medicine adulteration is not a new problem. The article describes a bitter tonic, Swertia chirata, substituted with the cheaper Andrographis paniculata.
Four questions molecular authentication could help answer Species identity. Chemotype classification. Cultivar identity. Geographic origin.
State testing law answers "what is in this product" and "how much." Not "what plant produced this." No state the article examined appears yet to require that answer.
California, Colorado and Michigan list their required tests. No botanical identity authentication requirement was identified.
What a certificate of analysis may imply A COA that includes no botanical identity authentication may implicitly represent that the product is what it claims to be at the species level.
Federal hemp law is being redefined. Section 781 of Pub. L. 119-37 amends the definition. Pub. L. 119-103 sets what applies before December 11, 2026.
FDA's 2016 Botanical Drug Development Guidance The article says it may be the most developed federal framework for botanical product identity authentication.
The UCC implies a warranty of merchantability. Merchantable goods must conform to the promise or affirmations of fact made on the container or label.

posts.title: Walk inside a piano
posts.summary: On a square in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week 2026, a Yamaha CP-70 electric grand piano was taken apart in sound. The model was first sold in 1976. Each key was wired to its own loudspeaker, hung in a bamboo frame that visitors walked through. Here is the instrument, the makers, and the part of the body built to catch it. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, filmed it with the Saturday press tour.

slides.alt: A yellow banner on bamboo poles reads Electric Grand above and below a black lightning bolt drawn from piano keys. Slide text: Every key of a Yamaha CP-70 electric grand got its own speaker.

Bamboo frames hung with upside-down terracotta pots and, lower down, black containers, visitors walking among them, a tall tower behind. Slide text: The speakers hung in a bamboo frame. You walked inside.
Diagram in three rows: one key, one amplified speaker, one volume control. Slide text: Each key wired to its own amplified speaker, each with its own volume control.
Inside a bamboo lattice, a keyboard stands over a tangle of cables on a wooden deck, listeners around it. Slide text: A live session, heard from inside the lattice.

Labeled textbook drawing of the outer ear cut open from the side: the curved auricle and the ear canal running inward through tissue and bone. Slide text: The outer ear's C-shaped curves direct sound toward the ear canal.

A tall bamboo pyramid hung with terracotta pots rises over a wooden deck under a blue sky, black containers hanging low, a few people among the frames and tall buildings behind. Slide text: Staged in 2021 at Boulevard in 's-Hertogenbosch. Seen at Dutch Design Week 2026 on Ketelhuisplein.

onScreen: A second reader checked all 136 claims in one long piece. 113 held. 22 were corrected. 1 was cut.
The draft said RN never saw the old lake bed. Her plane landed on it. Schiphol stands on the drained Haarlemmermeer, about 4 meters below the Dutch zero level.
The draft called Leeghwater a millwright. The source: a carpenter by trade who sometimes called himself a millmaker.
The draft said the museum named no maker. It names two. Engraved by Gerard Coeck after a design by Leeghwater, about 1640 to 1642.
The museum typed SAECVLV. The medal itself reads SAECVLA. When the object and its description disagree, the object wins.
Three checks that day: 16% to 28% of claims needed a fix. A second reader is in the standard for this reason.

posts.title: A park on the flat roofs
posts.summary: In a room at Stadslab Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week 2026, the park was on the ceiling and the sky was on the floor. Upside Park is a city idea for green, public roofs on Eindhoven's many flat post-war homes. RN Collins filmed the room. Here is what it showed, what the city has said, and what it has not.

A round green floor sticker reading Hier bouwen we aan de toekomst, We are building the future here, beside the wheel and frame of a mobility scooter. Slide text: We are building the future here.

The yellow Upside Park information board beside an ivy column under the UPSIDE PARK lettering, with a window behind it looking out on a rooftop and trees. A LEGO park built upside down on a green ceiling, with a wooden ladder, a wall of small photos, a bin of LEGO and a sky printed on the floor below. Slide text: Visitors built it in LEGO, upside down on the ceiling.

The Upside Park room: the green LEGO park hanging from the ceiling, ivy on a black frame, a yellow standing table and a wall screen, with a sky-printed floor at the bottom edge. Slide text: "A completely different vantage point that you just never otherwise get."

posts.title: Effortless for Whom?
posts.summary: When a service becomes easier for one person, the work behind it has to go somewhere. Five sets of public documents, from a Senate committee, a federal safety agency, the Treasury, the Federal Trade Commission and New York City, show where it went and who paid for it.

slides.alt: A paragraph of black report text on white. It says a rate of 600 means workers complete the same tasks every six seconds for a ten-hour shift, 5,400 times per day.
A page of report text under a bold heading about Project Elderwand. The last paragraph gives an upper limit of 1,940 repetitions in a ten-hour shift, about 216 items per hour.
A two-column table of Amazon warehouse injury rates per year: 7.25 in 2017, 7.74 in 2018, 9.01 in 2019, 6.59 in 2020, 7.64 in 2021, 6.97 in 2022 and 6.54 in 2023.
A scanned legal page headed Resolution and Amendment of Citation Items. A one-row table for site MDW8 shows an original penalty of $15,625 and an amended penalty of $145,000.
A table titled Direct File Costs per Filing Season. Tax year 2023: 140,803 filers, $31.8 million, $225.85 per return. Tax year 2024: 296,531 filers, $41 million, $138.27 per return.

The top of a court filing with a blue header line giving the case number, Document 490 and page 10 of 47. Numbered lines say that once a Prime member enters Iliad, they must reaffirm their desire to cancel on three pages.

A court order page with numbered lines and a blue header for Document 535. It requires cancellation through the same medium used to consent and a clear button to decline, which cannot say no thanks, I don't want free shipping.

posts.title: Who Sees Your Cannabis File
posts.summary: A dispensary may sit outside HIPAA. A door check, a state tracking system, a registry, police lookups and a provider's files each follow their own rules.

slides.alt: Part of page 5 of OMCCR's September 2024 newsletter. It says that while a medical cannabis dispensary may not be subject to HIPAA laws, Hawaiʻi Administrative Rules section 11-850-40 requires every dispensary to safeguard and keep confidential any personally identifying information and the medical condition of a patient.

Part of a page of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-850, section 11-850-33. A retail dispensing location must require a government-issued photo identification and a registration card before entry and must log the name and entry and exit time of every person who enters.

Part of 45 CFR 160.103 in the 2025 Code of Federal Regulations. It defines a covered entity as a health plan, a health care clearinghouse, or a health care provider who transmits health information electronically in connection with a covered transaction.

The text of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329-131, as printed from the saved web page. It says the prescription requirements of section 329-38 and the board of pharmacy licensure rules do not apply to the medical use of cannabis.

Page 850-48 of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-850, section 11-850-40, Confidentiality of information. It says a dispensary licensee shall safeguard and keep confidential any personally identifying information and the medical condition of a qualifying patient.

Part of page 5 of OMCCR's September 2024 newsletter. It says OMCCR does not share a patient's qualifying conditions with dispensaries, and that the 329 card registration number, name and date of birth are verified at a dispensary.

Part of page 850-60 of the dispensary rules, section 11-850-61(b) and (c). A dispensary shall track electronically all sales to patients from all dispensaries in the State and have a sales system that blocks sales over the legal limits and cannot be overridden manually.

The start of Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-160-56, Confidential information; exceptions. It says information the department keeps to administer the chapter is confidential except to employees and agents of the department, law enforcement, people with a court order, and others on a list.
The text of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-20, Law enforcement access to dispensary and production center records, as printed from the saved web page.

The definition of personal information in Hawaii Revised Statutes section 487N-1, as printed from the saved web page: a name combined with a Social Security number, a driver's license or Hawaii identification card number, or a financial account number with an access code.

A column of page 22715 of the Federal Register of April 28, 2026, in the Drug Enforcement Administration final rule that places FDA-approved products and marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license in schedule III and sets up an expedited registration process.

Part of the CMS web page Are You a Covered Entity, as printed from the saved copy. It says providers who submit HIPAA transactions, like claims, electronically are covered, and lists doctors, clinics, dentists and pharmacies as examples.

onScreen: Your dispensary may not be HIPAA. What protects you? OMCCR says a Hawaii dispensary may be outside HIPAA. A Department of Health rule still requires it to keep your information confidential.
Four places hold your file The certifying provider, the Department of Health registry, the dispensary and a statewide tracking system each hold part of it, under different rules.
What HIPAA covers A covered entity is a health plan, a clearinghouse, or a provider that sends certain health transactions electronically, such as claims or eligibility checks.
Why a dispensary may fall outside Hawaii law does not require insurance to cover medical cannabis, and prescription rules do not apply to it. Dispensary staff cannot issue certifications.
The rule that applies HAR 11-850-40 says a dispensary shall keep a patient's identifying information and medical condition confidential. Violations can bring penalties of $100 to $1,000 each.
What a dispensary sees Your card number, name and date of birth are verified. Dispensaries can see your purchase total across all dispensaries. Your qualifying condition is not shared.
Totals come from the law The tracking system must log each patient's purchases across all retail locations, and the sales system must block sales over the limit.
The registry has nine exceptions Registry information is confidential except for nine groups, including law enforcement, dispensary licensees verifying status and anyone you authorize in writing.
A second statute reaches dispensaries HRS 329D-20 requires the department to give dispensary files to agencies investigating crimes. It does not say whether patient sales data are included.
The breach law has a short list Hawaii's breach law covers a name plus a Social Security, license or ID, or financial account number. Medical information is not listed.
April 2026 federal change A DEA rule lets state-licensed medical marijuana dispensers register federally. The text I read does not mention HIPAA or patient privacy.

posts.title: Five rules for filming a design week
posts.summary: On the night before her first full day at Dutch Design Week 2026, RN Collins could not find the lens on her own camera. Four days later she had filmed makers, guides and a press tour on a camera smaller than a phone, with a second mic she handed to the people she met. Her cards show five working rules taking shape, each with a reason behind it.

slides.alt: RN Collins, in a dark head wrap and dark jacket, seen nearly full length in a mirror in a dim hotel room, holds a tiny camera on a grip at chest height, a blue ring light behind her. Slide text: "So I don't really know where the camera is." Friday night in Eindhoven. Five rules the footage shows her working out.

RN's hand holds out a small wireless mic to glass artist Eline Laauwen at her stand, who reaches to take it. Painted glass flowers hang on the board behind her; the lettering on the board is blurred. Slide text: Ask before you mic. Each of the three asks on tape got a yes.

A small clip-on mic with a gray fur windscreen sits on a black and white crochet top, beside a red and black woven guitar strap and the edge of a red guitar. Slide text: Hand over the second mic. It went to the makers.

A guide in a blue jacket with a press lanyard holds a bundle of microphone cables and a tote bag by a sheer curtain in a lounge. Slide text: Get their actual words. "I especially just wanna make sure I get everyone's like actually what they said and not what I think they said."

Rens of The Purple Show sits at a garden table in the sun and holds up a small wireless mic with a gray fur windscreen; brick houses and trees are behind, and the letters on the knit vest are blurred. Slide text: Point the camera at them. She told Eline Laauwen: "This isn't about me, this is about you."

A corner of the festival Business Lounge seen from above: gray felt chairs, a round felt table with a lit candle lamp and a paper cup, and a sheer curtain behind. Slide text: Film the room, not only the work. Tip from a workshop participant: three-second clips of everything.

RN's hand holds a second, gimbal-mounted camera in the hotel room on Friday evening, its set-up screen and brand name blurred, bedding behind. Slide text: Check the settings the night before. On Friday night, that meant the rotation and the lens.

In Dutch privacy law, a recognisable person in a photo is personal data. A public brand post falls outside the household exception.
Day 1, Eindhoven Centraal: built in 1956, a national monument since 2010. A platform sign names the place and shows no one up close.

The Evoluon, opened in 1966, stands in a public place. Dutch copyright law lets anyone publish pictures of it as it stands there.
Dutch Design Week 2026 ran under the theme R.A.W. Every design in a post carries its maker's name, and people stay small unless they agreed to be shown.
At the AI expo in the RAI, attending meant consent to the organizer's photos. That gives a visitor no right to post other visitors' faces. No trip frame comes from the expo.
Rijksmuseum: photos in public areas, none in the exhibition wing or the Cuypers Library. Garden photos are for private use only. The October 21 frames show the outside.

posts.title: Trauma-Informed Architecture
posts.summary: The argument: rooms act on the nervous system. The article says glare, echoes and mazes can trigger alarm, and daylight and wood can ease it. Next: what studies show.

slides.alt: Figure 16 of Justus and Raghani, Trauma-informed design: shelter homes for runaway children (2024): a design rendering of a shelter common room with arched alcoves, warm colours, cushions, plants and instruments, with two figures shown only as silhouettes. A building designed to be trauma-informed.
slides.credit: Source: Int J Adolesc Youth, CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: A long hospital corridor lit by overhead lights in Tuen Mun Hospital, Hong Kong. It does not show the study or findings the slide names.

Illustrative photo: Exterior of a former motel in Yaphank, New York, used as supported housing for US military veterans, shown with no residents in view. It is a shelter for veterans and does not show the permanent supportive housing study the slide names.
Illustrative photo: A bedroom with a bright window letting in daylight, with no person in view. It does not show the study, place or finding the slide names.

Figure 18 of the 2024 paper on shelter homes for runaway children: a design rendering of container homes placed around the site's existing trees, with a lawn and a deck, the paper's link to the outdoors.
slides.credit: Source: Int J Adolesc Youth, CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: Satellite view of the Za'atari refugee camp in Jordan on February 25, 2016: a dense grid of shelters in a rounded block, with roads, farm fields and desert around it.

Figure 13 of Al-Shoubaki and colleagues, A Human-Centered Shelter Design for People on the Move in the Al-Sahel Region (Sustainability, 2024): drawings of the proposed hexagonal shelter unit with a courtyard, in three options with two, three and four shelters.
Illustrative photo: Rows of tents in a military-run refugee camp at Oreokastro, Greece. It does not show the study or findings the slide names.

Page 1 of Valentine, Steffert, Mitcheltree and Steemers, Architectural Neuroimmunology: A Pilot Study Examining the Impact of Biophilic Architectural Design on Neuroinflammation (Buildings, 2024): the title, authors and abstract, which reports ten participants, lower relative delta power with more biophilic design, and no significant change in relative alpha power.
Illustrative photo: a Windows Mixed Reality virtual reality headset with two hand controllers. It does not show the study's virtual offices or participants.

Page 1 of Valentine, Architectural Allostatic Overloading: Exploring a Connection between Architectural Form and Allostatic Overloading (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2023): the title and abstract, which says there is yet to be a study of stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic load and advises a longitudinal public health study.

The Conclusions of Owen and Crane's 2022 review: the limited literature on trauma, design and housing is consistent with trauma-informed design principles, and three areas need future research, including how built-environment cues work over time.

The Conclusions of Valentine's 2023 paper: chronic or repeated exposure to stress may produce a cascade of allostatic events that ends in allostatic overload, and no study yet links stress-inducing architectural features to allostatic load. The basis for design that stops compounding stress.

onScreen: Can a building be trauma-informed? What the research says about spaces, stress and recovery. From RN Collins's article, Journal of Biophilic Design, Issue 17.
The argument: rooms act on the nervous system. The article says glare, echoes and mazes can trigger alarm, and daylight and wood can ease it. Next: what studies show.
A 2022 review of supported housing. Owen and Crane paired a scoping review with neuroscience. They found limited evidence that lines up strongly with trauma-informed design principles.
Three areas to research next. The review sets future research in three domains: safety and security, control, and enriched environments.
Shelters for runaway children. A 2024 paper lists open floor plans, sensory concerns, solitude, adaptability and a link to the outdoors. Hurdles: illiteracy, cost and varied trauma responses.
In Zaatari, residents redrew the grid. A 2025 survey of 102 households found refugees regrouped shelters into clusters around courtyards for privacy and safety. The model explained little overall.
A shelter design for the Al-Sahel. A 2024 design proposal: a unit for three to six people with patio options, for emergency, transitional and durable phases.
Evidence on shelter and health is thin. A 2022 review of shelters for displaced people found no clear guidance linking shelter quality to health, and called for more research.
A small EEG pilot: ten people. Participants viewed building images. Relative delta power fell as biophilic design rose. Relative alpha power showed no significant change.
A virtual reality test, 100 people. After a stress task, people in biophilic virtual offices recovered better, most in the first four of six minutes.
Long-term effects are unstudied. A 2023 paper says no study yet links stress-inducing architectural features to allostatic load. It proposes a longitudinal public health study.
What We Actually Know
Design cannot erase trauma. The article says it can stop compounding it. This is education, not medical or design advice. Sources are on the page linked in the post.

posts.title: Where she knew no one
posts.summary: In October 2026, RN Collins flew from Hawaii to the Netherlands for the first time, to a design week she had found by searching online, where she had met none of the people she had written to. Her camera caught her explaining why, again and again, to strangers who quickly stopped being strangers. Here is the trip in her own taped words, and the festival she walked into.

slides.alt: A close view of RN Collins looking up mid-sentence, a white curtain behind her. Slide text: "I just Googled what's going on in October in Netherlands." That is how she found Dutch Design Week.
An airport apron in early blue light, seen through the round window of a jet bridge. Slide text: First time in the Netherlands. First design week of any kind.

The Dutch Design Week desk under hanging PRESS and TOURS signs in a curtained lounge, a few people at the counter and blue sofas to the side. Slide text: Before she flew, she had emailed the festival's press office and some of the makers. She had met none of them in person.

Journalists with lanyards sit on wooden cubes in a lounge with curtains and ring lights, a water jug and a candle in front. Slide text: She came as accredited press, to a festival where she knew no one.

RN in a cream beanie and black hoodie talks at a wooden picnic table under a tree with a listener with long dreadlocks, in a sunny garden. Slide text: A storyteller, a researcher, a ceramicist and a technologist. "And so it felt like I could be a creative, or I could be an artist, you know?" she said on Sunday.

A staff member in a tan jacket and scarf, a paper cup in hand and a festival badge on a lanyard, stands talking with a seated person in a checked cap and headphones in a curtained lounge. Slide text: A festival staffer told her a visitor really needs a week.

Lines from Dutch Design Week's own press page: the 2026 edition was the 26th, under the theme R.A.W. (Rebel Authentic Worth), and over nine days around 2,500 designers showed their work across about 100 locations in Eindhoven. Slide text: 26th edition, 2,500+ designers, nine days.

posts.title: The Golf Balls Above Kaʻena Point Tracked America’s Early Satellite Programs
posts.summary: In 1959 the Air Force opened a tracking station on the ridge above Oʻahu's western tip. Its first job was a secret: helping bring film home from America's first photo satellites. The declassified histories, the newspapers of 1960 and the federal surveys of its buildings show what the station did, how it worked and how it changed.

slides.alt: A single white radome sits on a green ridge above the blue Pacific at Kaʻena Point Space Force Station, photographed in September 2022. It is the actual golf ball of the title, shown as it looks today, not in the CORONA era.
slides.credit: Photo: Brooke Wise, USSF, Public domain

slides.alt: A large white radome and a smaller one beside a dish antenna stand on a grassy ridge above the ocean at the Kaʻena Point Satellite Tracking Station, photographed in 2008. It shows the radomes the opening sentence describes.

Typed page 10 of the federal survey of the Kaʻena Point station, HAER HI-97. It lists the land's owners from the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi to the State and the Campbell Estate, with the Army and then the Air Force as lessees from 1958, and says the original site was land leased from the Territory of Hawaiʻi and private owners, 106 acres in 1958.

Typed Significance section of the federal survey, HAER HI-97 page 7. It says the station was established in 1958 to support the CORONA/Discoverer Satellite Program, that the nation's first satellite reconnaissance program was named Discoverer and became known by its codeword CORONA, and that the station, then known as HULA, supported it with data retrieval, tracking and relay.

The camera system built for the Discoverer and CORONA satellites on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2012: a long metal frame holding the camera and film machinery, with the gold capsule that brought the film back to Earth at its right end. It is the system that first returned photographs from orbit.

The CIA's line drawing titled Satellite Control Facility Operation in Recovery: three dashed satellite passes over Alaska, ENABLE commands from the control center and Vandenberg (STC, VTS) and a backup from Kodiak (KTS), Control arrows from the control center to the stations, and the Hawaii Tracking Station (HTS) at the bottom sending Control to a recovery plane near the capsule's impact point.
slides.credit: Source: CIA CORONA history, vol. 4, PD

slides.alt: Typed lines from page 229 of the NRO's declassification guide, section 5, Operations: MGS and RTS. Under Redact, item a reads: Redact specific details about the Mission Ground Station or Remote Tracking Station commands that were uplinked to the satellite, i.e., orbit adjustment, deorbit, camera operations, SIGINT payload operations, etc.
slides.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 229, PD

slides.alt: Typed list from page 52 of the NRO's declassification guide: Release fact that the following remote tracking stations supported DISCOVERER (CORONA) and/or SAMOS reconnaissance satellite programs, followed by ten sites from Annette Island, Alaska, to Vandenberg AFB, California, with Kaena Point, Hawaii, fourth.
slides.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 52, PD

slides.alt: Photograph of a CORONA parachute bag from the CIA Museum: an olive-green nylon pack with webbing straps and laced seams. It held the parachute that opened after the film capsule separated from the spacecraft and slowed it on the way down.
A black-and-white U.S. Air Force photograph of a C-119J Flying Boxcar towing a CORONA film capsule on its parachute after a midair catch. The photo is not identified as a Hawaiʻi recovery.
slides.credit: Source: U.S. Air Force, Public domain

A CORONA recovery vehicle, the gold-colored capsule shell that carried exposed film back through re-entry, on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2008. It is one of the very different machines in the chain of custody.

onScreen: The Golf Balls Above Kaʻena Point Tracked America’s Early Satellite Programs
From the Waiʻanae coast, the white radomes above Kaʻena Point look almost abstract: two geometric objects placed against a ridge.
In 1958, the United States Air Force began building what was then known as the HULA tracking station on land leased from the Territory of Hawaiʻi and private landowners.
Operations began in February 1959. Its initial mission supported Discoverer, the public-facing name associated with the classified CORONA reconnaissance-satellite program.
CORONA was the first American satellite program to return photographs from orbit.
Commands could concern orbit adjustments, camera operations and deorbit sequences.
CORONA exposed physical film in space. A reentry capsule separated from the spacecraft, descended toward Earth and deployed a parachute.
Recovery aircraft attempted to catch it in midair; ships could retrieve capsules that reached the ocean.
An official Air Force history of Kaʻena says aircraft from Hickam and ships from Pearl Harbor participated in recovery.
The capsule then had to move into secure processing and interpretation elsewhere. Kaʻena did not develop the film or interpret the photographs.
The first fully successful CORONA mission occurred in August 1960, after a string of failures that demonstrated how many systems had to work at once:
The station’s mission outlived CORONA. It became part of the Air Force Satellite Control Network and, in 2021, was renamed Kaʻena Point Space Force Station.

posts.summary: A faster pathway is not a lower bar. Breakthrough designation speeds development and review. Approval still asks for adequate and well-controlled investigations.

onScreen: Regulatory Clarity vs. Innovation Tension in Emerging Drug Classes A law-first look at FDA approval pathways, from Cannabis Law Report, Series 2 No. 2 of 20.
A faster pathway is not a lower bar. Breakthrough designation speeds development and review. Approval still asks for adequate and well-controlled investigations.

Substantial evidence has a statutory definition. Section 355(d) defines it as adequate and well-controlled investigations by qualified experts. FDA may accept one such study plus confirmatory evidence.

Accelerated approval rests on a surrogate endpoint. The effect must be reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Since 2022, FDA may use expedited procedures to withdraw approval if follow-up fails.
Trial design agreements are meant to hold. After testing begins, the written agreement changes only if the sponsor agrees in writing or a division director finds a substantial scientific issue.

FDA's August 8, 2024 letter named three issues. Reliable safety data. Durability beyond week 18. Bias, including prior MDMA use among participants. Psychotherapy questions were listed as not approvability issues.
FDA finalized its psychedelic trial guidance. Published July 14, 2026, it replaces the June 26, 2023 draft. Its recommendations are nonbinding.
The final guidance speaks to unblinding. It asks for blinded central raters, blinding and expectancy questionnaires, and says a factorial design may separate drug and psychotherapy effects.
Real-world evidence has a statutory hook. The 21st Century Cures Act, enacted December 13, 2016, required FDA to build a program. FDA published its framework notice on December 7, 2018.
Oregon has collected client data since January 1, 2025. Service centers collect client data and report totals to Oregon Psilocybin Services every quarter. Clients may opt out of submission.

onScreen: McDonald's Canada ran the same promotional idea twice, under two names. International Menu Heist in 2025, then World Menu Heist in 2026.
In June 2025, McDonald's Canada's International Menu Heist brought six items to Canada for a limited time, including Japan's Teriyaki Chicken Sandwich and Germany's Big Rösti burger.
The idea cast each item as a flavor taken in a “heist” from another country's McDonald's menu, Italy's McPizza Bites and Belgium's Biscoff McFlurry were also part of the 2025 lineup.
Then in August 2026, McDonald's Canada brought the idea back as World Menu Heist, with a new seven-item lineup including Australia's Chicken Parmi Burger and Spain's McExtreme Pulled Pork.
The 2025 and 2026 menus did not share a single item,
Japan's Teriyaki Chicken Sandwich never appeared alongside Australia's Chicken Parmi Burger.
Each year's campaign needs its own menu list, its own launch date and its own citation, 2025's International Menu Heist and 2026's World Menu Heist should never be cited as one continuous menu.

posts.title: After Hilo Had No Warning, Hawaiʻi Helped Build a Pacific One
posts.summary: On April 1, 1946, a wave from the Aleutian Islands reached Hilo almost five hours after it formed, and no one told the town it was coming. The reports, tide gauges and survivor accounts show what Hawaiʻi built next, and what a warning still cannot do on its own.

The facts, in numbers
Tide gauges could confirm abnormal sea-level movement. The Kahului, Maui, gauge as the 1957 tsunami arrived.
Museums, survivor accounts, school lessons, memorials and repeated drills preserve information the live sensor network cannot supply: what a confusing morning felt like, which cues people noticed,
why some instructions were trusted, where movement became impossible and how the coastline changed afterward.
In 1946, the Pacific had enough distance to permit a warning, but no institution capable of producing one.

onScreen: Designing for cognitive clarity Biophilic interiors and the science of mental recovery. From RN Collins's article, Journal of Biophilic Design, Issue 18.
The argument: a room can drain or restore. The article says clutter and glare keep the brain on alert, and daylight and natural textures help recovery. Next: the studies.
Walking in nature helped attention. In two experiments, walking in nature, or viewing nature pictures, improved directed attention on a backward digit-span task and the Attention Network Task.
The attention evidence is mixed. A review of 31 studies found support on three tasks and no marked effect in ten other analyses. What changes in attention is unclear.
A virtual reality test, 100 people. After a stress task, people in biophilic virtual offices recovered better from stress and anxiety, mostly in the first four of six minutes.

Sunlight and psychiatric stays. A 1996 paper reports sunny hospital rooms expedite recovery from severe depression. A 2001 paper reports morning sunlight shortened hospital stays in bipolar depression.
A Swedish psychiatric hospital study. A newer hospital with nine of ten stress-reducing features had fewer compulsory injections and half the restraints per restrained patient.
A theory for design choices. A 2010 paper applies salutogenic theory: people cope better when they can comprehend, manage and find meaning in a place. It cannot prove efficacy.
A design thesis on transitional housing. A 2024 Virginia Commonwealth University thesis asks how housing for women and children can support healing after domestic violence. A design project.
A Boston branch library, 2017. Utile designed a floor-to-ceiling wall covering for the children's reading room in the 2017 renovation of Boston's Jamaica Plain Branch Library.
What We Actually Know
We regulate inside our interiors. That is the article's closing idea. This is education, not medical or design advice. Sources are on the page linked in the post.

posts.title: c14-01 Steel guitar (Tech From Here, second run; its filmed Reel is the registry's c14-01 A; Hawaiian-language and cultural check before posting)
posts.summary: A boy from Lāʻie, a bar of polished steel and a new way to play the guitar. Old newspapers, discs, a patent and a Hawaiʻi law show how the sound left Oʻahu and how its name got lost along the way.

slides.alt: A handmade steel guitar in a Country Music Hall of Fame display case, shown with its museum label and a Milton Brown and His Musical Brownies poster. It opens the story because it puts a steel guitar inside country music, the place most listeners hear it.

A grainy 1912 newspaper halftone of Joseph Kekuku, seated in a pale suit and dark lei, both hands resting on an instrument laid flat across his lap, inside a printed frame. The Los Angeles Times printed it while he toured the mainland. It sits on the boundary slide because Kekuku is the name tied to the instrument, while the later accounts leave the first moment unrecoverable.

A halftone newspaper photograph of five men in matching white tunics with dark sashes, holding ukuleles and guitars, printed on page 6 of The Colville Examiner of July 22, 1916 under a headline about Hawaiian music at the Chautauqua; the article text names Kekuku's Hawaiian quintette. Cropped to the photograph from a full-resolution page image. It follows the boundary slide because the working life of a touring musician, not a single discovery, is where the story picks up.

Hawaiian steel guitarist Bobby Ingano seated on a folding chair on a cemetery lawn in Kāneʻohe, Oʻahu, in January 2024, a lap steel guitar flat across his knees and a small amplifier beside him, playing at the grave of the musician Gabby Pahinui. It shows a Hawaiian musician still performing the technique the slide names.
slides.credit: Photo: Michael Kiese / Puʻuloa Hawaiian Band, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.alt: Page 6 of The Original Guckert's Chords for the Hawaiian Steel Guitar, 1917: three chord grids for the key of C and, below, drawings of the steel bar held straight across the strings for C and slanted for F and G. It is an instruction book turning the technique into diagrams, the exact thing the slide says.
slides.credit: Page: Guckert, Union Music Co., 1917, PD, cropped

slides.alt: A Rickenbacker Electro B6 lap steel guitar from the late 1930s lying on a grey surface, photographed from above, with its chrome-covered horseshoe-magnet pickup set under the strings near the bridge. Commons describes it as having the Beauchamp horseshoe pickup. It shows the part the sentence names: the pickup that turns the vibration of the metal strings into an electrical signal for an amplifier.

A 1934 aluminum-cast Ro-Pat-In 'Frying Pan' electric lap steel guitar in a museum case at the Museum of Making Music. It is the instrument form the sentence describes, the lap steel tied to Beauchamp, Rickenbacker and the Ro-Pat-In company.

The 1931 one-piece maple prototype of the Rickenbacker Frying Pan electric lap steel guitar, a round solid body with a long neck and a pickup under the strings, standing in a glass display case with reflections and a museum label behind it. Commons credits its design to George Beauchamp, Paul Barth and Harry Watson. It is the kind of instrument the patent describes, an electrical stringed instrument with no conventional soundboard or resonance box. It is a photograph of the object, not of the patent.

Sheet 1 of the drawings for U.S. Patent 2,089,171, headed Aug. 10, 1937, G. D. Beauchamp, Electrical Stringed Musical Instrument, Filed June 2, 1934: the round solid body and long neck from the front, and the horseshoe magnet pickup under the strings. It is the patent's own drawing of an instrument with no sound hole or soundboard.

A 1938 Farm Security Administration photograph of a guitarist playing a steel-bodied guitar at a microphone during a Cajun band contest at the National Rice Festival in Crowley, Louisiana. It shows the technique far from Hawaiʻi, already part of another community's music.

posts.title: AI is leaving the screen
posts.summary: On Monday, October 19, 2026, Cities of Things presented its 2026 manifesto for designing with immersive AI at Stadslab Eindhoven, then sent plywood carts out onto the street with a person steering each one. RN Collins, an AI technologist, filmed the talk and the workshop. This piece reads the manifesto in full, sets it beside what the afternoon showed, and follows a second show in the same building that asks who gets a say.

slides.alt: A white flag printed with three stacked cubes and the words cities of things, pinned to a brown curtain. Slide text: Ten considerations for AI in rooms and streets.
A round sign reading stads lab in colored letters, in a white frame on a chipboard wall. Slide text: Cities of Things presented its 2026 manifesto at Stadslab during Dutch Design Week.

Iskander Smit of Cities of Things looks back at his slide, A rough timeline of generative AI, where the steps run from textual to agentic and end in physical. Slide text: Its argument: AI was leaving the screen and entering rooms and streets.

A screen slide listing five clusters: legibility interplay, intelligence is humble, design honesty, support community, provide openness. Slide text: Ten considerations in five clusters: legibility interplay, intelligence is humble, design honesty, support community, provide openness.

A talk slide titled Research, naming Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences, TU Delft and Cities of Things, with paper covers and small photos of field tests. Slide text: The manifesto page says it draws on conversations with more than 30 leading experts and seven years of applied research.

Hands hold a white two-stick radio transmitter over a square plywood deck on small black wheels, in a workshop with open tool cases; heather on a second cart shows at the bottom edge. Slide text: Then the workshop: a remote-controlled cart on a hoverboard and plywood.

On a brick path, a person at the left edge holds a white two-stick radio transmitter while a rider in black sits on a red seat on a plywood cart. Slide text: The carts were remote-controlled. Nobody pretended otherwise.

A plywood cart with a red chair and a box marked GIVE and TAKE waits in a corridor, beside an UPSTAIRS arrow sign and a panel titled Bewoners-in-the-loop, with a person reading it. Slide text: Same building, a second question: who decides? Bewoners-in-the-Loop's handbook listed 15 ideas, 18 experiments and 12 methods for involving residents.

posts.title: Why Human Review Requires Authority, Context and Time
posts.summary: Three public investigations looked at people placed beside automated systems: a test driver in Arizona, compliance officers in Australia and airline pilots over Indonesia and Ethiopia. Their reports show what each person could change, what each could see, and how many seconds or cases they were given.

slides.alt: The top of an NTSB table with columns for time to impact, speed, classification and path prediction, and system actions. At 5.6 seconds radar makes first detection of the pedestrian, classified as a vehicle; at 5.2 seconds lidar detects an unknown object.

Two rows of the NTSB table. At 1.2 seconds the bicycle is fully on the SUV's path, steering around it is no longer possible, and action suppression begins. At 0.2 seconds action suppression ends, and an auditory alert sounds.
A paragraph of NTSB report text saying that about five months before the crash the company began testing with one operator, removing a layer of safety redundancy and adding tasks for that operator.

A paragraph of report text: where compliance officers had been involved, the entire process would now be conducted online, the aim being to reduce (and preferably obviate) human involvement at the DHS end.

A red heading, 3.1 Staff concerns, above three paragraphs of report text. The last says that from around September 2015 compliance officers would no longer contact employers, and from January 2016 would no longer check a recipient's departmental file.
A paragraph of NTSB report text followed by four bullet points listing Boeing's assumptions, including that unexpected inputs are readily recognizable and that the pilot will take immediate action.

Three short paragraphs of guidance text. The middle one says oversight of a decision must be meaningful, rather than a token gesture, and carried out by someone with the authority and competence to change the decision.

onScreen: Uber's test car detected her 5.6 seconds before impact. It never decided what she was. The NTSB logged each change.
For one second, the system held back its own braking. No alert told the driver the pause had begun. Uber called it action suppression.
About five months earlier, Uber cut the second operator. The NTSB: that removed a layer of safety redundancy.
Robodebt aimed to reduce human involvement. And preferably to make it unnecessary, a Royal Commission found.
Officers stopped calling employers, then checking files. From September 2015 and January 2016.
Boeing assumed pilots would “take immediate action.” The NTSB found the crews did not respond that way.
Review counts only with authority to change the decision. Europe's data regulators, 2017 and 2018.

posts.title: Two strikes at once: where 'intersectionality' came from
posts.summary: The word began in a 1989 law review article about court cases. This is the story of those cases: five women laid off from a car plant, the judge who said their claim could not be "a combination of both," the courts that disagreed, and a hiring dispute at a law school in Honolulu.

slides.alt: Kimberlé Crenshaw in 2018, smiling and looking to one side, her hand under her chin, wearing a black top, silver necklaces and hoop earrings.
Seven lines of printed opinion text beginning Five black women have brought this action against their former employer, General Motors Corporation, and naming the United Automobile Workers Local 25.
Two facing typed pages of a bill with paper amendment slips attached, one typed and one handwritten, each with a round acceptance stamp.
A column of printed opinion text from The plaintiffs are clearly entitled to a remedy, through a new super-remedy, ending or alternatively either, but not a combination of both.
Seven lines of printed opinion text about creating a new classification of black women, ending clearly raises the prospect of opening the hackneyed Pandora's box.
A column of printed opinion text giving GM's hiring of black women by year, 155 of about 8,500 employees in late 1973, and 8,561 workers before the January 1974 layoffs and 6,378 after.

A column of printed opinion text beginning Recognition of black females as a distinct protected subgroup, ending the fact that black males and white females are not subject to discrimination is irrelevant.

posts.title: How a design-fiction workshop works
posts.summary: On Monday, October 19, 2026, RN Collins joined a Cities of Things workshop at Dutch Design Week, sat at one team's table for part of the afternoon and filmed the rest. Each table got a fixed, imagined 2050 future, a set of driver cards and a tray of LEGO. This piece follows the method step by step, and keeps every claim about 2050 with the person or team who made it.

slides.alt: A small LEGO figure holding a white bar and a green brick stands on a printed workshop canvas, beside the label CORE CAPABILITIES and yellow sticky notes. Slide text: What speculative design looked like at one table.

The Mobility Futures two-by-two chart on the presenter's screen: Mobility Patchwork, freedom meets friction, sits where market competition drives change and society is cautious about new technology. Slide text: Step 1: a fixed future. The table's was Mobility Patchwork, the TU Delft Mobility Futures (2025) scenario where markets lead and society is wary of new technology.

A strip of a printed workshop canvas reads 2050 is Mobility Patchwork, with tags for market-fragmented, unequal and fossil-fuel dependent. Slide text: The canvas described it as market-fragmented, unequal and fossil-fuel dependent.

A white card box lying on its side on a table, lettered The Work Kit of Design Fiction, a construction kit for imagining material cultural artifacts, by Near Future Laboratory. Slide text: Step 2: driver cards, then the Work Kit of Design Fiction from Near Future Laboratory.

Seen from above, a hand sets a small LEGO figure with a white visor bar on a blank workshop canvas, next to loose gray bricks and a sticky note with a drawing of glasses. Slide text: Step 3: build the object in LEGO.

Sticky notes on a workshop canvas: a pink note reads Happy Glasses, a yellow note reads Act above a pen drawing of a pair of glasses, and another reads wearable device. Slide text: One table's design fiction: 'Happy Glasses', an imagined wearable that would give 'social points' for acting.

A person in a navy T-shirt and jeans, seen from the chest down, holds a white radio controller over a robot made of taped cardboard boxes on a wheeled plywood base, on a patchwork carpet. Slide text: Step 4: share it. Then Cities of Things planned to take the robots into the street.

posts.title: The BILLY instructions and the creator brief
posts.summary: IKEA's assembly booklet for its BILLY bookcase hands a job to a stranger with almost no words. It lists the parts, orders the steps, marks the likely mistakes and ends with the bookcase fixed to a wall. A brief for a creator has the same job to do.

slides.alt: A finished IKEA BILLY bookcase in birch veneer standing against a wall at home, its shelves full of CDs and books, photographed in 2008. It is the finished object the instructions lead a stranger to, which is what the sentence describes.

Chart of what IKEA's BILLY booklet shows before step 1. Tools on page 6: flat screwdriver, cross-head screwdriver, pencil, hammer, measuring rule. Parts on page 7, each with its count: 16 wooden dowels, 12 cam bolts, 12 cam locks, 18 and 18 back-panel fasteners, 2 wall brackets with 2 screws and 4 washers, 16 shelf pins. Chart: RN Collins, from IKEA data.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from IKEA data

slides.alt: Chart of the BILLY booklet's twelve numbered steps in order, from 16 dowels into the shelf edges in step 1 to 4 loose shelves set on their pins in step 12; the frame is built lying down and raised in step 10. Chart: RN Collins, from IKEA data.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from IKEA data

slides.alt: Chart of every place the BILLY booklet draws a large X beside the right way: page 6, one person alone and boards on a hard floor; pages 7 and 14, a bookcase tipping over because it is not fixed to the wall; page 8, step 3, a panel turned the wrong way, shown twice; page 10, step 5, the end panel with its holes facing out. slides.alt: A tall white BILLY bookcase in a home in May 2020, standing upright with six shelves crammed with hardbacks and paperbacks. It is a finished BILLY doing its job, the finished state the card describes.

A narrow dark brown BILLY bookcase built and standing straight beside a door in August 2022, its shelves level, a row of books on one of them. It shows the finished state: the bookcase stands, aligns and works.

Chart setting the BILLY booklet beside a creator brief in four rows. Inputs: page 7's counted parts; in a brief, files, facts, allowed claims, rate and the disclosure line. Sequence: steps 1 to 12; in a brief, dates for draft, review, posting and take-down. Checks: the X marks at steps 3 and 5; in a brief, claims not to make and places a disclosure must not hide. Finished state: the cover drawing; in a brief, what the finished post looks like and how it is judged.

onScreen: IKEA’s BILLY bookcase instructions can guide a complete stranger from flat-pack parts to a finished bookcase without a single meeting.
They begin by showing the parts and tools before assembly starts.
Then each step arrives in a sequence the builder can follow.
Checks along the way prevent one early mistake from becoming the final result.
The finished state is visible:
the bookcase stands, aligns and works.
A creator brief works the same way: it’s the operating system that turns inputs, sequence and checks into a finished result anyone can build.
“Make it feel premium” hides a room full of unanswered decisions.

posts.title: Social points for reporting litter?
posts.summary: At a Cities of Things workshop during Dutch Design Week 2026, a slide offered "Social Credit System" as one possible force in an imagined future. Within the hour, one table had sketched glasses that reward people for reporting rubbish. This piece follows that idea from the slide to the sticky notes, then asks what research on rewards, clean streets and face-worn cameras says about its parts.

slides.alt: A workshop slide titled Political Driver with four teal text cards: Divided Societies, Pre-Crime Detection, Social Credit System and Polyarchy. The card pictures are blurred. Slide text: Political Driver: Social Credit System.

Two yellow sticky notes on the workshop canvas, handwritten: get social points for taking action, and, cut off at the top, ...ow to realize and take actions but also see happiness. These are the reward the quote on this slide describes. Slide text: That's how you're rewarded. Your glasses will show you it.

From above: the table's LEGO model, a figure in a white visor on a small street of white plates, sits on the blank workshop canvas beside a cut worksheet and loose dark plates, with a yellow chair at the edge. Slide text: It was a design exercise. The table's presenter called it "very feasible." Nothing on tape tested that.

A wall screen with the manifesto slide 4 support community and two points, Leverage Democratic Precedence and Ensure Distributed Sovereignty; the presenter leans toward the table beside a Cities of Things flag. Slide text: Who sets the points, and who gets to see them?

posts.title: A Right You Cannot Use
posts.summary: A check stopped before a hearing. A man crawled up courthouse stairs. A judge left one line on a form blank. Four Supreme Court cases show what turns a right on paper into a right a person can use.

slides.alt: Two columns of printed court opinion text side by side. The left says Angela Velez was cut off on March 11, 1968, because her husband allegedly visited every night, and that the tip came from her landlady and was untrue. The right says she and her four children were evicted before the decision.
slides.credit: Source: Kelly v. Wyman, 294 F. Supp. 893

slides.alt: A page of a 1970 Supreme Court opinion, headed 264, October Term, 1969, with a paragraph saying ending aid during a dispute may deprive an eligible person of the very means by which to live while he waits.
Opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying the delay between a hearing request and a decision is between 10 and 11 months and the full delay exceeds one year.

Printed federal regulation text headed section 404.1597a, in two stacked pieces, saying a person who wants benefits to continue must request reconsideration and continuation of benefits no later than 10 days after receiving the notice.

Opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying Lane was ordered to a second-floor courtroom with no elevator, crawled up two flights of stairs at his first appearance, and was later jailed for failure to appear.

Printed opinion text: the judge filled out a form titled Order for Contempt of Court with the line Defendant (was) (was not) gainfully employed and/or (had) (did not have) the ability to make these support payments when due, and left the statement as is.

Two columns of printed rule text side by side. The left begins section 303.6, Enforcement of support obligations, (c)(4) Establishing guidelines for the use of civil contempt citations. The right lists (i) screen the case for ability to pay, (ii) provide the court with that information, and (iii) provide clear notice that ability to pay constitutes the critical question.

Bar chart with four bars on a scale of 0 to 100 percent: 25 percent of serious problems got a search for legal help, 92 percent got no or not enough help, 46 percent of non-seekers named cost, and 49 percent of legal aid requests were turned away.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from LSC data

onScreen: New York cut off Angela Velez's welfare in 1968. The tip was false. Her family was evicted before she won.
In 1970 the Supreme Court said: hold the hearing first. A cutoff can take the means to live while a person waits.
By 1976, disability appeals took more than a year. The Court still did not require a hearing before the cutoff.
Since 1983, benefits can continue during an appeal. Ask within 10 days of the notice, Social Security's rule says.
George Lane crawled up two flights of stairs to reach court. The courthouse had no elevator. In 2004 the Court let his ADA suit go on.
The judge left the ability-to-pay line blank. He got 12 months in jail. The Supreme Court said that broke due process.
Since 2016, a federal rule requires a clear notice. Child support agencies must tell a parent that ability to pay is the critical question.
Too little or no legal help for 92% of serious problems. Low-income Americans, in a 2022 Legal Services Corporation study.

posts.title: Biophilic Design and Climate Change
posts.summary: Heat and mental health: 114 studies. A 2023 review: heatwaves went with 9.7% more hospital attendance or admission for mental illness (three studies). Much of the evidence was low certainty.

slides.alt: The title block of RN Collins's article Biophilic Design and Climate Change, subtitled Rethinking Mental Health infrastructure in a warming world, from Journal of Biophilic Design Issue 21, on her own site.
slides.credit: Source: RN Collins, JBD Issue 21 web text

slides.alt: Bar chart from Thompson and colleagues' 2023 review of 114 studies: hospital attendance or admission for mental illness rose 9.7 percent on heatwave days and 2 percent at the 99th versus 50th percentile of daily temperature; a 10 degree rise showed no significant association.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Thompson 2023 data

slides.alt: The National Weather Service Phoenix page Historical Extreme Temperatures in Phoenix, Yuma, and El Centro: a table in which the Phoenix column lists the longest stretch of 100 degree days as 113 (May 27 to September 16, 2024) and of 110 degree days as 31 (June 30 to July 30, 2023).

Page 1 of Baecker and colleagues, Impacts of extreme heat on mental health (2025): the title and abstract, which says four of 241 articles were eligible and gave limited evidence on stress, exercise and sleep.

Page 1 of Pihkala, Anxiety and the Ecological Crisis (Sustainability, 2020): the title and abstract, which says uncertainty, unpredictability and uncontrollability matter and most forms of eco-anxiety appear non-clinical.

Figure 3a of Hoffman, Shandas and Pendleton (2020): land surface temperature against the city average by HOLC grade across 108 US urban areas; grade A areas run cooler and redlined grade D areas warmest.

Page 1 of Hsu, Sheriff, Chakraborty and Manya, Disproportionate exposure to urban heat island intensity across major US cities (Nature Communications, 2021): the title, authors and abstract, which reports that the average person of color lives in a census tract with higher surface heat island intensity in all but 6 of the 175 largest urbanized areas.

Page 1 of Aram, Higueras Garcia, Solgi and Mansournia, Urban green space cooling effect in cities (Heliyon, 2019): the title and abstract, which reports the greatest cooling distance and intensity for large urban parks of more than 10 hectares.

Parc de Diagonal Mar in Barcelona's Sant Martí district, one of the parks in the Barcelona green-gentrification study: a lake crossed by steel pipe sculptures, trees, and new residential towers of Illa del Bosc behind it, May 2016.
The Tampines Park Connector in Singapore, part of the Park Connector Network, running through Sun Plaza Park as a paved walking and cycling path beside planted greenery.

The City of Portland page for Binding City Policy ENB-4.19, Green Streets Policy and Green Streets Cross-Bureau Phase 2 Report, showing its title and the first findings, which say 60 to 70 percent of Portland stormwater comes from paved streets and runoff directed from private property.
Page 7 of Baecker and colleagues (2025): the discussion says only four studies tested how heat harms mental health and that, taken together, the evidence base is lacking.
The Path Forward, the closing section of RN Collins's article on her own site, ending: the design ambition is to help people recover as well as endure.

onScreen: Biophilic design and climate change Rethinking mental health infrastructure in a warming world. From RN Collins's article, Journal of Biophilic Design, Issue 21.
Heat and mental health: 114 studies. A 2023 review: heatwaves went with 9.7% more hospital attendance or admission for mental illness (three studies). Much of the evidence was low certainty.
Phoenix heat data. The National Weather Service lists 31 straight days at 110°F or higher (June 30 to July 30, 2023) and 113 straight at 100°F or higher in 2024.
How heat harms the mind is thin. A 2025 review found only four eligible studies. They gave limited evidence for stress-axis activation, stress, less exercise and sleep disruption.
Climate anxiety is mostly non-clinical. Pihkala's 2020 analysis finds uncertainty, unpredictability and uncontrollability seem to matter in eco-anxiety, and that most forms appear non-clinical.
Redlined blocks run hotter. Across 108 US urban areas, formerly redlined neighborhoods were 2.6°C warmer on average, by as much as 7°C, in 94% of areas.
Unequal heat. In 175 large US urban areas, the average person of color lived in a tract with higher surface heat island intensity than non-Hispanic whites in all but 6.
Big parks cool more. A 2019 review of urban green space cooling studies found the greatest cooling distance and intensity for large parks over 10 hectares.
Greening can gentrify. A study of 18 Barcelona green spaces found signs of green gentrification in the old town and former industrial areas; elsewhere, vulnerable residents increased.
Singapore plans 500 km of connectors. NParks says it aims for 500 km of park connectors by 2030 so every household is within a 10-minute walk of a park.

Portland's green streets. Council adopted a binding Green Streets Policy on April 18, 2007. It says 60 to 70% of Portland's stormwater comes from paved streets and runoff gathered in the public right of way.
What We Actually Know
Recovery is a prerequisite. The article's closing idea: minds and bodies must recover from repeated heat. This is education, not medical or design advice.

posts.title: An anatomist reads a radio remote
posts.summary: On October 19, 2026, at Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, two plywood carts crossed a brick square with a person and a radio transmitter beside each one. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, filmed the transmitters and the hands that held them. This piece reads the remote first, then the thumb that works it, from its bones to the tendons at the wrist.

slides.alt: A white radio transmitter with two control sticks and red-tipped switches lies on a yellow bag over a green cutting mat. Its small screen reads FLY MODE OFF. Slide text: An anatomist reads a radio remote.

A gray-haired rider, seen from behind, rides a plywood cart with a red seat and a cardboard box down a brick street past parked cars. Slide text: At Dutch Design Week, Cities of Things took neighborhood carts into the street. They were remote-controlled, built on a hacked hoverboard under a plywood deck.

Black-and-white anatomical drawing from Gray's Anatomy, 1918, cropped to the wrist bones and the base of a thumb, with red outlines labeled opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis and adductor pollicis obliquus where those muscles attach. Slide text: Four thenar muscles form the pad at the base of your thumb.

Anatomical drawing from Gray's Anatomy, 1918, figure 426, The muscles of the thumb: opponens pollicis, in red, runs from the transverse carpal ligament to the thumb's metacarpal, with the two heads of adductor pollicis below it. Slide text: Opposition: opponens pollicis moves the thumb across the palm to the other fingers.

Anatomical drawing from Gray's Anatomy, 1918, figure 419, cropped to the back of the forearm: the muscles labeled abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis longus run down toward the wrist. Slide text: Three forearm muscles straighten (extend) the thumb: extensor pollicis longus and brevis, and abductor pollicis longus.

Two hands hold a white radio remote beside a plywood cart with a red seat, a cardboard box and a bottle, on brick paving; the rider is seen from behind. Slide text: Two hands, one thumb resting on a stick, one plywood cart. Shown by Cities of Things at Stadslab and the NRE site.

posts.title: Model Regulatory Framework for State Psilocybin Programs
posts.summary: Three states, three different programs. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico answered the same questions in their own ways.

slides.alt: The head of Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 475A, Psilocybin Regulation, 2025 edition, from the Oregon Legislature's site: the chapter title and the start of its list of sections.
Page 1 of Colorado Senate Bill 23-290 as signed, Concerning Natural Medicine, with its sponsors and the start of Section 1, one of the three state programs the slide compares.

Page 35 of Colorado Senate Bill 23-290: the state licensing authority must work with the Division of Professions and Occupations in the Department of Regulatory Agencies on an annual report, the two regulators that split Colorado's program.
The section list of ORS chapter 475A: the headings for the license to manufacture psilocybin products (ORS 475A.290), to operate a service center (475A.305) and to facilitate services (475A.325).
Oregon Administrative Rule 333-333-3050, Psilocybin Training Program Core Requirements: from January 1, 2025, core training of at least 128 hours of instruction.

Page 2 of New Mexico Senate Bill 219 (2025): a qualified patient is one diagnosed with a qualifying condition, and the list begins with major treatment-resistant depression and posttraumatic stress disorder.
ORS 475A.305(2)(d) and (e): a service center must not be within the limits of an incorporated city or town and zoned exclusively for residential use, and not within 1,000 feet of a school.
ORS 475A.350, Client information form: before an administration session the client must complete and sign a client information form.

ORS 475A.372: a service center operator compiles, for each three-month period, the number of clients served, administration sessions and adverse reactions, for a quarterly submission to the Oregon Health Authority.
ORS 475A.215: the Oregon Psilocybin Services Act may not be construed to require a person to violate a federal law or to exempt a person from a federal law.
ORS 475A.235, General powers and duties: the Oregon Health Authority holds the duties, functions and powers of the program, the one agency in charge in Oregon.
Page 6 of New Mexico Senate Bill 219: the Department of Health shall collaborate with the board, universities and providers and, by December 31, 2027, implement the program.

Psilocybe azurescens, a psilocybin mushroom, in a field photograph from November 4, 2024 at Fort Stevens State Park on the Oregon coast: two caramel brown caps on long pale stems among conifer needles and leaf litter, one tipped to show its dark gills. Psilocybin, the substance these state programs regulate, is made by this fungus and its relatives.
The last page of Colorado Senate Bill 23-290: the safety clause and the signatures of the Senate president, House speaker, their clerks and Governor Jared Polis, approved May 23, 2023.

onScreen: Model Regulatory Framework for State Psilocybin Programs Six design questions for legislators.
Three states, three different programs. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico answered the same questions in their own ways.
Question 1: who runs it? Oregon puts one health agency in charge. New Mexico uses its Department of Health. Colorado splits the work between two regulators.
Question 2: which licenses exist? Oregon's statute names manufacturer, service center, facilitator and testing laboratory licenses. The article proposes six types.
Question 3: how much training? Oregon's rules now require 128 hours of core instruction and 40 hours of practicum. The article proposes a 150-hour floor.
Question 4: who can get services? Oregon sets no diagnosis rule. New Mexico requires a qualifying condition. The article proposes two tracks, clinical and general.
Where a center may sit is a statute question. ORS 475A.305 ties service center location to city limits and residential zoning. The article proposes setbacks from sensitive places instead.
Question 5: what must clients be told? Oregon requires a signed client information form before any session. The article proposes written disclosure of risks, credentials and the right to withdraw.
Question 6: what gets counted? Oregon requires service centers to report quarterly on clients served, sessions and adverse reactions. The article says new programs should build that in from launch.
All of it sits under federal law. Oregon's statute does not exempt anyone from federal law. The article flags section 280E for session-fee businesses as unresolved.

posts.title: Case-based learning, with LEGO
posts.summary: At a Cities of Things workshop during Dutch Design Week 2026, small tables were handed a fixed future, asked to name the forces in it, given LEGO to build an object and then asked to present it. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, joined one table for part of the afternoon and filmed the rest. This piece sets those four steps beside the way medicine has taught from cases since 1900, and reports what education research says about each one.

slides.alt: A printed journal column from 1900 headed THE CASE METHOD OF TEACHING SYSTEMATIC MEDICINE, by W. B. Cannon, Student, Harvard Medical School, above the paper's first paragraph. Slide text: Four moves a design-fiction workshop shares with medicine's case method.

Ten lines of a printed 1900 journal column comparing a medical society's case papers with the proposed case system, in which the students must speak from a common study of the same hospital reports. Slide text: Fix the scenario. The workshop handed each table a 2050 scenario already written. In 1900, Walter Cannon wanted a case class to argue from the same printed hospital reports.

Two numbered paragraphs from a 1906 book on case teaching; the second reads: 5. We can teach the student how to group isolated symptoms into well-knit diagnoses. Slide text: Name the drivers. Driver cards asked each table to name the forces shaping its future. Cabot's 1906 case book set out to teach students to group symptoms into a diagnosis.

Seen from above, a hand holds a half-built LEGO figure with a yellow head, a green brick and a white bar like a visor over a blank sheet, with loose gray LEGO plates beside it and a yellow sticky note with a drawing of glasses. Slide text: Make something. Each table built a LEGO object in a timed round against the clock. A case can ask learners to make something, too.

Eight lines of a printed 1900 journal column: the instructor first calls upon one of the students to state the case, on another to analyze the symptoms and venture a diagnosis, on another to present the differential points, on still another to suggest treatment. Slide text: Share the thing. A presenter from each table stood and explained the object to the room. In Cannon's 1900 case conference, students stated the case and argued it out loud.

A Cities of Things talk slide titled Future research for scenarios, showing the cover and pages of the Mobility Futures report that the workshop's scenarios were based on. Slide text: Workshop by Cities of Things at Dutch Design Week 2026. Scenarios based on TU Delft's Mobility Futures (2025).
