posts.title: Independent Oversight Structures for Psychedelic Service Centers
posts.summary: Advisory boards advise. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico each have one. In each state the agency, not the board, holds the licensing power.

slides.alt: The Oregon Health Authority's page for the Oregon Psilocybin Advisory Board: established by ORS 475A, the board makes recommendations to OHA; members are appointed by the Governor.
ORS 475A.230, Duties of Oregon Psilocybin Advisory Board: the board shall provide advice and make recommendations to the Oregon Health Authority.
OHA's rulemaking page: the rulemaking process is informed by recommendations from the Oregon Psilocybin Advisory Board, rules advisory committees and public comment.

OAR 333-333-6150, Inspections: the authority may inspect a licensed premises at any time, unannounced when necessary, and will not inspect client areas during sessions unless needed to prevent a serious danger.
OAR 333-333-5120(10) and (11): a facilitator shall not engage in any romantic relationship, sexual contact or sexual intimacy with a client during services or for one year after the last service.
Oregon's psilocybin rules on sanctions: civil penalties under ORS 475A.513 and the five violation categories, Category I to IV by risk and Category V for data reporting under OAR 333-333-4910.
ORS 475A.498: a client may purchase, possess and consume a psilocybin product only at a psilocybin service center and only under the supervision of a facilitator.
Page 1 of the May 30, 2025 opinion and order in Cusker v. Oregon Health Authority, District of Oregon: the plaintiffs allege a Title II ADA violation, and the defendants' motion to dismiss is denied.

onScreen: Independent Oversight Structures for Psychedelic Service Centers Who watches the service center?
Advisory boards advise. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico each have one. In each state the agency, not the board, holds the licensing power.
Oregon's board recommends. OHA decides. OHA says its rulemaking is informed by board recommendations, committees and public comment. It then writes a letter explaining its decisions.
Oregon can inspect at any time. Rules allow inspection of a licensed premises at any time, unannounced when necessary. Client areas stay off limits during sessions unless danger is serious.
Oregon's rules bar sexual contact with clients. That covers every session and one year after a client's last service.

OHA can suspend, revoke or fine. The rules sort violations into five categories: four by risk, one for data reporting. A revocation or refusal to renew generally goes through a contested case under ORS chapter 183.
Where a center may sit shapes who can reach it. ORS 475A.305 ties location to city limits and residential zoning. Consumption is allowed only at a licensed center.

posts.title: The robots run on people
posts.summary: On October 19, 2026, two plywood carts rolled through a Dutch Design Week workshop in Eindhoven, and a person with a radio walked beside each one. The carts made no secret of it. This piece follows those operators, then the people behind other street machines: a hidden chess player, a driver dressed as a car seat, remote helpers for robotaxis, and the workers who plot routes for delivery robots.

slides.alt: Iskander Smit kneels on a low plywood platform on wheels in a maker space, holding a radio remote, beside workbenches and a 3D printer. Slide text: The robot ran on people. A person with a remote did the steering.

Iskander Smit of Cities of Things smiles from the seat of a plywood cart in a hall, while an operator in a white shirt stands behind him holding the white radio transmitter that drives it. Slide text: "There's no sensors, it's just humans." Iskander Smit, Cities of Things.

Two plywood carts coupled end to end on brick paving, one with a red chair and one with cardboard boxes, each riding on black hoverboard wheels. Slide text: The Wijkbot: a hacked hoverboard under a plywood deck.
Two hands hold a white two-stick radio transmitter at the right, while Iskander Smit stands behind among workbenches. Slide text: Steered with one stick on a radio. Open-source firmware.

An operator's hands hold a white radio transmitter in the foreground, while ahead Iskander Smit rides a plywood cart with a red seat across a brick square past parked cars. Slide text: Remote-controlled, by a person.
An operator in a striped shirt holds a white radio remote and presses a button beside the blue doors of a freight lift. Slide text: Who is helping whom? The question the afternoon left.

posts.title: Shoes with archaeological heels
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, a pair of black pumps stood on heels of weathered oak, each marked with a find number. This is what the excavation documents, the museum entries and the Dutch rules on keeping finds can tell us about them, and what they cannot.

slides.alt: A black leather pump on a plinth with a heel of dark, weathered wood, seen from behind, with a second shoe beside it. It is from TERRA FIRMA by Judith Sanders. Slide text: Shoes with archaeological heels.

A white display case under an acrylic cover with rows of small round dishes of ground and broken material in browns, reds and grays, and a drawer of colored cards below. Slide text: EX SITU gave nine makers archaeological finds that museums did not keep, including mammoth bone.

A black leather pump with a heel of weathered wood, painted with the numbers 7074 and 7144, in an acrylic case, with a brown sneaker of patched old leather in a second case and the EX SITU title wall behind. Slide text: Judith Sanders cut these heels from oak the show said held up a Roman road in 125 AD.
slides.credit: Photo: B. Bollmann / Dutch Design Week

posts.title: Between Lights
posts.summary: Teresa van Dongen's Between Lights put solar harvesting where people look. The published numbers on see-through solar cells show what that costs, and what the public documents leave open.

slides.alt: The designer's visualization of Between Lights: a three-pane window looking out over a lake and hills, with a band of blue square modules patterned with yellow diamonds running across all three panes, above a window seat with cushions and candles. It is a visualization from the press kit, not a photograph of the installation. Slide text: A window that makes power by day and light by night. Teresa van Dongen's Between Lights, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, as she pictured it.
slides.credit: Image: Teresa van Dongen, DDW press kit

slides.alt: A gloved hand holding a small square organic solar cell of the polymer-blend kind, a reddish, partly see-through glass slide with rows of round silver contacts. It is a lab-scale cell of the kind the festival text names; it is not Between Lights. Slide text: Its panels used organic solar cells, which can be printed thin. They collected sunlight and indoor light, the festival text said.

Bar chart of two see-through lab solar cells. The color-neutral cell let 43.3 percent of visible light through and turned 8.1 percent of sunlight into power; the green-tinted cell 45.7 and 10.8 percent. Slide text: A see-through solar cell trades view for power. In a 2020 lab test, one cell let 43 percent of visible light through and turned 8 percent of sunlight into power.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from PNAS 2020 data

slides.alt: Bar chart of yearly output in a Dutch test: a south panel tilted at about 35 degrees is 100, an upright south-facing panel about 70, and an upright panel turned 60 degrees east or west about 65. Slide text: A window also faces the sun at a poor angle. In a Dutch test, upright south-facing panels made about 70 percent of a tilted panel's yearly power.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Hanze 2019 data

slides.alt: A microscope view of the pointed tip of a Canadian pondweed leaf, its cells packed with green chloroplasts along a central vein, against a black background. Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens; it is not Between Lights. Slide text: The designer named photosynthesis as her inspiration. Over a year, plants turn about 1 to 2 percent of sunlight into biomass, a U.S. energy lab said in 2011.

Bar chart of typical indoor light levels from a 2021 review: homes about 200 lux, offices about 500 lux and workshops about 1,500 lux; sunlight is about 1,000 times stronger. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: The panels collected sunlight and indoor light, and lit LEDs at dusk. What we don't: How much power that made, how much was stored, how long the LEDs ran.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from ChemSusChem data

slides.alt: The Klokgebouw at Strijp-S in Eindhoven under a blue sky: a white former Philips factory block with a clock tower. It is the building where Between Lights was shown. Slide text: Would you trade some of your view for your own power? Between Lights was shown in the Klokgebouw, Eindhoven, at Dutch Design Week 2026.

posts.title: The Lab Rules
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi has posted eight versions of its medical cannabis rules since 2015. Here is what the lab must look for today, what happens to a batch that fails, and why every licensed product in the state passes through one lab on Oʻahu.

slides.alt: The summary page that opens the Department of Health's adoption of Chapter 11-850, Hawaii Administrative Rules, dated December 7, 2015, which says the chapter, entitled "Medical Marijuana Dispensaries," is adopted.

Appendix I of the compiled chapter 11-850 effective November 17, 2025, showing Table 6, microbial contaminants that must not be detected in one gram: Escherichia coli, Salmonella species and four Aspergillus species, above Table 7 for mycotoxins.

The text of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-8, Laboratory standards and testing; laboratory certification, with the list of what the Department shall do when setting standards, including considering the retail cost to the qualifying patient.

Page 850-49 of the 2015 rules: moisture content under 15 percent, then microbiological impurities with count limits for total viable aerobic bacteria, yeast and mold, coliforms and bile-tolerant bacteria, then E. coli and Salmonella not detected in 1 g and limits for three Aspergillus species.

Page 850-106 of the Ramseyer version effective February 24, 2022. Deleted count groups are struck through, and an underlined lead-in reads "The following microbial contaminants, which must not be detected in one gram," followed by E. coli, Salmonella and four Aspergillus species.

Part of the Department of Health's executive summary of major changes to chapter 11-850, under Testing: revised microbial contaminants list, allow non-plating methods, and a change from moisture content to water activity for cannabis.
The Department's one-page summary of changes effective April 29, 2022, with a bullet on laboratory analysis that says to remove Aspergillus terreus from the microbial contaminants list.

The Department's list of amendments effective November 17, 2022, item 4 on laboratory testing, which adds Aspergillus terreus and replaces the water activity or moisture content language with water activity alone.

Section 11-850-135(c) of the compiled chapter 11-850 effective November 17, 2025, where item (E) refers to the microbial contaminants listed in Table 6 in Appendix I, which must not be detected in one gram of cannabis or manufactured cannabis product.
The Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation page titled Certified Cannabis Testing Facilities, with the statute excerpt on transporting samples and a list that shows one laboratory.

Two callouts from OMCCR's July 2024 newsletter guide to reading a certificate of analysis: foreign matter, and microbials, which says contaminants must not be detected in one gram of cannabis or manufactured cannabis product. Part of the sample certificate beside them is cut off.

Page 2 of the Department's Medical Cannabis Testing Facility Application, with the microbiology boxes for E. coli, Salmonella species and four Aspergillus species, and a section on ISO 17025 accreditation status.
The Department's web page listing every posted version of chapter 11-850, from December 2015 through November 2025, with links to the rules and to the lists of changes.

Page 850-115 of the compiled chapter 11-850: paragraph (i) of section 11-850-135 on disposing of a batch that does not conform, under video surveillance within thirty days, with the quarantine rule and the start of the section's history note.

Before and after 2015: count limits for four microbe groups. Today: six named organisms that must not be detected in one gram.
The statute sets the frame HRS 329D-8 tells the Department to set testing standards and certify labs, and to consider the cost to the patient.
2015: counts and a short list Rule 11-850-85 set count limits for four groups. It also required no pathogenic E. coli or Salmonella in a gram.
February 24, 2022: counts out The count limits were struck. A not-detected list took over: E. coli, Salmonella and four Aspergillus species.
The Department's two lines Its summary says: revised microbial contaminants list, allow non-plating methods. It gives no reason.

posts.title: Soil, land, 'up to'
posts.summary: A sign at Dutch Design Week 2026 said that 40% of the world's soils are degraded. RN Collins photographed it on a press tour. This piece follows the number back through UN reports, a 1990 world map and a 2000 farm study, and asks the question every percentage needs: of what?

slides.alt: A black sign on a red frame reading of global soils are degraded. Due to intensive farming practices, with the top of a large red 40% cut off, over a red box of loose dark soil holding clear acrylic plates. Adults stand behind. Slide text: Soil, land, 'up to'. Three words that change a statistic.

Inside a large industrial hall with a steel roof: a ring of hanging white curtains under a round lighting truss, spotlights, iron columns and a row of white stands in the distance. Slide text: Where the sign stood: the Secrid Talent Podium in Eindhoven's Klokgebouw, beside Aeropod, a soil capsule by Lu Afolayan and Ocean Hu of Muju Earth.

posts.title: Can the Institution Be Answered?
posts.summary: A computer called workers cheats and no person checked. Teachers could not test their own scores. An agency left airbags out of its reasons. A cabinet memo gave a reason the Supreme Court found contrived. Four disputes show what it takes to answer an institution, and to make it answer back.

slides.alt: A page of a 2019 federal appeals court opinion with two paragraphs: from October 2013 to August 2015 the system alone decided fraud and no human being took part, and the questionnaires went to online accounts, many of them dormant.
slides.credit: Source: Cahoo v. SAS Analytics (6th Cir.)

slides.alt: Printed court opinion text quoting a questionnaire: a yes or no question about giving false information, then eight numbered reasons starting with I needed the money, and a sentence saying the form gave no information about why the agency suspected fraud.
slides.credit: Source: Cahoo v. SAS Analytics (6th Cir.)

slides.alt: Bar chart with three bars on a 0 to 100 percent scale: 85 percent of fraud findings made by the computer alone reversed, 44 percent of findings sent to staff reversed, and, for comparison, 41 percent of all appeals reversed or changed by judges.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Michigan UIA data

slides.alt: Two pieces of a printed state law joined by a thin gray line: the heading Act No. 226, Public Acts of 2017, approved by the Governor December 20, 2017, then subsection (m) saying the agency shall not make a determination based solely on a computer-identified discrepancy, and enacting sections giving July 1, 2018.

Scanned court opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying trade secrets do not let a school district violate its employees' rights, and that the proper remedy is to overturn the policy while leaving the trade secrets intact.
slides.credit: Source: HFT v. Houston ISD (S.D. Tex.)

slides.alt: Two pieces of a 1983 Supreme Court page, 48, October Term 1982, joined by a thin gray line: the heading, then lines saying the agency did not even consider requiring airbags in its 1981 rulemaking and that not one sentence of its statement discusses the airbags-only option.

Three pieces of a 2019 Supreme Court page headed Department of Commerce v. New York, 28, joined by thin gray lines: the heading, lines saying the sole stated reason seems to have been contrived, and the closing words what was provided here was more of a distraction.
slides.credit: Source: Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752

slides.alt: A table row from a federal technical report headed NIST AI 100-1, AI RMF 1.0, reading MEASURE 3.3: feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes are established.

onScreen: Michigan's computer decided unemployment fraud with no person involved. That is what people suing said of 2013 to 2015, and a federal court took it as true.
Flagged workers got two questions and ten days to answer. The form never said why the agency suspected them.
When the agency rechecked in 2017, it reversed 85% of computer-only fraud findings. Where an investigator took part, it reversed 44%.
Michigan's law bars fraud findings based only on a computer mismatch. An agency employee must examine the facts first. This version applied from July 2018.
Houston rated teachers with scores no teacher could check. In 2017 a federal judge said the remedy was to overturn the policy and leave the trade secrets intact.
In 1983 the Supreme Court found a safety agency never considered requiring airbags. "Not one sentence of its rulemaking statement discusses the airbags-only option."
In 2019 the Court said the census question's stated reason "seems to have been contrived." It sent the decision back to the agency.
A 2023 federal framework lists ways for people to appeal what an AI system decides. NIST calls the framework voluntary.

onScreen: Civil Rights Safeguards in Psychedelic Service Delivery Models A law-first look at access, disability, data and Indigenous rights, from Cannabis Law Report, Series 2 No. 5 of 20.
Who gets in is a civil rights question. In 2025, 1,652 of the 2,825 clients who gave an income bracket reported household income above $95,375.
A federal court let the ADA claim proceed. On May 30, 2025 the court denied Oregon's motion to dismiss, saying the remedy rests on physical access, not drug distribution.
It is still an early-stage case. On March 17, 2026 the court again let the facilitators' ADA claim proceed but ruled one plaintiff lacked standing. No merits ruling.
Title II of the ADA covers public entities. 42 U.S.C. 12132: no qualified individual with a disability may be excluded from or denied the benefits of a public entity's services.

Oregon logged 258 denials in 2025. Reasons include ineligibility (147) and requests outside a center's business model (94). The summary does not say whether any denial raised a discrimination question.
Clients can opt out of data submission. On the 2025 race and ethnicity question, 387 clients chose "don't want to answer." Clients may also opt out of submission altogether.
A UN declaration names traditional medicines. Article 24 of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples recognizes a right to traditional medicines and health practices.

Oregon law already names an enforcer. ORS 659A.403 bars discrimination in places of public accommodation. ORS 659A.800 gives the Bureau of Labor and Industries general jurisdiction over unlawful practices.
The article proposes eleven safeguards. They include a sliding-scale session target, aggregate-only data reporting, an 18-month retention limit and an independent civil rights monitor.

posts.title: License or buyout?
posts.summary: In 1984 a film producer ordered special effects shots, and no one said a word about who would own them. The court case that followed, and four others like it, show what a payment buys, what it leaves behind, and why the answer belongs on paper before the work travels.

slides.alt: Larry Cohen, left, beside Merv Bloch outside the Gartenbaukino cinema in Vienna during the Viennale film festival, October 26, 2010, under a white sign with red letters. In 1984 Cohen ordered special effects shots for his film The Stuff with no written deal about who would own them.

Page 3 of the U.S. Copyright Office's Circular 30, Works Made for Hire, under the heading Specially Ordered or Commissioned Works: four tests a commissioned work must meet to be made for hire, ending with the line that a work failing any of them is not a work made for hire.
slides.credit: Image: U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 30, page 3, public domain

slides.alt: The Transfer of Copyright Ownership paragraph from page 3 of the Copyright Office's Circular 1: a transfer generally must be in writing and signed by the owner, and transferring a right on a nonexclusive basis does not require a written agreement.
slides.credit: Image: U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 1, page 3, public domain

slides.alt: The Copyright Act's definition of a transfer of copyright ownership, from section 101 of Title 17: an assignment, mortgage, exclusive license or other conveyance, but not including a nonexclusive license.
slides.credit: Image: U.S. Code, Title 17, section 101, via GovInfo, public domain

slides.alt: Page 489 of the Supreme Court's 2001 opinion in New York Times Co. v. Tasini: the publishers engaged the freelance writers under contracts that in no instance secured consent to placing an article in an electronic database.

slides.alt: The cover of an early printed edition of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring for piano four hands. Stravinsky licensed the music to Disney in 1939 for one motion picture, and his publisher later sued over whether that wording reached videocassettes.

onScreen: Wood: the multisensory, physiological magician A look at the research behind wood and the nervous system. From RN Collins's column, Journal of Biophilic Design, Issue 22.
Real findings, honest limits. The column says direct experiments remain limited on long-term exposure and optimal wood proportions. The frames show what the cited sources support.
Stress is an ongoing assessment. McEwen and Akil (2020): the stress system continually assesses the environment, and ongoing overload can harm brain health and raise risk for depression.
Forest research in Japan. A review by Tsunetsugu, Park and Miyazaki summarizes forest-bathing studies by the five senses, including the odor of wood and the sound of running water.
Rooms with different wood. A 2007 study compared how rooms with different wood quantities affect the body. The column cites 45% against 90% coverage.
Classroom noise matters. A 2003 review covers speech intelligibility in classrooms, effects of noise on children's academic performance, and classroom noise levels. It does not test wood.
Buildings and emissions. IPCC's 2022 buildings chapter puts buildings at 12 GtCO2-eq in 2019, 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and 31% of global CO2 emissions.
Wood can store carbon. 50 case buildings, four European scenarios: wooden construction could capture 1 to 55 Mt of CO2 a year, 1% to 47% of European cement industry CO2.
Forests are a carbon sink. Inventories give a total forest sink of 2.4 Pg C a year, 1990 to 2007, and a net 1.1 Pg C after tropical land-use change.

Certification verifies sourcing. FSC forest management certification requires managers to maintain or enhance High Conservation Values, such as rare species, ecosystems and critical ecosystem services.
Mass timber and fire. A 2016 Fire Engineering article explains that char insulates the wood beneath and slows burning. Codes reference a specification for exposed fire-resistance rated wood.
What We Actually Know
Responsibly sourced, thoughtfully used. The column's conclusion: wood works best with certification, accountability and attention to equity. This is education, not medical or design advice.

posts.title: Why Evidence Systems, Not Model Intelligence, Are the Missing Layer
posts.summary: Courts in New York and London have now ruled on filings built from answers that no one checked, and Parliament had to undo hundreds of convictions that rested on a computer's word. The court papers show where each evidence path broke, who was supposed to catch it, and what it took to repair the damage.

slides.alt: A paragraph of court text numbered 39. It quotes typed requests to ChatGPT, including provide case law in support, show me specific holdings in federal cases and show me more cases.

slides.alt: Two numbered paragraphs of court text. The second says the lawyer who signed the filing was not its author, reviewed it for style, and did not review any judicial authorities cited in it.

A dense paragraph of judgment text saying that in the Horizon cases there was no evidence of a shortfall other than the Horizon data, and that if the data was not reliable there was no basis for the prosecution.

Then: the OMCCR form After you recover, OMCCR asks you to submit a form. Email or phone is required, name is optional, a description is required.
A form for the product A separate form takes a product complaint. Name is optional, and you can attach up to 10 files.
Dispensaries must report Rule 11-850-126: a dispensary must tell the Department within 48 hours after learning of an adverse event tied to its product.

posts.title: Governance Design for Psychedelic Authorities: Lessons from Gaming & Utilities Commissions
posts.summary: Psilocybin programs sit inside existing agencies. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico did not create a new commission. The article asks what a purpose-built authority could borrow.

slides.alt: The head of Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 463, Licensing and Control of Gaming, the gaming law the article borrows from, with the start of its section list.

NRS 463.030: the Nevada Gaming Control Board, consisting of three members, is created; NRS 463.040 sets the members' qualifications.
NRS 463.310: the Board makes investigations and, if satisfied a license should be limited, conditioned, suspended or revoked, initiates a hearing before the Commission by filing a complaint.
NRS 463.023(4) and 463.024: not more than three Commission members of the same major political affiliation; the Governor appoints the members; terms are 4 years.

onScreen: Governance Design for Psychedelic Authorities Lessons from gaming and utilities commissions.
Psilocybin programs sit inside existing agencies. Oregon, Colorado and New Mexico did not create a new commission. The article asks what a purpose-built authority could borrow.
Nevada splits the job in two. The Gaming Control Board has three members. The Gaming Commission has five.
One investigates. One decides. The Board investigates and files a complaint. The Commission hears it and can limit, condition, suspend or revoke a license.
The Governor appoints both bodies. Terms are four years. No more than three of the Commission's five members may share a political affiliation.
Conflict rules are in the statute. Board members must give full time and may not be pecuniarily interested in a licensee. Commissioners swear they hold no direct interest in gaming.
Secrecy is written in too. Nevada law makes audit and investigation files confidential. Meeting minutes and license application files are open to the public.
Federal guidance on gaming commissions. NIGC says a commission's law should state that it is an independent body and that its purpose is regulatory, not managerial.

California's utilities commission has an advocate. The Governor appoints five Commissioners, Senate-confirmed, to six-year staggered terms. The Public Advocates Office advocates solely for ratepayers.
FDA seats consumers and patients. Its advisory committees typically include a consumer representative and a patient representative by topic. The article proposes a seat for lived experience.
The article proposes building in phases. Day one: conflict rules and a coordination plan. Year one: a client advocate. Later, at set size thresholds: a two-tier board and commission.

posts.title: Beyond Personal Software: Your AI Is Becoming a Private Institution
posts.summary: A judge in New York ordered OpenAI to keep chats its users had deleted. European law lets people take their data with them, but official guidance leaves out what a system inferred about them. Read in order, the court orders, laws and regulator files show what a person can ask of a system that acts for them, and where those rights end.

slides.alt: A typed court paragraph directing OpenAI to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted, then So Ordered, dated May 13, 2025, with the judge's e-signature.

Typed court text with two numbered paragraphs: one ends the obligation to preserve deleted output logs as of September 26, 2025; the other keeps logs already preserved, except those from the European Economic Area, Switzerland or the United Kingdom.

A paragraph of court text on the order to produce the entire de-identified 20 million log sample, listing three privacy protections: a smaller sample, de-identification and the existing protective order.
Two paragraphs of guidance text saying inferred and derived data, such as a health assessment or a credit score, are created by the controller and fall outside the right to data portability.
Printed legal text headed Automated individual decision-making, including profiling, ending with the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision.
slides.credit: Source: GDPR Art. 22, OJ L 119/46, © EU

slides.alt: A typed order headed Data Collection and Use, asking each company about the personal information it collects, any summaries or inferences it makes from users' chats, how long data is kept and how long it stays after a deletion request.
Italian court text under the heading P.Q.M., annulling decision no. 755 of 2 November 2024 of the data protection authority, dated Rome, 18 March 2026, and signed by the judge.

onScreen: In May 2025, a judge ordered OpenAI to keep chats its users had deleted. A delete button is a promise. A court can override it.
The order ended for new chats on Sept. 26, 2025. Chats already kept stayed kept, except those from the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK.
Then a court ordered 20 million kept chats handed over. Personal details removed first, and a protective order limits who sees them.
EU law lets you take the data you provided. Official guidance says what a system inferred about you does not travel with you.
A recourse template already exists: a human to step in, a chance to be heard and a way to contest an automated decision.
The FTC asked seven chatbot companies in 2025: Do you draw inferences from users' chats? How long do you keep data after a deletion request?
Italy fined OpenAI 15 million euros in 2024. In March 2026, a Rome court annulled the fine: the wrong regulator had issued it.

posts.title: The ceramicist at DDW26
posts.summary: RN Collins is a ceramicist, and Dutch Design Week 2026 had more clay than one person could reach in three days. Eight works shown that week never made it into her footage: porcelain made new, clay that goes back to nature, and vessels used as tools. This piece follows all eight from what their makers published, then ends with the ceramics she did see.

posts.title: All Media, Now Known or Hereafter Devised
posts.summary: Six words in a license can reach screens that do not exist yet. Court fights over deals going back to 1930, for films, songs and books, show what those words carry, and what a short, named license keeps.

slides.alt: Page 484 of Boosey and Hawkes v. Disney (1998): Stravinsky's 1939 grant to Disney, for 6,000 dollars, of the right to record his music in any manner, medium or form.
Page 152 of Bartsch v. MGM (1968), quoting the 1930 grant: all other rights now in existence or which may hereafter come into existence shall be reserved to the owner.
Page 154 of Bartsch v. MGM (1968): the court reads the assignment's words as giving the broadest rights, since exhibit means to show by any method.
Page 483 of Boosey and Hawkes v. Disney (1998): Stravinsky's 1939 licence for The Rite of Spring, and the suit over Fantasia's later release on videocassette and laser disc.
Page 1 of the U.S. Copyright Office's Circular 12, Recordation of Transfers and Other Documents: owners can record transfers and other agreements about their works with the Office.
Page 484 of Boosey and Hawkes v. Disney (1998), quoting the 1939 agreement's type-of-use terms: one motion picture, any length, music that may be adapted or changed, and the title that may be used.
Page 620 of Random House v. Rosetta Books (2001): the court finds the grant to print, publish and sell the work in book form does not include the right to publish it as an ebook.

posts.title: A Public Lab for Patients

onScreen: A public lab for patients Hawaii has one certified cannabis lab. The state asked for a reference lab. Here is what the sources show.
Every dispensary batch needs this lab A dispensary may not dispense unless a Department-certified lab has analyzed a sample. OMCCR lists one lab.
The law lets patients test HRS 329D-8 says the rules must let patients and caregivers get testing directly from certified labs on their island.
A patient may carry a sample A patient or caregiver may take a small sample to a certified lab, with an appointment and a confirmation in hand.
But not between islands The statute's interisland exceptions list dispensaries and labs. A patient carrying a sample between islands is not among them.
Half the patients live off Oahu On August 31, 2026, 14,671 of 29,315 patients lived in the three counties other than Honolulu. The lab's drop-off is on Oahu.
The state asked for a reference lab The Department asked for $2,100,000 in special funds to establish a state reference laboratory for medical cannabis and hemp.
The Legislature funded part of it Its worksheet shows $500,000 for "reference library" against the $2.1 million request. Patients are not mentioned in the request.
UH can run testing programs HRS 304A-1865 lets the University of Hawaii set up medical cannabis testing programs, subject to Department certification.
A UH Hilo page lists a state award It lists "HDOH, Cannabis Analysis," August 2026 to July 2031. The page does not say what the work is.
The argument of this piece: pay for patient tests The law promises patients testing, but one Oahu lab does it. A subsidy would pay the lab fee for registered patients.

posts.title: A top printed from a map of the skin
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the designer Laura Civetti showed Adaptive System, a sleeveless top printed in layers from maps of the body. RN Collins was in the same building that week but did not see it. This piece explains how the top was designed and made, and what skin and sweat science says about the idea behind it.

slides.alt: The back of a person in a sleeveless printed top against a gray wall: rows of cream fins run down both sides of the spine over a green lattice. Slide text: A top printed from a map of the skin. Laura Civetti's Adaptive System, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026. RN Collins did not see it in person.

The front of the printed top on a blue backdrop: a curved yellow, teal and cream lattice over the chest, with pale fins along the shoulder and armhole. Slide text: Body curvature, heat and sun exposure were mapped into three layers. Movement, ventilation, protection: one layer for each, as the press kit describes it.

An old black and white drawing of a slice of the outer skin, with five labeled layers from the stratum corneum at the top, through the stratum lucidum and granulosum, down to the stratum germinativum. Slide text: Skin is not the same everywhere. Most of the body has thin skin with four layers. Only the palms and soles have thick skin, with a fifth layer.

Bar chart of sweat in grams per square meter per hour, 3 of 9 regions: forehead 1,710, upper back 1,197, palms 119. Slide text: Sweat has a map too. In male athletes running hard, the upper back sweated about ten times faster than the palms. The authors said the data could help clothing design.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Smith 2011 data

slides.alt: Close view of the printed top at the back of the shoulder, below the back of the head: overlapping cream fins laid over a green grid. Slide text: It is a proof of concept, printed in 18 parts. A size chart starts from an average body. This top starts from maps of simulated body data. That is the shift the maker is after.

posts.title: Federal-State Tensions in Psychedelic Regulation: Where Preemption May Emerge
posts.summary: Federal law leaves room for state law. Section 903: no field preemption. State law yields only on a positive conflict where the two cannot consistently stand together.

onScreen: Federal and State Tensions in Psychedelic Regulation Where preemption may emerge. A law-first look from Cannabis Law Report, Series 2 No. 7 of 20.
Federal law leaves room for state law. Section 903: no field preemption. State law yields only on a positive conflict where the two cannot consistently stand together.
Raich decided federal power over local marijuana. On June 6, 2005 the Supreme Court held Congress may prohibit local cultivation and use of marijuana that complies with California law.
Congress cannot commandeer state officers. New York v. United States (1992) struck a take-title provision. Printz v. United States (1997) struck the Brady Act duty on local officers.
Oregon's statute disclaims any federal exemption. ORS 475A.215(7): the Psilocybin Services Act may not be construed to exempt a person from federal law or obstruct its enforcement.
The Ninth Circuit upheld DEA's registration rule. On February 13, 2025 (No. 22-1568), the court denied a petition over DEA's refusal to exempt a physician from registration.
Banking risk runs through money laundering law. The article ties it to 18 U.S.C. 1956, which carries up to 20 years in prison for laundering proceeds of specified unlawful activity.
The article reads Wyeth as the test for approved products. Decided March 4, 2009, Wyeth v. Levine held FDA approval of a label did not pre-empt a state failure-to-warn claim.
Enforcement discretion has lived in memos. The August 29, 2013 Cole memorandum says it creates no enforceable rights and that state law is no defense to a federal violation.
A 2026 executive order funds state partnerships. Executive Order 14401 (April 18, 2026) directs HHS to allocate at least $50 million from existing funds to partner with state psychedelic programs.

posts.title: Glass and pumps: the hidden infrastructure
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, a TU Delft student team showed two works about systems most people never see: the glass that carries the internet, and the pumps that keep low Dutch land dry. RN Collins did not see them at the festival. This piece is built from the program, the press kit, the team's own pages and the public sources behind both systems.

slides.alt: A long lit cylinder of clear glass-like rods lies across a dim floor while a few people stand at a control stand behind it. It is Illumina. Slide text: The internet runs on glass. Much of Dutch land runs on pumps working around the clock. Two works by TU Delft student team Emergence Delft at VEEM. Not seen in person; this is from the program.

Close view of a fan of clear rods glowing cyan and pink against black. It stands in for optical fiber. Slide text: Illumina followed a message as light: device, router, provider, undersea cable. The team's site says 95% of international data runs through submarine cables. That figure is theirs.

The end of Illumina's cylinder: dozens of clear rods held in a ring, their tips lit blue against a dark background. Slide text: The kit says it shows how glass quietly holds our society together. A sculpture of clear rods stands in for the optical fiber the internet travels through.

Two clear tanks lit blue in a dark room, joined by two angled tubes in an X shape. It is SYNC's closed water loop. Slide text: SYNC used data from real pumping stations, the kit says. The kit says that with a quarter of the country below sea level, continuous pumping keeps the land dry.

Close view of an Archimedean screw inside a clear tube lifting water, which spills into a clear tank, all lit deep blue. Slide text: 'Can we keep pumping forever?' That is the team's own question. In SYNC, Archimedean screws turned in a loop that never stopped. Which infrastructure do you only notice when it fails?

posts.title: What does a new material story forget?
posts.summary: An exhibition at the Gasfabriek in Eindhoven told fifty years of Dutch biological and biobased building. VIBA's own chronology shows ministers, pavilions and a permanent expo in the 1990s, and national monitors show how small the share still is.

A paragraph of the exhibition’s DDW press kit: knowledge and experience gained in the Netherlands over the past 50 years, many well-developed building products made from natural materials now, and the foundation ready for a mature bio-logical building culture.

The exhibition's DDW press kit: this exhibition is inspired by 50 years of the Association for Integral Bio-logical Architecture (VIBA), with examples of research, design and construction by the pioneers of bio-logical building in the 1970s and 1980s.

The Dutch text of the exhibition’s press kit naming the organization in full: Vereniging Integrale Bio-logische Architectuur (VIBA), 50 years, the pioneers of the 1970s and 1980s, and Professor Peter Schmid of TU Eindhoven.

onScreen: “New” in what way?
An idea can have a history before its current object appears.
VIBA dates its founding to December 15, 1976. That date marks an organization. Present-day materials need their own dates.
The DDW exhibition gathers drawings, publications and projects
around fifty years of Dutch biological and biobased building.
That gives the exhibition’s named organization a dated public source.
Is the change in composition, joining or intended use? The comparison depends on the question.
Two dated documents can show what changed and what continued.
An earlier ambition and a current ambition still need their own performance evidence.
What We Actually Know
A story of change can keep its predecessors in view. What is actually new here?

posts.title: Tiers, Targets, and the Guidance Gap
posts.summary: Multi-target pharmacology appears to be something close to the default operating mode of plant-derived bioactive compounds. The article adds that "default" may overstate how uniform the underlying biology actually is.

slides.alt: Page 1 of FDA's Botanical Drug Development Guidance for Industry (December 2016, Revision 1): the title, the nonbinding-recommendations box and the introduction on development plans for botanical drugs.

Young leaves of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis, ready for harvest at the Berlin Botanical Garden. Tea makes EGCG, one of the three plant-derived compounds in the 2019 study the article uses to show that plant compounds act on many targets.

21 CFR 314.126 in the 2025 Code of Federal Regulations: reports of adequate and well-controlled investigations are the primary basis for substantial evidence, and such a study needs a clear statement of objectives and a valid comparison with a control to give a quantitative assessment of drug effect.
Chart: the 2019 reverse docking pipeline identified 151 nonredundant protein targets for acteoside, 143 for quercetin and 128 for EGCG; no cannabinoid was tested.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Zhang et al. data

slides.alt: Chart: 24 squares for the 24 ingredient-target complexes the 2019 reverse docking study predicted; 16 are filled, the cases with binding modes highly similar to known complexes.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Zhang et al. data

slides.alt: Chart: binding free energy after 100 nanoseconds of molecular dynamics for the study's three selected complexes: acteoside and NOS2 minus 264.1, quercetin and PDE5A minus 185.5, EGCG and WARS minus 55.8 kilojoules per mole.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Zhang et al. data

slides.alt: The EMBL Grenoble outstation, a cream-colored laboratory building with the EMBL logo and a sign pointing to reception. The sentence reports crystal structures from researchers at this EMBL site.

Page 1 of Eymery, McCarthy and Hausmann, Linking medicinal cannabis to autotaxin-lysophosphatidic acid signaling (Life Science Alliance, 2023): the title and abstract, which report inhibition in enzyme assays, X-ray crystal structures and cell experiments, the kinds of evidence the tiers sort.

Page 35 of the Supreme Court's slip opinion in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024): "Chevron is overruled. Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, as the APA requires."
slides.credit: Source: Loper Bright, slip op. at 35

slides.alt: Page 43 of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm (1983) in the United States Reports: the agency must examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.

Page 593 of Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (1993) in the United States Reports: a key question is whether a theory or technique can be and has been tested, and another is whether it has been subjected to peer review and publication.

The table of contents of FDA's 2016 Botanical Drug Development Guidance: introduction, background, regulatory approaches and the sections for Phase 1, 2 and 3 studies, from raw materials to clinical pharmacology, with no section on computational methods.

FDA's notice in the Federal Register of September 4, 2026, Advancing Development of Botanical Drug Products; Request for Information: the heading, docket number FDA-2026-N-9550 and the summary opening a public docket for comments.

Close view of a flowering top of Cannabis sativa against a dark background: pale, hair-like pistils and leaves covered in tiny glandular trichomes, the resin glands where the plant makes cannabinoids such as THC. Photograph by Alex Abair, United States, 2016.

Federal Rule of Evidence 702 in the 2024 U.S. Code: an expert may testify if it is more likely than not that the testimony rests on sufficient facts or data, is the product of reliable principles and methods, and reflects a reliable application of them to the case.

Eymery, McCarthy & Hausmann, Life Science Alliance 6:e202201595 (2023)
FDA, Advancing Development of Botanical Drug Products; Request for Information, 91 FR 56887 (Sept. 4, 2026)

onScreen: Tiers, Targets, and the Guidance Gap A Proposed Evidentiary Framework for Computational Pharmacology in FDA Botanical Drug Proceedings

Multi-target pharmacology appears to be something close to the default operating mode of plant-derived bioactive compounds. The article adds that "default" may overstate how uniform the underlying biology actually is.
FDA's approval framework appears to have been designed around the single-target model. One compound, one receptor, one measurable clinical outcome.
A 2019 study identified 151 protein targets for acteoside, 143 for quercetin, and 128 for EGCG. The paper is a reverse docking study of three herbal ingredients. No cannabinoid was among them.
The paper reports that 16 of 24 predicted complexes had highly similar binding modes. Nothing about this pipeline should be read as establishing that any particular predicted target is real.
Molecular dynamics refines a docking prediction. The study ran 100-nanosecond simulations on three selected complexes using GROMACS.

In 2023, EMBL Grenoble researchers reported crystal structures of THC bound to autotaxin. The Protein Data Bank entries are 7P4J and 7P4O. EMBL's announcement says in vivo studies are necessary to confirm that the binding is linked to therapeutic effects of THC administration.

posts.title: A robot that writes and wipes history
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Groningen studio Paul&Albert showed a robot arm that writes on glass with a marker and wipes the words away with a sponge. It was made for a history museum that has not opened yet. Here is the machine, the gas story its programme text points to, and what the public sources say about how that story was told.

slides.alt: A white robot arm inside an orange glass vitrine in a dark blue room covered in handwritten notes. It is the installation the post is about. Slide text: A robot arm wrote history on glass, then wiped it away. Writing History, by Paul&Albert. The DDW program said it wrote Groningen gas headlines.

The robot arm holds a marker against the glass of its case, with handwritten names and dates on the panes. It shows how the text is written. Slide text: The press kit says it works from news reports about Groningen gas. Early headlines told a story of prosperity and progress. Later ones turned to subsidence and earthquakes, the kit says.

Close view of the robot arm behind glass covered in white handwriting, with dates from Groningen. It shows the written layer the robot keeps changing. Slide text: The risks were not unknown, the press kit says. Warnings came early. The main story, pushed in part by the government and NAM, played them down.

The white robot arm turns inside the orange case, seen through glass with large handwritten letters. It shows the arm that writes and wipes. Slide text: It wrote with a marker and wiped with a sponge. The studio says its text comes from a database of Groningen history, with live water level, traffic and weather data added.

The robot's gripper in sharp focus, with blurred handwriting on the glass behind. It closes on the hand that does the writing. Slide text: The press kit asks a question: who writes history? It says history is also shaped by 'which stories receive space.' Its makers describe a programmed robot and a database of facts.

posts.title: Luxury Agents: The Next Status Symbol Is Protected Attention
posts.summary: A New York hotel put a telephone in every room in 1904 and later sold a butler to answer for the guest. Software agents now promise the same kind of help online. Read in order, the court orders, rules and regulator files show what the law already asks of anything that guards a person's attention, and what it asks when that person wants to leave.

slides.alt: Numbered court filing text with a bold heading about a four-page, six-click, fifteen-option cancellation process, and a line saying customers could enroll with one or two clicks.

slides.alt: Numbered lines of a court order headed Simple Cancellation Mechanisms, saying cancelling must not be difficult, costly, confusing or time consuming.
slides.credit: Source: W.D. Wash., Dkt. 535, pp. 6 to 7

slides.alt: Two narrow columns of rule text headed Simple cancellation, Click to Cancel, saying the way to cancel must be at least as easy to use as the way the consumer consented.

slides.alt: A numbered paragraph from a state order saying Honda's cookie tool lets consumers accept all cookies with one click but requires at least two clicks to opt out.
Two lettered regulation paragraphs saying an authorized agent must keep a consumer's information secure and use it only for the consumer's requests.

onScreen: Leaving Amazon Prime took six clicks and fifteen options, the FTC charged. Joining took one or two clicks.
A 2025 court order binds Amazon for ten years: cancelling must not be difficult, costly, confusing or time consuming.
In 2024, the FTC wrote the same idea into a rule for every seller: leaving must be at least as easy as signing up.
In July 2025, an appeals court struck the rule down. It faulted the process the FTC used, not the goal.
EU law bars online platforms from deceptive design. It names leaving that is harder than joining as one practice the Commission may address.
California counted Honda's clicks: one to accept cookies, at least two to opt out. Honda agreed to pay $632,500 and add a Reject All button.
California already has a rule for agents that act for a person: keep the data safe, and use it only for the task.

posts.title: One shared wage, one big body
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, a small show in Eindhoven asked how people act together. One studio pours its income into a single bank account. One artist blew a body up to giant size in ship camouflage. This piece is built from the makers' own pages, the press kits, the festival's photos and the public documents behind each work. RN Collins has no footage of the show.

slides.alt: Two people, seen from behind, stand by a tall magenta sign reading The Collective Response, Design for Shared Action, next to a glass case with a screen. It is the entrance to the show. Slide text: A Rotterdam studio started pooling income into a stable monthly wage, the festival says. The Income Pool, by Extra Practice, at Dutch Design Week.

An oversized soft human figure in a bright dazzle print of yellow, red, white and black stripes, hanging at an angle under purple light. It is My Body is a Battleship. Slide text: Questions Collective made a body larger than life, printed in dazzle camouflage. Ships wore dazzle in World Wars I and II to confuse the enemy about their course and speed. Here it helps a body claim space.

Four boxes naming the works and makers: The Income Pool, Extra Practice; Citizens' Assemblies, Bureau Burgerberaad; It Takes a Village, Yamuna Forzani; My Body is a Battleship, Questions Collective. Slide text: Four ways to act together, in one show at Foundation We Are. Which would you try first: a shared income pool, a citizens' assembly, a soft room or a bigger body?

posts.title: Inhaled Residue
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi tests dispensary cannabis against a list of 56 pesticides, each at one limit. Food runs on a different rulebook. Here is how the two systems work, how other states set their numbers, and where the public sources stop.

slides.alt: Part of page 850-110 of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-850-135. It lists heavy metal limits in Table 3 and then says pesticides listed in Table 4 each have a limit of 1.0 parts per million.

The start of 21 U.S.C. section 346a in the 2024 United States Code. Paragraph (a)(1) says a pesticide chemical residue in or on a food shall be deemed unsafe unless a tolerance is in effect and the residue is within its limits, or an exemption from the tolerance requirement is in effect.

Part of EPA's Regulation of Pesticide Residues on Food web page, printed from the saved copy. It says EPA sets tolerances, which are the maximum amount of a pesticide allowed to remain in or on a food.

Part of 21 U.S.C. section 346a in the 2024 United States Code, the determination of safety. Safe means a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure, including all anticipated dietary exposures and all other exposures for which there is reliable information.

Part of an EPA slide, Cannabis Status Update, from the November 1, 2017 Pesticide Program Dialogue Committee meeting. It says there are no pesticides registered by EPA specifically for use on marijuana and no tolerances established for marijuana or hemp.
Part of 7 U.S.C. section 136j in the 2024 United States Code. Item (G) makes it unlawful to use any registered pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling.

The top of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture Pesticides Branch document, Criteria for Pesticides Used in the Production of Medical Marijuana in the State of Hawaii, January 2017. It says no products are registered for use on marijuana with EPA or the department and lists requirements for a product that may be used. The page is cut short so that no email address appears.

Part of page 1 of EPA's May 19, 2015 letter to the Colorado Department of Agriculture. It lists five similar-use criteria, including use on food and use on tobacco in order to have a pyrolysis study of breakdown products formed when treated plant material is burned.
slides.credit: Source: EPA letter, May 19, 2015, p. 1, PD

slides.alt: Page 850-111 of the dispensary rules, the start of Table 4 in section 11-850-135. It lists pesticides alphabetically from abamectin with their Chemical Abstracts Service registry numbers.

Part of section 11-850-135(h) of the dispensary rules. It says if any limit is exceeded the dispensary shall not dispense the nonconforming batch, and it lists what may be remediated: heavy metals, foreign or extraneous material, microbial contaminants, mycotoxins and water activity.

Part of page 4 of OMCCR's July 2024 newsletter, a sample certificate of analysis. A callout says all pesticides that are tested are listed and points to Hawaii administrative rules 11-850-135. The page is cut short so that no email address appears.

Part of page 1 of OMCCR's December 2024 newsletter, Know Before You Grow Part 4, with the outdoor pest management bullets. One says to avoid spraying flower buds with pesticides, even organic ones, and to wash buds after harvesting if you do spray.

Part of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-8, as printed from the saved web page. Item (3) says the department shall review and take guidance from the testing programs and standards for pesticides under the regulations of the United States Environmental Protection Agency.

Part of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity Pesticides Branch web page, printed from the saved copy. It lists a notice about chlorpyrifos and a link to guidance on pesticide use on medical marijuana, dated January 2017.

How the food system works Federal law deems a pesticide residue on food unsafe unless EPA has set a tolerance or an exemption for it.
A tolerance is a maximum EPA defines a tolerance as the maximum amount of a pesticide allowed to remain in or on a food. It sets different tolerances for different foods.
Safe means aggregate exposure EPA may set a tolerance only if there is a reasonable certainty of no harm from aggregate exposure, including all anticipated dietary exposures.
EPA found none for cannabis In 2017 EPA said no pesticides were registered for marijuana and no tolerances were established for marijuana or hemp.
The label is the law Federal law makes it unlawful to use a registered pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling.
Hawaii's agriculture guidance In 2017 the Department of Agriculture said no products were registered for marijuana. A usable product must be EPA registered or a minimum risk pesticide.

posts.title: When does a find become a feedstock?
posts.summary: Dutch law says every archaeological find from an excavation must be kept. EX SITU, at Dutch Design Week 2026, worked with finds that were deselected. The government inspectorate's own 2025 report shows how that decision gets made, and what is still unsettled.

slides.alt: A cardboard box of large pale bones and stones, deselected archaeological finds from South Holland, photographed in storage. The vertical EX SITU wordmark is printed at the right edge. The page names mammoth bone among the materials and lists this photograph under Shahar Livne's HUBRIS.

Dark, worn leather pieces including part of a shoe, lying in a clear plastic find bag with a paper label inside. They are deselected finds from South Holland that Judith Sanders reworks in TERRA FIRMA at EX SITU. The bag label is the find documentation the slide asks about; it is only partly legible.

Overhead photograph on white of eight dark bowls holding sorted archaeological materials from South Holland. The STRATA page lists eight materials: flint, mammoth bone, ceramics, wood, glass, iron, natural stone and leather; the photograph does not say which bowl holds which. Natasja van der Meer turns such materials into glazes in STRATA, an experiment shown at DDW 2026 before the finished objects planned for 2027.

A cracked cream-colored Roman jug stands on a bare floor with other pots behind it in a storage room of the Provincial Archaeological Depot of South Holland, photographed in 2009. It shows the kind of storage the fact card refers to.

An aisle with yellow floor markings and a pedestrian symbol beside metal racks that hold dark waterlogged wood and standing stones, with numbered shelf labels. It appears to be the archaeological depot storage floor; the DDW page does not caption it.

Stacked dark archaeological oak logs with cut ends, kept in storage. The DDW page lists this photograph under Daan Simons' Footed Remembrance Pot, made from archaeological wood. The logs are stacked rather than boxed.

A hand holds a medieval Pingsdorf pottery sherd with painted stripes over a table at the Provincial Archaeological Depot of South Holland, with labeled find bags beside it. It shows the handling and study step that is separate from borrowing, photographing and transforming a find.

An excerpt of this post's essay: “All archive items must be marked or labelled with a unique identifier.” (EAC Guidelines 1, 2014). It gives a vocabulary for what a before-and-after photograph would need behind it.

A necklace by Judith Bloedjes, Thread of Time, made with fragments of archaeological clay pipes strung on a wire with metal rings, photographed on white. It shows how a find is given another interpretation as jewelry in EX SITU.

Iridescent shards of archaeological glass, a bottle neck, bowl bases and curved fragments, lying on a gray tray and in a clear plastic find bag, with the vertical EX SITU wordmark at the right edge. DDW lists this photograph under Bernard Heesen’s glass project at EX SITU. It shows the kind of deselected find the program says the project uses.

Three red Roman sigillata pottery shards on brown card, one a curved rim fragment and two flat pieces with a molded ridge, with the vertical EX SITU wordmark at the left edge. DDW lists this photograph under Lotte Douwes’s Future Unearthed. It shows single pieces whose individual status the essay says it cannot establish.

Close-up of a necklace by Judith Bloedjes: pieces of archaeological flint set in white metal rings joined by a thin wire, photographed alone on white and cropped to the rings. It is the single new object of the close, shown without its source documentation.

onScreen: State Psilocybin Implementation Statutes A drafter's comparison.
Three statutes, three designs. Oregon's voters enacted ORS 475A. Colorado's legislature rewrote its voters' measure. New Mexico's legislature wrote its own bill.
Oregon: one agency licenses everyone. ORS 475A makes the Oregon Health Authority the regulator and creates manufacturer, service center, facilitator and testing laboratory licenses.
Oregon sets no diagnosis rule. OHA may not require a medical condition, and a service center is not a health care facility under ORS chapter 441.
Oregon's law does not override federal law. ORS 475A.215 says the act may not be construed to exempt anyone from a federal law or obstruct its enforcement.
Colorado split the job in two. SB23-290 puts facilitators under a professional licensing division and businesses under a state licensing authority. A 15-member board advises both.
Colorado bars a revolving door. Regulators who oversee natural medicine licensees may not work for or consult for one for six months after leaving.
Colorado kept amending. HB25-1063 carves FDA-approved psilocybin prescription products out of state Schedule I. SB25-297 directs state health data collection.
New Mexico wrote a medical program. SB 219 limits access to qualifying conditions, has clinicians deliver care, excludes synthetic psilocybin and exempts FDA-approved products.
New Mexico set a deadline and a report. The law requires implementation by December 31, 2027, and an annual assessment from the Department of Health.
Texas backed a trial, not a program. SB 2308, signed June 11, 2025, lets the state match funds for an FDA drug trial of ibogaine run by a public university.

posts.title: Who gets to escape a flood?
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, a young designer showed two survival kits for a Swedish peninsula flooded in a story set in 2081: one to escape in style, one to stay and patch. The peninsula is real, and so is its new wall. RN Collins has no footage of the work. This piece reads it from the press kit, then checks the story against the sea.

posts.title: The Internet Used To Be A Home
posts.summary: Trisha Koevoets framed leaving Big Tech as a house move. EU law gives you two ways to take your data with you. The European Commission's own papers suggest the harder part is finding the door.

slides.alt: A screenshot of the project website: huge white letters Big Tech Verhuis Service over a blue sky, a red starburst reading Claim back your web, and pop-up windows titled Claim back the web and Alert, Verhuis je data, with a blue button reading Niet mijn data (Not my data). Slide text: What would you pack if you moved out of a platform? Trisha Koevoets's project posed as a Big Tech moving service, at Dutch Design Week 2026.

Bar chart titled Which internet do you prefer? The internet of the past got 20 dots, the middle line 3 and the internet of now 3, from dots on the maker's posters in public space in 2026. Slide text: On her street posters, 20 dots went to the old internet. 3 went to today's. A small, self-selected sample. She warned that nostalgia may explain much of it.

The opening words of GDPR Article 20(1), set in type on a pale card, with provided to a controller and without hindrance highlighted, and the Official Journal reference below. Slide text: Since 2018, EU law has let you take the data you gave a service. GDPR Article 20: in a machine-readable format, sent on without hindrance.

A crop of page 10 of the data portability guidelines: a printed paragraph saying the term provided by the data subject should exclude inferred data and derived data, for example algorithmic results. Slide text: What a platform works out about you stays behind. EU guidance leaves inferred and derived data, such as algorithmic results, out of that right.

Digital Markets Act Article 6(9), set in type on a pale card with marked omissions, with free of charge, tools and continuous and real-time access highlighted. Slide text: The EU's Digital Markets Act asks the biggest platforms for more. Free tools, and continuous and real-time access to your data. Article 6(9).

Bar chart of designated core platform services per gatekeeper: Alphabet 8, Meta 5, Apple 4, Amazon 2, Microsoft 2, Booking 1 and ByteDance 1. Slide text: Seven companies run the 23 services the law covers. Alphabet runs eight of them, from Search to YouTube.

A crop of page 10 of the Commission staff working document: a printed paragraph saying thousands of end users are using the data portability solutions to download their data, and around 40 authorised third parties have integrated with the gatekeepers' APIs. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: Thousands of users and about 40 third parties use the tools, the Commission says. What we don't: What share of users that is, or how easy the tools are.

A screenshot of the Commission's DMA web page headed What does Article 6(9) mean?, listing three duties: data portability, free tools to make it easy, and continuous and real-time access. Slide text: Pick one account. What would you pack, and where would you go? The Commission lists each gatekeeper's tools on its DMA website.

posts.title: A university for 2070
posts.summary: An Irish design studio built a model of one river region and asked visitors to imagine enrolling there in 2070. RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, has no footage of it from Dutch Design Week. This piece follows the project back through its reports, its tools and its open questions.

slides.alt: A gray relief model of a hilly landscape seen from above, dotted with small wooden blocks and pale stone-like pieces, on wooden trestles. It is the Shannon bioregion model. Slide text: A university for 2070, built as a model of one Irish river region. The Pluriversity, by Studio Saol, began as a strategy job for an Irish university. From the DDW press kit.

The long relief model on wooden trestles in front of a dark brick wall, with wooden blocks, pale stacked forms and green-and-bronze rings on it. It shows the installation. Slide text: People played prospective learners in the year 2070. Three viewports opened onto 'living systems labs', each with a mission, a learner's story and an object from the future.

Close view of the gray landscape model with small pale wooden blocks standing on it, and a person's forearm and hand at the left edge. It shows the wooden pieces. Slide text: The studio says the model uses materials native to each campus. The English text lists reclaimed brick, copper, native Irish oak and bog oak. The Dutch text lists brick, limestone, clay, ash and bog oak.

A wooden viewport stand on tall legs beside the relief model, in front of a dark brick wall. It is one of the windows into the imagined labs. Slide text: A question the studio asks too: who would a river-basin university answer to? Three years of research, eight scenarios, one that kept returning. Medicine has asked a version of it since a 1995 WHO paper.

posts.title: What does “buy” mean?
posts.summary: A movie bought for $19.99 shows up in a folder called "Purchased." The terms behind the button describe a license that can end. Courts, Congress's advisers and California have each looked at that gap, and the same three questions sit inside every creative deal.

slides.alt: A phone held at an angle showing the iTunes Music Store page for an album: a blue price button sits beside every track (the visible tracks read $15.00) and one beside the album. It opens the story because the price button is the one-tap Buy the sentence describes; the photo shows the buttons, not the terms behind them.

A television wall-mounted in a room showing the Apple TV sign-in screen, with fields for an Apple ID and password and the line asking whether to use different Apple IDs for iTunes and iCloud. It sits under the slide because buying on Apple's services runs through one Apple account, and access follows the service terms tied to it; the photo shows the sign-in, not the terms.
Section 202 of the Copyright Act: ownership of a copyright is distinct from ownership of the material object, and transferring the object does not convey rights in the work.

A first-generation Apple iPad showing the Apple Books (then iBooks) app open to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. It stands for what an Apple purchase delivers, a book you can read inside Apple's app; the photo does not show the Buy button or the terms behind it.

An iTunes gift card printed with the Apple logo, lying on a wooden table. It is a physical way to pay into Apple's store; it is not the store's terms and shows nothing about what a purchase gives you, how you may use it or who owns it.

Page 559 of Effects Associates v. Cohen (1990): Cohen paid almost 56,000 dollars for the footage but received only a nonexclusive license; copyright is a bundle of rights and Effects gave up one stick.

A flat lay of eleven removable storage formats on a pale surface: 8-inch, 5.25-inch and 3.5-inch floppy disks, a cassette and an 8mm tape, two CDs, CompactFlash and SD cards, and a USB drive. Each is a different container for delivering files, which is why naming the deliverable matters; the photo does not show a final, editable or source file.
Page 557 of Effects Associates v. Cohen (1990): a written agreement forces a party to negotiate with the creator to determine precisely what rights are being transferred and at what price.

A 1954 black-and-white photograph of a hand writing with a pen in a notebook on a table, from a Norwegian national archive. It stands for writing the terms down; it is not the written terms themselves.
A green running-figure exit sign mounted above a wooden door in Australia. It stands for an exit route; it is not a deal document and says nothing about any term or contract.

Photo of a hand holding an Amazon Kindle 2 whose screen reads 'Thank you for your purchase' for a travel guide, with a 'Purchased by Accident? Cancel this Order' link. It shows the moment right after Buy, where the transaction starts; it is Amazon's flow, not Apple's, and does not show the licence language.

FDA's letter is public. Signed August 8, 2024, it says the agency could not approve the application in its present form.
The advisory committee voted twice. 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness. 10 to 1 that benefits did not outweigh risks.
The letter named three issues. The reliability of the safety data. Whether the effect lasts beyond 18 weeks. Bias from participants who had used MDMA before.
Resilient resubmitted in August 2026. The company formerly known as Lykos filed again without a new Phase 3 trial.
FDA issued final psychedelic trial guidance. Published July 14, 2026, it finalizes a draft first issued on June 26, 2023.

An executive order added vouchers and a scheduling review. Executive Order 14401, signed April 18, 2026, directs priority vouchers and an Attorney General review of Schedule I products that finish Phase 3.
Compass Pathways reported two positive Phase 3 trials for psilocybin. On November 9, 2026, it said it had completed its FDA application.

posts.title: A castle of concrete sandbags
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the artist Yvonne Mak stacked hundreds of sandbags into a castle on the lake at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven. Every bag was cast in concrete. Here is what a sandbag does in a flood, why concrete has a climate problem, and what the materials in the castle try to change.

slides.alt: A small castle of stacked gray sandbag shapes with a wooden door and red flags, on a floating platform on a lake beside a museum wall. It is the work the post is about. Slide text: A castle of sandbags on a museum lake. Every bag is cast in concrete. Sandbag Castle, by Yvonne Mak, Van Abbemuseum. Concrete guards against rising water, and making it emits a lot of CO2. From the press kit.

Eight boxes: calcined clay, geopolymers, recycled or dredged, CO2 use, lighter aggregates, enabling additives, self-healing, and more. Slide text: The festival's English text counts almost twenty lower-carbon concrete approaches in the bags. Its Dutch text says more than ten. They run from calcined clay and geopolymers to CO2 use and self-healing concrete.

Two boxes. Bone: clot, callus, new bone. Concrete: crack, mineral fill, still a crack. Slide text: Bone mends its breaks. Two products in the castle aim to let concrete seal cracks. Analogy only: a sealed crack is still a crack, filled with a brittle mineral.

onScreen: Congressional Action on Psychedelics: Scheduling and Agency Authority A law-first look from Cannabis Law Report, Series 2 No. 9 of 20.
Congress has funded psychedelic research. Section 723 of the FY2024 NDAA (December 22, 2023) set up a Defense Department process to fund research on PTSD and brain injury.
The law names the conditions and substances. Covered conditions: PTSD and traumatic brain injury. Covered substances: MDMA, psilocybin, ibogaine, 5-MeO-DMT and plant-based alternative therapies.
The money sits in a funding table. The Defense Health Program table lists $10 million, shown as 10,000 in thousands, for a clinical study on treatment with psychedelic substances.

HHS gets the first word on scheduling. Before DEA starts a scheduling proceeding it must request HHS's scientific and medical evaluation. HHS's recommendations are binding on scientific and medical matters.
FDA approval starts a 90-day clock. If HHS recommends schedule II to V for an approved drug, the Attorney General must issue an interim final rule within 90 days.
Psilocybin is a statutory Schedule I substance. 21 U.S.C. 812(c) lists psilocybin and psilocyn in Schedule I. Schedule I means no currently accepted medical use and high abuse potential.
Right to Try does not displace the CSA. On February 13, 2025 the Ninth Circuit said the Right to Try Act does not exempt investigational drugs from CSA oversight.
Tax law follows the schedules. Section 280E denies deductions for a business that traffics in Schedule I or II controlled substances prohibited by federal or state law.

posts.title: A chair for two, with two snake heads
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the artist Melyssa Lim showed Vis à vis, a two-seat chair bent from metal tube into a snake with a head at each end. RN Collins has no footage of it. This piece reads the chair from its program text, the press photos and an earlier interview with its maker, then follows its shape back through two centuries of seats for two, the metalwork it names and the body of the animal it copies.

slides.alt: Close view of a curved metal tube ending in a brass snake head with an open mouth. It is one of the chair's two heads. Slide text: A two-seat chair shaped like a snake with a head at each end. Vis à vis, by Melyssa Lim, began with a 2019 dream of a snake that 'became one with the form,' she writes. DDW press kit.

The metal tube chair on a concrete floor, two seats of translucent sheet set between looping tubes, with small brass snake heads. It shows the whole chair. Slide text: It was built from standard round tube, cut, turned and joined again. The maker calls the result a 'second skin', both classic and complex.

Diagram of four rows: cut curved tubes, rotate the pieces, reassemble as curves, and the techniques used: weld, braze, cast. Slide text: More than five metalworking techniques went into one chair. DDW names two kinds of welding, brazing and brass casting.

posts.title: Matching Patients and Growers
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi lets a registered caregiver grow medical cannabis for a patient who cannot grow their own. The state publishes how many caregivers there are and no list of who they are. Here is the law behind both facts, and what the numbers show.

The first page of Act 46, Session Laws of Hawaii 2025, S.B. No. 1429, where the first section says some patients may not be able to grow because of limitations such as disability or lack of space.
The definitions section of the medical use of cannabis law, Hawaii Revised Statutes 329-121, including the definition of primary caregiver.

The first page of the Department of Health's August 2026 registry data report, with the in-state patient data box showing patients with a valid registration, applications issued, caregiver totals and physician and APRN totals.

The next page of section 11-160-56, with the remaining exceptions for dispensary system licensees and others deemed necessary by the Department, and the line that the Department may publish non-identifying aggregated data or statistics.
