onScreen: No public list of caregivers Hawaii counts its caregivers but does not list them. Why, and what a careful match could look like.
Some patients cannot grow Act 46 says patients with a disability or no space should keep the option of a caregiver growing for them.
What a caregiver is A person 18 or older who agrees to manage a patient's well-being for medical use and registers with the Department of Health.
The state publishes counts August 31, 2026: 2,342 caregivers and 29,315 patients. Honolulu 1,348, Hawaii 605, Maui 320, Kauai 67. No names.
The limits are in the law One caregiver per patient. Up to five patients per caregiver. Up to five patients per grow site.
The registry is confidential Rule 11-160-56 bars disclosure of registry files except to listed parties, and allows non-identifying statistics.
Who can say yes The consent exception names the patient. A caregiver's own permission is not listed, and neither is a public directory.
State law backs privacy Hawaii's constitution recognizes privacy. The public-information law lists medical history, diagnosis and treatment as significant privacy interests.
Providers are listed. Caregivers are not. OMCCR posts a certifier list with a not-endorsed notice. No caregiver list appears on its registry pages.
How people find help now OMCCR's public deck tells new growers to talk to other patients, caregivers and cultivators: cannabis is community.
The patient names the caregiver The 2026 guide has the patient pick who grows and upload the caregiver's ID. It shows no matching step.

posts.title: Linoleum, off the floor
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Studio RENS and Tarkett hung linoleum on the wall to show the side a floor keeps hidden. RN Collins has no footage of the show, so this piece reads it from the festival's and the makers' own pages, then follows the material back through its factories, its chemistry and the earlier times it left the floor.

slides.alt: A person in black holds up a framed linoleum panel with a black center and a wide woven border, in front of a larger framed panel, with green and yellow linoleum rolls below. They show STILLS works. Slide text: A floor you never look at, hung on the wall to be looked at. STILLS, by Studio RENS with Tarkett linoleum. From the Dutch Design Week program and press kit.

Seen from above, a black linoleum sheet with a circle cut out lies on a woven brown backing, with a pale yellow lens-shaped piece set in the hole. It shows backing and cut edges. Slide text: The works showed the side of linoleum that is normally hidden: the backing, the fibers, the cut edges and the colors under the surface.

Two boxes. On the floor: top color shows, backing hidden. On the wall: backing shows, cut edges show. Slide text: Under your feet, versus in view: what the floor hides becomes the picture. It picks up from Lino Undercover, their 2023 research with Tarkett.

onScreen: Who gets credit for a new material?
Designed. Wove. Photographed. Curated. Each verb names a different contribution.
The object and its photograph can have different authors.
Those two lines describe different contributions.
Collection-wide or exhibition-wide credits do not explain every individual sample.
An object’s maker marks do not establish the photograph’s reuse rights.
Whose contribution is named, and whose remains missing?
The maker explains who created the object. The photographer explains who created this view of it.
What We Actually Know
The credits are part of the story.

posts.title: No Standard of Care, No Medical Status, Full Liability: The Facilitator Malpractice Question Oregon's Framework Raises
posts.summary: Oregon's Measure 109 created a new professional category and, in the same set of rules, appears to have disclaimed its clinical character.

onScreen: No Standard of Care, No Medical Status, Full Liability The Facilitator Malpractice Question Oregon's Framework Raises
Oregon's Measure 109 created a new professional category and, in the same set of rules, appears to have disclaimed its clinical character.
A psilocybin service center is not a health care facility subject to ORS chapter 441. Oregon Revised Statutes 475A.305(1)(b).

The same rules set a duty of care. Facilitators have a duty to put clients' interest above their own and to use a standard of care that other reasonable facilitators would use under similar circumstances.
The gap between the disclaimer and the duties may be where a malpractice claim would ultimately need to be litigated.
Facilitators must monitor clients continuously. OAR 333-333-5200(4): keep visual and audio contact during an administration session.
Oregon's required client-form questions do not name SSRIs. The article calls SSRI use perhaps the most significant unaddressed standard-of-care question in the framework.
Three liability categories the rules appear to create Contraindication screening failure. Session management failure. Boundary violation.

By several counts, a third or more of Oregon's licensed service centers have closed. The article asks whether a closure leaves any duty to clients. It says that question does not appear to have been litigated.
Licensed health care providers can also hold a facilitator license. In administration sessions, ORS 475A.338 allows it only if the provider does not provide health care services at the same time.

posts.title: A 1932 play, woven in blue
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Carla Schwering showed woven pieces built on a forgotten play from 1932. Behind them sit three older stories: a writer the stage lost, a blue print made by sunlight, and a loom that read punched cards.

slides.alt: A blue woven hanging held up in a studio shows a long-haired figure in a dress sitting on a large rock; only the holder's hands show, at the top corners. It is one of the woven hangings. Slide text: A man pulls a woman from his pond in a 1932 play. A designer wove it. The Voice from the Water, by Carla Schwering, at Dutch Design Week. From the program and press kit.

Close view of a sheer hand-woven textile in pale blue, cream and green stripes, hanging in soft folds. It shows the weave the work is built from. Slide text: The play is Anna Gmeyner's Automatenbüfett. In the play, Adam pulls Eva out of his pond and brings her to his wife's automated snack bar, where she upsets the order.

Strips of paper typed with German words, from a line about machines and people, woven into a dense cream mesh. It shows text made into textile. Slide text: Text and textile share a Latin root, texere: to weave. She wove cyanotype prints on digital jacquard, making a fragile image durable. The kit's point: weaving ran on coded patterns long before computers did.

posts.title: Risk-Based Auditing for New Drug Regulatory Bodies
posts.summary: Small programs cannot inspect everyone equally. The article asks a regulator to spend limited audit time where harm is most likely.

slides.alt: The cover of the California Department of Finance's June 2025 performance audit of the Department of Cannabis Control, with the seal of the Office of State Audits and Evaluations.

Finding 7 of California's 2025 cannabis control audit: controls over remediation plan reviews, case prioritization and inspections can be enhanced, with cases not always prioritized by policy and higher priority issues delayed.
slides.credit: Source: Calif. DOF, DCC audit, Finding 7

slides.alt: FDA's web page FDA's Risk-Based Approach to Inspections: the criteria it uses to rank facilities, including facility type, compliance history, hazard signals such as recalls, and inherent product risk, with the sterile-site example.

OAR 333-333-6200(4), Violation sanctions, in the Oregon Health Authority's rules effective January 1, 2026: Exhibit 1 lists the proposed sanctions for single or repeat violations within two years for each violation category, as guidelines the Authority may raise or lower.

ORS 475A.385, Authority to inspect books and premises: the Oregon Health Authority may examine a licensee's books after 72 hours' notice, and may at any time examine a licensed premises to determine compliance.

onScreen: Risk-Based Auditing for New Drug Regulatory Bodies A scorecard for small programs.
Small programs cannot inspect everyone equally. The article asks a regulator to spend limited audit time where harm is most likely.
FDA ranks facilities by risk. It weighs facility type, compliance history, recall signals and product risk. A never-inspected sterile site making high-risk products would likely rank higher.
Oregon already ranks violations by risk. OHA's rules sort violations into five categories, four by risk and one for data reporting, and set sanctions by category for single or repeat violations.

Oregon's rules allow unannounced inspections. The statute behind them, ORS 475A.385, lets OHA examine a licensed premises at any time. The rules add notice, except when an unannounced visit is necessary.
A rule is not a schedule. The article says Oregon publishes no risk score or inspection schedule. None appears in the rules or OHA pages opened for this carousel.

posts.title: No Organic Seal for Cannabis
posts.summary: One sentence in Hawaiʻi's dispensary rules hands the word organic to Washington, D.C. Here is what federal law does with it, why hemp gets a path that medical cannabis does not, and what the 2026 rescheduling order leaves in place.

slides.alt: Part of a page of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-850-143. Subsection (g) says a dispensary licensee shall not label as organic any cannabis or manufactured cannabis product unless permitted by the United States Department of Agriculture in accordance with the Organic Foods Production Act.

Part of 7 CFR section 205.2 in the 2025 Code of Federal Regulations. The definition says organic is a labeling term that refers to an agricultural product produced in accordance with the Act and the regulations in this part.

The start of 7 CFR section 205.100, What has to be certified. It says each operation that produces or handles agricultural products intended to be sold, labeled or represented as organic must be certified, except for exempt operations.

Part of 7 U.S.C. section 6502 in the 2024 United States Code. Paragraph (1) defines agricultural product as any agricultural commodity or product, raw or processed, marketed in the United States for human or livestock consumption.

Part of USDA's National Organic Program instruction NOP 2040, effective November 26, 2019. The policy section says only hemp produced under the U.S. Domestic Hemp Production Program or the 2014 Farm Bill may be certified as organic, if produced under the organic regulations.

Part of the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service hemp FAQ, printed from the saved web page. The answer says the legal difference between hemp and marijuana is the amount of THC, and that a hemp license cannot be used to produce medical or recreational marijuana.
slides.credit: Source: USDA AMS, hemp FAQ, Public domain

slides.alt: Part of 21 U.S.C. section 812 in the 2024 United States Code. Schedule I includes item 10, marihuana, and item 17, tetrahydrocannabinols, except for tetrahydrocannabinols in hemp.

Part of page 22719 of the Federal Register of April 28, 2026, in the Drug Enforcement Administration final rule. It says any form of marijuana other than an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license remains a schedule I controlled substance.

Part of slide 52 of the Know Before You Grow deck hosted by the Hawaii Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation, cropped to the USDA organic seal and its caption: Federal Cert, but cannabis is still federally illegal, no cert. Part of a photo of a cup of compost tea is also visible.
slides.credit: Source: Hawaiʻi DOH, OMCCR deck, slide 52

slides.alt: Part of the California Department of Food and Agriculture OCal Cannabis Certification Program page, printed from the saved copy. It says only the National Organic Program can authorize the word organic and that cannabis products are not eligible for the organic designation.

Part of page 2 of OMCCR's October 2024 newsletter, in the Nutrients paragraph. It says to use organic nutrients and pesticides, whenever possible, to minimize toxic chemicals in your medical cannabis.

Part of the Federal Register notice of April 28, 2026, page 22777, in which the Drug Enforcement Administration sets a hearing on the proposed rescheduling of marijuana to begin June 29, 2026 and to conclude not later than July 15, 2026.

Part of the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service hemp FAQ, printed from the saved web page. It answers whether hemp produced under the domestic hemp program may qualify for organic certification: it may, under USDA organic regulations.
slides.credit: Source: USDA AMS, hemp FAQ (organic), PD

slides.alt: Part of 7 U.S.C. section 6503, National organic production program, in the 2024 United States Code. Subsection (a) says the Secretary shall establish an organic certification program for producers and handlers of agricultural products produced using organic methods.

posts.title: NAITURE
posts.summary: Merel Mierop's NAITURE set image predictions of decay beside buried fabric. What would make that comparison fair, and what does EU law say about labeling the AI side?

slides.alt: Two dug-up fabric pieces on white: a loose cotton mesh clogged with soil on the left and gray felt with soil and pale roots grown through it on the right. Slide text: An AI guessed how buried fabric letters would decay. Then the letters were dug up. Merel Mierop's NAITURE, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026.

Two lines of printed text from the NAITURE press kit saying that after one month to one year, the letters are dug up and compared with the AI's predictions. Slide text: The letters spent one month to a year underground. An AI got a photo of each letter and a prompt about material, place and conditions, and its guess was set beside the real thing.

Bar chart of weight lost after four months buried in soil: cotton about 90 percent, Tencel 60 percent, PET polyester none, acrylic none. Slide text: The fabric changes what the soil does. In a 2019 burial test, cotton lost about 90 percent of its weight in four months. Polyester lost none.

Bar chart of days for half of each fabric to break down in warm, moist soil: rayon 22, cotton 40, Tencel 94. Slide text: Even plant fabrics rot at different speeds. Buried in warm, moist soil, rayon lost half its mass in 22 days, cotton in 40 and Tencel in 94.

Bar chart of physics scores out of 3 on chemistry scenes for four image models: the best scored 0.84 and the lowest 0.23. Slide text: Image models were weak at picturing chemical change. In a 2024 test with prompts like a rod rusting for decades, the best model scored 0.84 out of 3.

A crop of the Official Journal page that adds paragraph 4 to Article 111: providers of AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026. Slide text: EU law: image generators must mark their output as AI-made. Tools on the market before August 2, 2026 had until December 2, 2026 to comply.

The three EU label icons on a paper band: a black circle with the letters AI, and two black pills that add a word for fully AI-made and partly AI-modified content. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: Letters spent months in soil and were set beside AI guesses. What we don't: The AI model, the number of letters, the soil, the labels.

onScreen: Digital, AI and Psychedelic Convergence What this means for regulators. A law-first look from Cannabis Law Report, Series 2 No. 1 of 20.
The test case is one session with a drug, a device and software. Federal law sorts products into drugs, devices and biologics. Combinations have their own definition, 21 CFR 3.2(e).
A combination product has several modes of action. 21 CFR 3.2(m): the primary mode is the one expected to make the greatest contribution to the intended therapeutic effects.
A statute picks the lead FDA center. Section 353(g): the center follows the primary mode of action, the single mode expected to contribute most to the intended therapeutic effects.
FDA's 2021 plan for AI software has five parts. The January 2021 plan covers AI and machine learning software as a medical device, from the device center, CDRH.

HIPAA's Privacy Rule dates from December 28, 2000. The final rule covers health plans, clearinghouses and certain health care providers. The article argues AI-derived inferences sit outside that frame.
The FTC has a biometric information policy. Its statement covers technologies that claim to infer traits such as personality, aptitudes or demeanor, and applies Section 5 of the FTC Act.
FDA defines an adaptive trial design in writing. The November 2019 guidance: prospectively planned modifications to one or more aspects of the design based on accumulating data from subjects.
FDA has a draft framework for designing a REMS. On May 7, 2024 FDA announced a draft REMS Logic Model guidance, Docket FDA-2024-D-1032, for applicants designing and assessing a REMS.
DEA's scheduling power sits in section 811. The Attorney General may by rule transfer a substance between schedules, after the chance for a formal hearing.

Since the article: FDA finalized psychedelic trial guidance. On July 14, 2026 FDA announced the final guidance Psychedelic Drugs: Considerations for Clinical Investigations, finalizing the June 26, 2023 draft.

posts.title: c14-04 Two versions of the law (Tech From Here, second run)
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi has two official languages, and its courts run in one of them. In January 2018 a Maui courtroom found out what happens when a person who speaks both chooses the other. The laws, cases and bills behind that morning reach back to 1896.

slides.alt: A black-and-white photograph from about 1870 of Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu, a two-story stone government building with a clock tower and a tall flagpole in an open yard. It was the Kingdom government building that later housed its Legislature and Supreme Court.
slides.credit: Photo: HABS / Hawaii State Archives, PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_EXTERIOR_VIEW_OF_NORTHEAST_(FRONT)_ELEVATION_FROM_EAST_(Photo_ca_1870,_from_original_in_Hawaii_State_Arvhices).__Photocopy_1966_-_Aliiolani_Hale,_463_King_Street,_Honolulu,_HABS_HI,2-HONLU,3-21.tif (HABS HI-2-HONLU-3-21, 1966 photocopy of a c. 1870 print in the Hawaii State Archives; cropped to the print)

slides.alt: Page 6 of the Compiler's Preface to the 1846 Statute Laws, in old printed type. It says the code went to the king's cabinet for discussion, then to the Rev. William Richards for faithful translation into the native language, then to both houses for three readings, debated section by section.

Page 259 of volume 1 of the Hawaiian Reports, headed 1856, Hardy vs. Ruggles, in old printed type. The lines read that where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian, the latter must govern, because it is the language of the legislators of the country.

Page 367 of the 1859 Civil Code, Chapter XLI, General Provisions, in old printed type. Section 1493 says that if a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian versions of any part of the Code, the English version shall be held binding. The page ends with the approval of May 17, 1859, signed Kamehameha.

Four lines of old printed type from the same page of Hardy v. Ruggles. They read that the English and Hawaiian may often be used to help and explain each other where the meaning is obscure, or the contradiction slight, but where the omission in the Hawaiian is clear, it is impossible to reconcile them.

A printed act headed An Act for the Construction of Statutes Where the English and Hawaiian Versions Do Not Agree. Its one section says that whenever a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian version of any of the laws of the Kingdom, which have been, or may hereafter be enacted, the English version shall be held binding. Approved January 10, 1865, signed Kamehameha R.
slides.credit: Source: Laws of 1864 to 1865, p. 68, PD

slides.alt: A 1943 session-law page headed Promulgation of Laws. Act 218 rewrites the rule so that the secretary of the Territory publishes the laws once in the English language in a Honolulu daily newspaper. The Hawaiian-language publication is gone from the text.

Two crops of a 1979 session-law page, Act 97, S.B. No. 45. It rewrites section 1-13: English and Hawaiian are the official languages of Hawaii; where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian version of any state law, the English version shall be held binding; Hawaiian shall not be required for public acts and transactions.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 16, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined new text adds a proviso to section 1-13: if a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian and its English version was translated from it, and the law has not been subsequently amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English, the Hawaiian version shall be held binding.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 109, S.D. 2, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined text adds the same proviso for laws originally drafted in Hawaiian and not later amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English. Its last line reads: This Act shall take effect on July 1, 3000.

A typed bill page, H.B. No. 2433, H.D. 1, S.D. 1, with numbered lines. The sentence making the English version binding is struck through. New underlined text gives priority to the language that aligns with the intent of the legislature as evidenced by legislative history, context and purpose. Seven lines of old printed type from page 480 of volume 8 of the Hawaiian Reports, April 1892, In re Ross. They read that the English version shall be held binding, that the two versions constitute but one act, that there is no dual legislation, and that as a rule one version is the translation of the other.

The top of page 69 of volume 2 of the Hawaiian Reports, 1858, Levi Haalelea v. Daniel Montgomery, in old printed type. It reads that the deed is a printed formula in two languages, that the English version of this formula is, of course, the original, and the Hawaiian merely a translation.

Voters approved Measure 110. Lawmakers changed it twice. Senate Bill 755-C took effect July 19, 2021. House Bill 4002 re-criminalized possession on September 1, 2024.
Proposition 122 was an initiated statute. The initiative text adds article 170 to title 12 of the Colorado Revised Statutes. It is a statute, not a constitutional amendment.
The initiative text names one department. In the text on file, the department is the Department of Regulatory Agencies. The article places a two-agency split in that text.
Colorado's initiative bars local bans. Localities may regulate time, place and manner. They may not ban or completely prohibit licensed healing centers (section 12-170-107).
Oregon's measure let localities opt out. Section 128 lets a city or county adopt an ordinance to prohibit or allow centers, sent to voters at the next statewide general election.
Oregon's residency rule had an end date. The enrolled text requires two years of Oregon residency for owners. ORS 475A now requires the proof only until January 1, 2025.
Both states wrote federal law into the text. Colorado's section 12-170-111(k) says the act may not exempt anyone from federal law. Oregon's ORS 475A.215(7) says the same.
Lawmakers added client data reporting in 2023. Oregon Senate Bill 303 (2023) requires service centers to collect client data from January 1, 2025 and report it quarterly.

posts.title: Bricks on steel wire
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Lynn van der Vleuten set brick cylinders on thin steel wires so that they seemed to float. This piece follows the brick behind them: the river clay, the kiln, the monks, and the wall that now hangs on wire.

slides.alt: Dozens of short orange brick cylinders standing on thin steel wires at different heights, lit warmly against a dark ground. It is the Steentijd installation. Slide text: Brick cylinders, balanced on steel wire, so the wall's building block seems to float. Steentijd, by Lynn van der Vleuten, at Dutch Design Week. From the press kit.

Close view of rough orange brick cylinders on thin wires, tilted at angles above a dark stepped steel platform. It shows the brick's texture up close. Slide text: The press kit opens with Louis Kahn's idea that even a brick wants to be something. Here each cylinder stands alone, at its own height.

Long shadows of the brick cylinders and their wires fall across a concrete floor from two angled steel platforms. It shows how the light builds the piece. Slide text: Brick once carried buildings. The kit calls that role largely lost. Stepped steel platforms raise the work like a low pyramid, and the light throws its shadows across the floor.

Two press photos side by side, cropped: at left, a hand placing a brick cylinder on a wire; at right, the artist seated, her hand at her cheek, with brick pieces at the lower edge. Slide text: Van der Vleuten's site says her work began with surplus bricks. Where do you notice brick?

posts.title: dust vessel for a lasting memory
posts.summary: Xiaotong Li used dust to think about data storage. The EU asks data centers for numbers, and the first reports show how much of the picture is still missing.

slides.alt: A polished metal disc with a round center hole, tilted on its edge on a plain pale gray surface: the press kit's only image, captioned memory platter. Slide text: The cloud is a building. Xiaotong Li's project looked at its dust. dust vessel for a lasting memory, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026.

A crop of a printed page headed Project Information (EN) with two short sections, Material Conditions and Dust within a Dust-Free Zone. Slide text: It set dust against the dust-free rooms where technology is made. The festival text called data storage a physical system, not something purely digital.

The slim steel arm of a hard drive reaches in from the left; its tiny head sits at the edge of a stack of mirror-polished platters, close up. Slide text: A drive's head flies less than 5 nanometers above the disk. A micron-wide dust grain is over 200 times that gap, a 2020 Berkeley paper shows.

A crop of a printed page listing five ways to destroy storage media: disintegrate, incinerate, melt, pulverize and shred, each with a short definition. Slide text: One US way to destroy a drive is to grind it to dust. A 2025 federal guide lists pulverizing among the methods, and warns it is not enough for sensitive data.

A crop of a printed legal page with the heading Article 12 on data centers above three numbered paragraphs. Slide text: Since 2024, big EU data centers must report their energy use. The rule covers sites with at least 500 kilowatts of IT power, every year.

Bar chart of the Dutch data center file: 104 entries, of which 47 give total energy, 50 give total water and 62 answer the waste heat question. Slide text: The Dutch public file listed 104 data centers. Most energy cells were blank. Only 47 gave total energy use, 50 water, and 62 answered on waste heat.

Bar chart of the first EU reporting round: 36 percent of expected data centers reported across the EU and 44 percent in the Netherlands. Slide text: The first EU round caught about a third of data centers. 770 reported, about 36 percent of those expected. In the Netherlands, 85 of about 192.

A crop of a presentation slide with a blue heading about the owner and operator of a data center and two bullet points of gray text. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: EU data centers report as buildings. What we don't: Which building holds your files, or what the vessel was.

A sample label with an EU flag, placeholder fields, a QR code, a pie chart and two colored A to G scales for power and water. Slide text: Do you know which building your photos live in? A planned EU label would grade each building A to G. It would not name the customers inside.

posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Studio Dwarshuis showed tables, bowls and candle holders made of pruned branches cast in a matte resin. A bowl of round branch slices and short strips set in dark resin holds a potted pink-flowering plant on a branch-patterned table. It is a Raw Willow bowl. posts.title: Hawaiʻi's 2027 session and the cannabis bills
posts.summary: Four sessions in a row, a bill to legalize cannabis for adults reached the Hawaiʻi Legislature, and four times it stopped. The House Journal, the committee reports and the bill status files show where each one stopped, who said what, and what the 2027 session starts with.

slides.alt: The Hawaiʻi House chamber seen from the gallery: curved rows of wooden desks on red carpet, members at their seats, the rostrum at right with the United States and Hawaiʻi flags, and a gold sphere light hanging from the ceiling.
slides.credit: Photo: Kerry Gershaneck, U.S. Navy, PD

slides.alt: A printed page of the Hawaiʻi House Journal: the Speaker's answer, Representative Quinlan's remarks for the motion, and the paragraph saying the motion to recommit H.B. No. 1246 carried, with six members voting no.
Printed law text, section 3 of Act 273, with underlined new words making possession of three grams or less of marijuana a violation punishable by a fine of 130 dollars.

The entrance to the Hawaiʻi State Senate chamber: a curved wall of tall dark glass panels between two pale columns, a door marked Senate at each side, and rope barriers on the paved floor in front. No people.
A typed committee report page listing three amendments, including changing the effective date to July 1, 3000, and recommending that the bill be referred to the Committee on Finance.
Numbered lines of typed bill text, section A-52, Personal cultivation of adult-use cannabis: no more than six living plants per person, and no more than ten plants at any private residence.

Typed bill text, section 3: the ballot question asking whether the constitution should be amended to let people 21 and older use and possess personal-use amounts of cannabis, and to require the legislature to pass laws on it.
A chart titled How far each bill got: seven bills from 2023 to 2026, each a bar from Introduced toward Governor. S.B. 3335 of 2024 is longest, reaching House Finance; none reaches the governor.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Legislature data

slides.alt: A bar chart titled The expungement pilot, Hawaiʻi County: 2,268 arrests flagged as possibly eligible, 1,321 expungement orders granted, 87 found not to qualify and 860 still to review when the pilot ended.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from AG data

slides.alt: The Hawaiʻi State Capitol in Honolulu on a sunny day: a flat upper block of offices raised on tall, tapered columns over the curved chamber walls, with a lawn and a low concrete wall in front.

onScreen: Four sessions, four stops. From 2023 to 2026, a bill to legalize cannabis for adults reached the Hawaiʻi Legislature each year. None reached the governor.
Feb. 6, 2025: sent back. The House returned H.B. 1246 to the two committees that had passed it two days earlier. Six members voted no.
Three grams or less: a $130 fine. Act 273 of 2019 made it a violation. More than three grams and under an ounce is still a petty misdemeanor.
The Senate passed it twice. S.B. 669 passed 22 to 3 in 2023. S.B. 3335 passed 19 to 6 in 2024. Neither got a final House vote.
2024: an effective date of July 1, 3000. A House committee set that placeholder date and sent S.B. 3335 to Finance. Finance would not hear it, and the bill died.
H.B. 1246: six plants, ten per home. As amended in 2025, it would have let adults 21 and older grow six plants, with no more than ten at any home.
2026: a ballot question, never heard. S.B. 2420 would have let voters decide on adult use. It needed two-thirds of each chamber to reach the 2026 ballot.
How far each bill got. S.B. 3335 came closest in 2024. No adult-use bill reached the governor.
What passed: 1,321 arrests cleared. Old Hawaiʻi County possession arrests, cleared by the state for free. 860 were left when the pilot ended in 2025.
Jan. 20, 2027: every bill starts over. No 2026 bill carries over. Watch how many committees a bill gets, whether one is Finance, and the decking deadline.

posts.title: Wool, tufted like rock layers
posts.summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Mexican studio Kaustik showed Strata, wool tufted by hand into layers that read like rock. What follows is the studio's own account of the work, how a tufted surface is built, what geologists mean by strata, and what is known about the dyes.

slides.alt: A large round white tufted panel with wavy raised layers hangs on a white wall in an exhibition hall. It is Kaustik Studio's Blanco de Río, from the Strata press kit. Slide text: Hand-tufted in layers that read like rock strata. Strata, by Kaustik Studio, at Dutch Design Week 2026. RN Collins has no footage of it. Shown: their piece Blanco de Río, from the Strata press kit.

Close view of white tufts in wavy ridges and shelves, like layers of sediment. It shows the tufted relief. Slide text: The studio's starting point: rock layers as natural archives of pressure, erosion and time. Color, volume and relief stand in for those layers.

Two boxes. In the ground: layers, erosion, minerals. In Strata: tufted wool, relief, natural dyes. Slide text: From a geology idea to a textile surface: pressure, erosion and sedimentation become color, volume and relief, the kit says.

Close view of white tufts pushed through a backing cloth in loose wavy bands, mid-making. It shows the hand-tufting process. Slide text: The kit describes 'subtle variations that make every fibre and tonal transition unique.' Kaustik Studio is a design studio based in Mexico, founded by Isaías Osorio.

Close view of woven baskets on a white table, with a bowl of dark red seeds, a basket of dried bark and a tuft of red fiber, from the press kit's photo of dye materials. Slide text: The wool is colored with natural pigments and dyes. The kit does not say which. What would you want to know about a dye before you lived with it?

posts.title: What is the sensor actually telling you?
posts.summary: KojiGotchi turns sensor readings into a face. Its open code, its raw data, its guidebook and the parts' own datasheets show what that face can and cannot say.

slides.alt: A hand holds the 3D-printed, egg-shaped KojiGotchi test container. A small digital thermometer in its window shows 30.7 degrees C and 37 percent with a smiley-face icon, and steamed rice sits in the clear chamber below. It is the kind of sensor display the cover asks about, from the team's fourth experiment.

Sensor boards wired to boxes of steamed rice on the shelves of an incubator, from the KojiGotchi team's third experiment, where it tested temperature, humidity, oxygen, moisture and color sensors. It shows where each quantity is measured, at a place and in a unit.

a handheld thermal camera in a bright hall, its screen showing people as bands of color, taken at the KojiGotchi team's user study. It is a real case of someone choosing colors to stand for a reading. It is not the KojiMoji avatar or the device's own mapping.

a hand holds the yellow KojiGotchi device over a table of grain bowls at the team's user study while another arm reaches in. It shows people being guided in handling the device. It does not show an instruction being given or what it said.

A two-pronged soil moisture sensor on a metal surface, its board edges and contacts corroded. The KojiGotchi team saw this after about 72 hours of continuous measurement and replaced it with an oxidation-resistant type.

A small sensor board with a 100 nanofarad capacitor added, held in tweezers on a round black base. The team added the capacitor because the air-quality board gave unreliable readings without it, and swapped the moisture sensor as well.

the yellow KojiGotchi device lying on a wooden board among bowls of grain at the team's user study, its small screen at the top and clear chamber at the bottom. The screen is where the avatar face appears but it is too small to read here.
A hand holds the KojiGotchi container at hour 48 of the proof-of-concept experiment. The clear polystyrene chamber shows the rice and koji directly, which is what the team chose over a color sensor.

The open 3D-printed container of the second KojiGotchi experiment, held against a gray cloth: a small digital thermometer sits inside the black shell beside a paper sachet, its display showing a number and a small face icon, with pink string attached. The team says this sensor gave only hourly readings. It shows the kind of logged readings the essay has not reviewed.

A participant at the KojiGotchi user study holds the whole yellow device against their chest, small screen at the top and clear rice chamber at the bottom, with grain bowls on the table. No face is shown.

onScreen: What is the sensor actually telling you?
Measurement: A quantity, at a location, in a unit.
Interpretation: Someone chooses how to represent that reading. A handheld thermal camera in a bright hall.
Instruction: What should the person do next? A hand holds the yellow KojiGotchi device.
Another number can add data without adding understanding.
A friendly face connects these stages. It should not make their differences disappear. The yellow KojiGotchi device lying on a wooden board.

A rug drawn from folded paper
posts.summary: Rug Aya began as a small paper study at Dutch Design Week 2026. Here is what the maker published about it, and what paper, wool and a tufting gun bring to the story.

slides.alt: A pale rectangular rug seen from above on black, with crisp folded-paper edges and diamond-shaped bands of sheen across it. It is the Aya rug. Slide text: A sheet of paper, folded and opened again, became a 2 by 3 meter rug. Rug Aya, by Irena Egelkraut, at Dutch Design Week. This is from the program and press kit.

The corner of the pale rug laid on dark grass, its edge stepped like folded paper, with bands of shinier fiber. It shows how the fold lines carry into the rug. Slide text: The folds did not disappear when the paper opened. They stayed in the surface, the maker writes, like a memory. Traced as lines, those creases became the first sketch, then were tufted by hand.

Close view across the rug: matte pale wool beside a wide band of shinier, silkier fiber, with a raised seam between them. It shows the wool and Tencel areas. Slide text: New Zealand wool for softness, with areas of Tencel for a silky shine. Different pile heights make the surface change with light and angle.

Black and white photo of a model in black lying face down on the pale rug, head resting on folded arms, eyes closed. It is a press image of the rug in use. Slide text: Made to be touched as much as seen. In 2026, the kit called Reni Rugs, the label behind Aya, 'soon-to-launch.' Would you lie on a rug shaped by a fold?

posts.title: One face, many times
posts.series: Tech From Here: NL, beyond Dutch Design Week
posts.summary: Van Gogh painted himself about 35 times in less than four years. The paint changes in every one, while the bones under it stay where they are.

slides.alt: Van Gogh in a blue smock behind an easel, holding a palette and brushes, red beard, in a gilded frame with a dark band on a cream museum wall. Slide text: Van Gogh painted his own face about 35 times. An anatomist sees the same skull under every one.

A Van Gogh self-portrait of 1887: head turned slightly, red beard, short blue brushstrokes on a pale ground around the head, in a wide gilt frame. Slide text: He wasn't chasing a likeness. The Van Gogh Museum says the self-portraits were practice in portrait painting, not an attempt at realism.

Van Gogh self-portrait from 1887 in the Rijksmuseum: gray felt hat, red beard, blue background in short strokes. Slide text: Find the brow ridge first. The frontal bone thickens above each eye socket. That ridge is where his brows sit.

Van Gogh self-portrait in a yellow straw hat with a red-edged collar, against pale dashes of blue, in a wide gold frame. Slide text: Then the orbit, the bony socket of the eye. Seven skull bones build each one. Here he painted one eye blue and one green, the museum notes.

A dark, realistic oil portrait of Van Gogh in three-quarter view, holding a brush, in an ornate gilt frame. Slide text: A friend painted the same face in 1886. John Peter Russell's portrait. An artist who knew them both called it 'an admirable likeness,' more than any by Van Gogh himself or by Gauguin.

A small, muted Van Gogh self-portrait from 1887 (Van Gogh Museum s0155V1962) in a deep gold frame on a gray wall. Slide text: Cheekbone, jaw, brow: the bones don't change. The light, the brush and the mood do. Next time you see a self-portrait, look for the skull first.

posts.title: Klokgebouw, 2015 to 2025: a former Philips factory in the Dutch Design Week archive
posts.summary: A former Philips factory on Strijp-S, followed through the national monument register, a 2022 building survey, period newspapers, the redevelopment of Strijp-S, Dutch Design Week's own old websites and its photo archive.

slides.alt: The Klokgebouw entrance during Dutch Design Week 2019: a gray banner reading Klokgebouw hangs above the doors, and a few visitors walk in, one pulling a suitcase. It shows the venue the carousel is about.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Inside a Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2021: visitors walk between tall white banners beneath steel roof trusses and stage lights. It shows the factory interior the 1928 and 1929 dates belong to. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A wide view from above of an exhibition hall full of visitors in the Klokgebouw during Dutch Design Week 2015, with display cases, white partition walls and an orange robot arm at the right edge. Photographed by Sjoerd Eickmans.
slides.credit: Photo: Sjoerd Eickmans / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A high view of the crowded Klokgebouw main hall during Dutch Design Week 2016: visitors at long exhibit tables under tall dark banners, with the words Mind the Step partly visible on the signage. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A zigzag white exhibition wall with small screens and blue-toned objects on low plinths in a Klokgebouw hall, with a few visitors walking past and steel roof trusses above, during Dutch Design Week 2017. Photographed by Ruud Balk.
slides.credit: Photo: Ruud Balk / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A high view into a Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2018: hanging white fabric panels, benches, a yellow road bicycle at the right and visitors gathered near a screen. The photo is titled Hal3 in the archive. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A figure in a white dress with a wide hat on a plinth in front of a wall printed with yellow DRIVER tape lettering, with visitors around it, inside the Klokgebouw during Dutch Design Week 2019. The photo is titled Driving Dutch Design. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Tall white banners reading Willem de Kooning Academy, Design Academy Eindhoven, Minerva Art Academy and ArtEZ University of the Arts hang in a dark Klokgebouw hall while visitors walk through, during Dutch Design Week 2021. The photo is titled Class of 21. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Tall white banners and a large screen showing a woman’s portrait in Hall 1 of the Klokgebouw during Dutch Design Week 2022; the banners read Get set for global wellbeing, and two visitors stand in front. Photographed by Cleo Goossens.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: A ticket desk with a queue of visitors under tall banners printed with the Dutch Design Week logo and the words e-tickets only, inside a Klokgebouw hall on October 20, 2024. Photographed by Max Kneefel.
slides.credit: Photo: Max Kneefel / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Visitors stand and walk through a bright Klokgebouw hall with white walls, hanging textiles and colorful displays, during Dutch Design Week 2025. Photographed by Boudewijn Bollmann.
slides.credit: Photo: Boudewijn Bollmann / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: a wide view of a Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2015, with large silver air ducts and lighting trusses under the dark ceiling, white concrete columns, exhibition banners and stands, and visitors walking between them, most of them blurred or seen from behind. Photographed by Sjoerd Eickmans. It illustrates the venue and is not the subject of the sentence.
slides.credit: Photo: Sjoerd Eickmans / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: a dark Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2021 under steel roof trusses, with tall white banners naming art academies, lit display stands and a few visitors in the distance. From the 2021 album, the largest in the archive. It illustrates the venue and does not show the archive counts.
slides.credit: Photo: Cleo Goossens / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: two visitors seen from behind stand in front of a tall lime-green wooden frame with leaf patterns in a Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2024, with scaffolding displays behind. Photographed by Max Kneefel. It illustrates the venue and is not the subject of the sentence.
slides.credit: Photo: Max Kneefel / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: a bright Klokgebouw hall in 2022 with tall white banners carrying printed text, white hanging letter shapes overhead and visitors walking through, mostly seen from behind. It illustrates the venue and does not show the limits of the record.
slides.credit: Photo: Max Kneefel / Dutch Design Week

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: a white pavilion titled The Sensory Experience, Smurfit Kappa, in a large Klokgebouw hall during Dutch Design Week 2017, with visitors lying on white cardboard loungers inside, a few people walking past and cardboard stools in front, under steel roof trusses and green light. Photographed by Ruud Balk. It illustrates the venue and is not the subject of the sentence.
slides.credit: Photo: Ruud Balk / Dutch Design Week
